#80. Nvidia’s interim CEO spent 13 years behind the scenes at Microsoft

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words)

Nvidia’s interim CEO spent 13 years behind the scenes at Microsoft

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/nvidias-new-interim-ceo-spent-13-years-at-microsoft-far-from-the-spotlight/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 10:45 amNovember 12, 2026 at 12:22 pm.
  • Colette Kress, named Nvidia’s interim CEO on Thursday after Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation, spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, including four as chief financial officer of the Redmond manufacturer’s Server and Tools business.
  • But to say she was under the radar would be an understatement: a search of Seattle-area news archives turns up a single mention of her name from her Microsoft years, in a 2007 press release listing her as a presenter at a Hotel 1000 seminar on Microsoft’s budgeting software.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 10:45 amNovember 12, 2026 at 12:22 pm.

Colette Kress, named Nvidia’s interim CEO on Thursday after Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation, spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, including four as chief financial officer of the Redmond manufacturer’s Server and Tools business.

But to say she was under the radar would be an understatement: a search of Seattle-area news archives turns up a single mention of her name from her Microsoft years, in a 2007 press release listing her as a presenter at a Hotel 1000 seminar on Microsoft’s budgeting software.

According to recent reports, of course, that’s to be expected. Divisional finance execs aren’t typically public faces at Microsoft or anywhere else. But now she finds herself in the global spotlight, running the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom — at least for the time being.

It has been revealed that nvidia revealed Thursday that Huang resigned as president, CEO and a member of the board, effective immediately, following reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly concluded was a Chinese spy, and a second affair with a direct report.

In a recent development, kress will remain CFO while the board searches for a permanent CEO, considering internal and external candidates. Director Harvey Jones, the former Synopsys CEO, becomes Nvidia’s first board chair. Nvidia shares fell more than 13% in early trading.

It has been revealed that wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note Thursday morning that Kress has built “enormous credibility” inside and outside Nvidia. “We always believed she would eventually be CEO of a major public tech tech giant, but she would have to leave Nvidia after many years there,” he wrote.

Kress joined Microsoft in 1997 after finance roles at Texas Instruments, and held senior positions in corporate planning and finance before becoming chief financial officer of the Server and Tools business, which sold Windows Server, SQL Server and Visual Studio. Her LinkedIn profile lists her as a Microsoft corporate vice president from April 2006 to November 2010.

Server and Tools was also a training ground for Microsoft’s current leadership. Satya Nadella took over the business in 2011, after Kress left, and used it as a springboard to the CEO job three years later. Amy Hood, now Microsoft’s CFO, served as its chief of staff earlier in her career.

From Microsoft, Kress went to Cisco as senior vice president and CFO of its Business Technology and Operations Finance organization. Nvidia hired her as CFO in September 2013, ending a search of more than two years.

Now as Nvidia’s interim CEO, her first major test comes promptly. Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday, Nov. 17, with an earnings call scheduled for 2 p.m. Pacific.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 9:56 amNovember 12, 2026 at 11:05 am.

As the fallout from Jensen Huang’s affair came to a head with his resignation as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, attention has turned in part to his wife, Lori Huang, who has stayed largely in the background during their 41-year marriage.

A New York Times profile, and other media coverage, placed Lori Huang alongside two familiar Seattle names — MacKenzie Scott, ex-wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Melinda French Gates, ex-wife of Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates — as tech billionaires’ spouses who have faced infidelity playing out in public.

It has been revealed that huang acknowledged to employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. The admission followed Times reporting last month that a Chinese businesswoman he had become close to had been identified by U.S. officials as an intelligence asset. China has denied the espionage claims.

On Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, citing five people who worked at the company.

Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Kress spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Industry observers note that huang was worth about $145 billion as of Wednesday’s close, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, nearly all of it from his roughly 3.4% stake in Nvidia. That figure doesn’t reflect Thursday’s drop: Nvidia shares fell more than 13% at the open, pushing the firm’s market value below $4 trillion, CNBC reported. Huang’s fortune peaked at as much as $195 billion in May, according to Bloomberg.

More than half of his 922 million shares belong to a trust where he and Lori Huang are co-trustees, the Times reported, and she solely controls a separate trust holding about $5 billion in Nvidia stock.

Industry observers note that scott and French Gates each came out of their divorces with vast fortunes. Scott, whose split from Bezos was declared in 2019, left with about $38 billion. French Gates, who divorced Gates in 2021, received an estimated $25 billion in a settlement that was never publicly disclosed, The Independent reported.

It has been revealed that both have since steered billions into philanthropy. Scott has donated $26 billion through her organization, Yield Giving. French Gates left the Gates Foundation in 2024 with $12.5 billion for her own work.

George Rush, who co-wrote the Daily News gossip column Rush & Molloy, told the Times that the Huang situation differs from the Bezos and Gates splits in one key way: this relationship has the potential to move markets and carry global consequences.

There has been no report of any plans by the Huangs to separate. Lori Huang did not respond to the Times’ request for comment. In his message to employees, Huang asked for privacy for his family, saying they bear no responsibility for his choices.

The couple’s story has Pacific Northwest roots. Jensen Huang, born in Taiwan, was sent as a child to live with relatives in Tacoma, Wash., and later went to high school in Beaverton, Ore., according to Quartr. Lori Huang also graduated from an Oregon high school.

Industry observers note that the two met in the early 1980s at Oregon State University, where Lori Huang, then Lori Mills, was one of only a handful of women studying engineering, the Times reported. They were paired as lab partners in an electrical engineering fundamentals class, and Huang later told OSU that meeting her was “the most vital, single event of OSU, and of my life.”.

In a recent development, after graduating and marrying, the Huangs moved to Silicon Valley to work as chip designers. Lori Huang worked at Silicon Graphics, where she earned more than her husband did at LSI Logic, he told The New Yorker in 2023. Just before Nvidia’s founding in 1993, she gave up her career to raise their two children, Spencer and Madison, who both now work at Nvidia.

Recent findings suggest that huang has frequently credited her support. Speaking on a podcast in May, he recalled missing the kids’ karate tournaments while building the organization and mentioned she never complained. “That’s the gift that she gave me,” he said.

Lori Huang is president of the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation, which had $9 billion in assets as of 2024, according to the Times. The couple gave $50 million in 2022 to launch a research complex bearing their names at Oregon State. Last month, the foundation gave the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, led by Nobel laureate David Baker, nearly 7 million GPU hours of cloud computing.

#85. Agent fleets drag the messaging layer from afterthought to AI’s coordination core

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words)
AI & Tech

Agent fleets drag the messaging layer from afterthought to AI’s coordination core

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/13/data-center-telemetry-runs-nats-graduates-from-cncf-kubeconna/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Data center telemetry, sandboxed AI workloads and fleets of agents are pushing more machine-to-machine traffic through infrastructure than ever before, exposing the limits of messaging systems built for steadier demand.
  • That shift is drawing attention to the Neural Autonomic Transport System, an open-source messaging system that lets applications and services exchange messages by topic.
  • Sources indicate that “What’s changed in the current context, or landscape, is everything is really ephemeral.

Data center telemetry, sandboxed AI workloads and fleets of agents are pushing more machine-to-machine traffic through infrastructure than ever before, exposing the limits of messaging systems built for steadier demand.

That shift is drawing attention to the Neural Autonomic Transport System, an open-source messaging system that lets applications and services exchange messages by topic. Created in 2010, NATS graduated from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation in November 2026. Its simple design suits AI workloads, according to Andrew Connolly (pictured, left), NATS project maintainer at Synadia Communications Inc., a provider of managed NATS services. When AI tools like Lovable can turn a plain-language prompt into a working web app, the messaging layer has to keep updates flowing as sandboxes come and go.

Sources indicate that “What’s changed in the current context, or landscape, is everything is really ephemeral. If you take the Lovable example, connections coming and going really fast, tons of churn, tons of sandboxes, all these things spinning up, spinning down,” Connolly remarked. “Not every technology can handle that.”.

Recent findings suggest that connolly and Waldemar Quevedo (right), project maintainer of NATS at Synadia, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how NATS handles traffic from short-lived sandboxes, carries data center telemetry and helps AI agents hand off work. (* Disclosure below.).

In a recent development, the demands go well beyond app sandboxes. The project itself has grown from single-cluster deployments into a system that spans data centers, regions and clouds, with one AI app builder recently rebuilding its real-time service on NATS to serve millions of subscriptions, Quevedo noted.

“NATS has evolved to be able to communicate multiple data centers with a super cluster topology with the gateways,” Quevedo said. “It is smart [at routing] the interest graph out to multiple regions, multiple availability zones, multi-cloud.”.

In a recent development, some data center operators use NATS to carry power and cooling telemetry, and Nvidia Corp. built its AI factory event bus on the system as part of its DSX reference architecture, Connolly said. NATS can also route messages across fleets of AI agents, with its JetStream persistence engine and key-value store preserving the state agents need to hand off work.

According to recent reports, “In some sense, agentic systems are just microservices systems, but at a bigger scale,” Connolly stated. “NATS was good for microservices. It’s going to be great for AI agents.”.

#86. ‘Water for life, not data’: Amazon data center proposal draws Eastern Washington protests

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (845 words)

‘Water for life, not data’: Amazon data center proposal draws Eastern Washington protests

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/water-for-life-not-data-amazon-data-center-plan-draws-eastern-washington-protests/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 9:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 10:35 am.
  • Amazon’s intends to build a data center campus near the Columbia River in Eastern Washington drew pushback Monday at a meeting of the Walla Walla County commissioners.
  • Some attendees held handmade and printed signs reading “Amazon lies,” “Major tech is shady.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 9:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 10:35 am.

Amazon’s intends to build a data center campus near the Columbia River in Eastern Washington drew pushback Monday at a meeting of the Walla Walla County commissioners.

Some attendees held handmade and printed signs reading “Amazon lies,” “Major tech is shady. No more data centers” and “Water for life, not data,” according to the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin and its photos of the event.

The majority of the roughly 56 public comments were opposed to or had concerns about data center development, including worries about groundwater supplies, effects on agriculture and wildlife, and a lack of transparency, the Union-Bulletin reported. Supporters pointed to potential benefits from job creation and economic development.

Sources indicate that the meeting highlighted continued resistance to data centers from communities concerned about higher electricity bills, depleted freshwater supplies and other environmental and social repercussions. Over the past year, tech giants including Amazon and Microsoft have pledged to limit those impacts and invest in host communities, but those commitments have not ended the opposition.

Elected officials are increasingly considering legislation and local ordinances to set standards and require greater transparency — an approach some tech leaders say could help address public concerns.

“There is a role for good laws, and if laws emerge that require that everybody do this work in a responsible way, I think that might be part of the solution,” Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, recently told reporters at a company event.

It has been revealed that commissioners in Western Washington’s Skagit County last month adopted significant restrictions on data center development. The facilities are prohibited in unincorporated areas, with some exceptions, and upcoming caps on size and electricity usage will limit the technology to small-scale operations.

The planned Walla Walla County campus is one of two projects that would mark Amazon’s first large-scale data center developments in its home state. The second is in West Richland, part of the Tri-Cities. Amazon already operates smaller data centers in Washington.

Recent findings suggest that the Walla Walla County campus would occupy roughly 134 acres at Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. Its three proposed single-story data center buildings would create about 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

According to a company fact sheet, the campus would use roughly 14 million gallons of water from the public utility to cool its equipment during its first year of operation. Amazon indicates it is working with the port to build a system that would replace the utility-supplied cooling water with nonpotable water drawn from the Columbia River. Wastewater from the campus “will meet industrial reuse standards,” the company stated.

The campus would also use about 6 million gallons of utility-supplied water annually for employee needs.

Amazon’s fact sheet says the firm will cover the electricity costs associated with the data center and that the “expenses aren’t added to the bills of local residents or businesses.”.

It has been revealed that the tech giant is also working with partners to develop a nuclear power plant using small modular nuclear reactors near the Tri-Cities. The proposed plant could begin operating in the 2030s and “will provide net-newly introduced carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon noted.

Despite Amazon’s assurances, many attendees at Monday’s meeting called for a one-year, countywide moratorium on fresh data center development, the Union-Bulletin reported. Commissioner Bertha Clayton mentioned she would consider a pause on new applications to give officials time to draft an ordinance to better regulate the developments.

Clayton said zoning changes adopted now would be unlikely to affect the current phase of Amazon’s project. The other two commissioners have previously said they do not support a moratorium, according to the Union-Bulletin.

Sources indicate that the proposal is undergoing an environmental review under Washington’s State Environmental Policy Act, or SEPA. The review will assess potential environmental impacts and identify measures to address them. It will also determine whether the project requires a more detailed environmental impact statement.

Harbinger raises $240M after expanding into defense

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Sumber: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/05/harbinger-raises-240m-after-expanding-into-defense/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Electric truck startup Harbinger has raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications.
  • Recent findings suggest that the funding comes almost one year to the day after the Los Angeles-based firm declared a $160 million Series C, which included an initial truck order from FedEx.

Electric truck startup Harbinger has raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications.

Recent findings suggest that the funding comes almost one year to the day after the Los Angeles-based firm declared a $160 million Series C, which included an initial truck order from FedEx. Harbinger has now raised more than $650 million to date, according to Bloomberg News, which first reported the round.

Sources indicate that the Series D was co-led by Tiger Global, Capricorn’s “technology impact fund,” and defense-focused firm Ridgeline. FedEx invested again after leading last year’s round, and other repeat investors included Maniv, Greycroft, and Leitmotif, a VC firm backed by Volkswagen. Also investing this time was institutional giant Fidelity Management, which tends to invest in pre-IPO startups. (Harbinger is reportedly weighing going public.).

Industry observers note that while it didn’t lead this round, FedEx’s relationship with Harbinger continues to deepen. The shipping giant’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, Paul Melander, has joined Harbinger’s board of directors. FedEx also recently placed its first large order with Harbinger — a deal for 2,000 trucks valued at more than $300 million.

Founded in 2022 by former employees of now-defunct EV startup Canoo and battery manufacturer QuantumScape, Harbinger started by focusing on making one electric truck chassis. The company has steadily expanded its efforts since. It bought autonomy startup Phantom AI, has begun developing hybrid emergency vehicles, and revealed a driverless hybrid electric platform for the military.

#88. Tech Report: From Palestine to Gibraltar, 10 cases of home games played elsewhere

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16 min read (3166 words)
General

Tech Report: From Palestine to Gibraltar, 10 cases of home games played elsewhere

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read | Sumber: https://qz.com/national-teams-home-games-abroad

💡 Key Takeaways
  • National teams playing home games abroad usually face war, travel limits or failed stadium checks, and these 10 cases from football and cricket show why.
  • According to recent reports, A home game is a line on a fixture list before it is a place on a map.
  • That gap between label and location explains why national teams playing home games abroad have become a recurring feature of international sport.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

National teams playing home games abroad usually face war, travel limits or failed stadium checks, and these 10 cases from football and cricket show why.

According to recent reports, A home game is a line on a fixture list before it is a place on a map. The team named first usually wears its first-choice kit and uses the home dressing room. Nothing in that arrangement requires the match to be played inside the team's own borders. When a country cannot host, the fixture moves abroad and keeps its home label.

That gap between label and location explains why national teams playing home games abroad have become a recurring feature of international sport.

It has been revealed that the decision rarely rests with the team alone. In football, FIFA and continental confederations such as UEFA set rules on where competitive internationals may be staged. Those rules cover security, stadium inspections and licensing. In cricket, a home board needs visiting teams willing to tour. Without them, it must find another venue.

Three causes recur across these cases. The first is war or a security threat serious enough that teams, officials and fans cannot be protected. The second is restricted movement, which can stop players from reaching a venue or crossing borders to train together. The third is infrastructure. A stadium can fail an inspection or lack the license a competition demands, even in a country at peace.

The 10 cases that follow are a selection, not a complete list. Nine come from international football and one from cricket. They cover Europe, the Middle East, North Africa, the Caribbean and Central and South Asia. Some relocations followed a single event, such as the 2009 attack on the Sri Lanka team bus in Lahore. Others grew out of long-running conflict or security restrictions, as in Libya and Iraq. Gibraltar's case had nothing to do with security.

Recent findings suggest that A relocated home match still counts as a home fixture in the competition's records. What changes is the setting. The team plays on a pitch abroad, and the size of its crowd depends on which supporters can travel or live nearby. Several hosts in this selection are neighbors, such as Jordan for Palestine, Tunisia for Libya and Tajikistan for Afghanistan. Others sit farther away, such as Malaysia for Syria and Hungary for Israel.

Taken together, the cases show a fixture list responding to events outside sport: conflict, restricted movement and stadium standards.

Palestine's national football team has repeatedly staged home fixtures outside Palestine because of movement and security restrictions. Jordan has hosted some of those matches at the Amman International Stadium.

Recent findings suggest that the team also has a home venue inside the West Bank. The Faisal Al-Husseini International Stadium in Al-Ram has hosted Palestine home matches as well.

That gives Palestine two kinds of home ground. One sits in Palestinian territory. The other is in Amman, the Jordanian capital, on the far side of an international border.

Sources indicate that A fixture at Al-Ram is a home game in both senses. The town lies in the West Bank. A match there is played on Palestinian soil.

Recent findings suggest that A fixture in Amman is a home game on the schedule only. Palestine is still the named host. The stadium, however, is in another country.

In a recent development, the venue for a Palestine home match is therefore not settled by geography alone. Over the years, the team's home fixtures have been played both in the West Bank and in Jordan.

Movement restrictions bear on who can reach a ground. A home international needs players, coaching staff, match officials and the visiting team to arrive and leave on schedule. Security restrictions add a second test: whether the host can protect everyone inside the stadium. When those conditions cannot be met in the West Bank, Amman provides a stadium across the border.

It has been revealed that ukraine could not play competitive home matches on its own soil after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. In Euro 2024 qualifying, its home game against England was played in Wrocław, Poland. Its home game against Italy was played in Leverkusen, Germany.

Sources indicate that the obstacle was security, not facilities. Ukraine had stadiums built to international standards, including Kyiv's Olimpiyskiy Stadium, which hosted the Euro 2012 final. Air-raid alerts and missile strikes ruled out staging a fixture with visiting players, officials and fans inside the country.

Recent findings suggest that wrocław sits in southwestern Poland, near the German and Czech borders. It was one of the host cities when Poland and Ukraine jointly staged Euro 2012. Its stadium was built for that tournament and already met UEFA standards.

Leverkusen is a city in the western German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. It is home to the Bundesliga club Bayer Leverkusen. The match against Italy was played at the BayArena, the club's ground. Germany was also the host of Euro 2024, the tournament Ukraine was trying to reach.

Ukraine did reach those finals, though not through its qualifying group. It advanced through the playoffs and then played its tournament matches in Germany.

The displacement extended beyond the national team. Ukrainian clubs could not host European ties at home either. Shakhtar Donetsk had already left Donetsk after fighting began in eastern Ukraine in 2014. After the full-scale invasion, it staged Champions League home matches in Warsaw and later in Hamburg.

Industry observers note that domestic football took a different route. The Ukrainian Premier League restarted in August 2022. Matches were played behind closed doors and halted when air-raid sirens sounded. That kept a league running inside the country while the national team relied on borrowed venues abroad.

It has been revealed that the invasion also changed the fixture list for the other side of the conflict. FIFA and UEFA suspended Russia's national teams and clubs from their competitions in February 2022. Russia was left without competitive international fixtures, home or away.

Haiti played its home matches in 2026 World Cup qualifying in Curaçao rather than in Haiti. Gang violence at home ruled out hosting, and the Ergilio Hato Stadium in Willemstad served as the team's stand-in home ground.

The move took the national team away from its usual base. Haiti has traditionally played home internationals at the Stade Sylvio Cator in Port-au-Prince, the capital. Armed gangs have taken control of large parts of Port-au-Prince in recent years. The violence has displaced residents, shut businesses and forced repeated closures of the city's international airport.

Recent findings suggest that the Ergilio Hato Stadium is Curaçao's national stadium and the home ground of Curaçao's own national team. It is named after Ergilio Hato, a goalkeeper from the island.

Curaçao is a small island in the southern Caribbean, off the coast of Venezuela. It is a constituent country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and Willemstad is its capital. Like Haiti, Curaçao belongs to CONCACAF, the confederation that governs football in North America, Central America and the Caribbean. CONCACAF organizes World Cup qualifying for the region.

The arrangement left Haiti without a guaranteed home crowd. Supporters based in Haiti had to leave the country to watch matches billed as Haiti home games.

The 2026 tournament is the first World Cup to feature 48 teams, up from 32. The U.S., Canada and Mexico co-host it, and all three qualify automatically. CONCACAF received six direct places, including the three hosts' automatic spots. The region also received two places in an intercontinental playoff. That expansion opened more routes to the finals for teams such as Haiti.

Sources indicate that haiti's only World Cup finals appearance before the 2026 cycle came in 1974, in West Germany. At that tournament, Emmanuel Sanon scored against Italy, ending goalkeeper Dino Zoff's long run of international minutes without conceding. Sanon also scored against Argentina, giving him both of Haiti's goals at the finals.

Syria played its home leg of the 2018 World Cup Asian qualifying playoff against Australia in Malaysia. The match was staged at the Hang Jebat Stadium in Malacca and finished 1-1.

Syria's civil war, which began in 2011, left the country unable to host international football. Its national team had to find venues abroad for competitive home matches. It also played its other home matches in that final qualifying round outside Syria.

It has been revealed that the playoff was a two-legged tie between the third-placed teams from the two groups in Asia's final qualifying round. Australia finished third in one group. Syria finished third in the other, which also included Iran and South Korea. Away goals would break a tie on aggregate. The winner moved on to an intercontinental playoff for a place at the tournament in Russia.

According to recent reports, syria clinched third place on the final matchday. Omar Al Somah scored a late equalizer in a 2-2 draw away to Iran. The country had never qualified for a World Cup. The playoff left its team two rounds from a first appearance.

It has been revealed that malacca is a historic port city on Malaysia's west coast, southeast of Kuala Lumpur. The Hang Jebat Stadium takes its name from a warrior in Malay legend. Hosting there meant the Syrian squad traveled to Southeast Asia for a fixture listed as its own.

Recent findings suggest that robbie Kruse put Australia ahead in Malacca. Omar Kharbin equalized for Syria with a late penalty. The result left the tie level but gave Australia an away goal heading into the second leg in Sydney.

Sources indicate that australia won that match 2-1 after extra time. Tim Cahill scored both Australian goals. Al Somah gave Syria an early lead and later hit the post with a free kick in extra time. A goal there would have put Syria through on away goals.

Australia went on to beat Honduras in the intercontinental playoff and qualified for the 2018 World Cup. Syria's campaign ended in Sydney.

Libya's national football team has played home matches in neighboring Tunisia. Years of conflict left Libya without venues approved to stage international fixtures.

According to recent reports, those games keep their Libyan label. Libya is still listed as the home side, even with the match played across the border.

Industry observers note that the conflict traces back to the 2011 uprising that ended Muammar Gaddafi's rule. Rival armed groups and competing administrations later fought for control of the country.

In a recent development, venue approval decides where a competitive international can be played. A stadium must be cleared before it can host one. Libya's grounds lacked that clearance during the years of conflict. The national team needed a host abroad.

Tunisia lies along Libya's western border. Its stadiums gave the team a home base in North Africa.

Recent findings suggest that the disruption reached beyond single fixtures. Libya had been chosen to host the 2017 Africa Cup of Nations. The tournament was moved because of the security situation. Gabon staged it instead.

The same conditions that sent individual matches to Tunisia also cost Libya a full continental tournament.

In a recent development, afghanistan's national football team has played home matches in Dushanbe, the capital of Tajikistan. Security conditions inside Afghanistan kept the country from hosting those games.

In a recent development, the obstacle was security, not the condition of a stadium. A pitch that meets the regulations is only part of what a competitive international requires. Visiting players, referees and spectators must also be able to travel to the venue and stay there safely.

Dushanbe sits across the border from Afghanistan. Tajikistan shares a frontier with northern Afghanistan, and much of it follows the Panj River, one of the headwaters of the Amu Darya.

The Afghanistan Football Federation runs the national team. It belongs to FIFA and to the Asian Football Confederation. Those two bodies set the rules on where the team's competitive matches may be staged.

A match in Dushanbe still counts as an Afghanistan home fixture in the competition's records.

Pakistan's national cricket team played its home international series in the United Arab Emirates for years after gunmen attacked the Sri Lanka team bus in Lahore in March 2009. Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Sharjah became its main home venues.

Sources indicate that the attack took place on March 3, 2009. The Sri Lankan squad was traveling to the Gaddafi Stadium for the third day of a Test match against Pakistan. Several Sri Lankan players were wounded. Pakistani police officers escorting the convoy were among those killed.

In a recent development, international sides stopped touring Pakistan after the shooting. Visiting boards declined to send teams, which left Pakistan with no opponents willing to play on its soil.

The fallout reached beyond bilateral tours. The International Cricket Council removed Pakistan as a co-host of the 2011 Cricket World Cup. The tournament went ahead in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

Recent findings suggest that the UAE already had grounds built for international cricket. The International Cricket Council has had its headquarters in Dubai since 2005. The Emirates are also home to large South Asian expatriate communities, including many Pakistanis.

Each of the three venues has its own history. Sharjah Cricket Stadium staged one-day international tournaments from the 1980s and has hosted more one-day internationals than any other ground. Sheikh Zayed Cricket Stadium in Abu Dhabi opened in 2004. The Dubai International Cricket Stadium, in Dubai Sports City, opened in 2009.

Industry observers note that the UAE was not Pakistan's only stand-in host. In 2010, Pakistan staged a two-Test home series against Australia in England. Lord's and Headingley hosted the two Tests.

Industry observers note that domestic cricket moved to the Gulf too. The Pakistan Super League, the country's professional Twenty20 competition, launched in 2016 with its first season played in the UAE.

In a recent development, cricket relocations differ from football ones in a practical way. A cricket tour often runs for several weeks and can include Tests, one-day internationals and Twenty20 internationals. That means the stand-in country hosts an entire visiting tour, not a single match night.

Industry observers note that gibraltar played home qualifiers at the Estádio Algarve in Portugal because its own ground, the Victoria Stadium, did not meet UEFA's requirements for some competitive internationals. The move had nothing to do with war or security. It came down to whether a venue passed the governing body's standards.

Recent findings suggest that gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory on the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula. It joined UEFA as a full member in 2013. That gave its national team a place in European qualifying competitions. Gibraltar later became a FIFA member in 2016, which opened World Cup qualifying as well. Membership did not come with a stadium ready for every fixture those competitions involve.

UEFA sets infrastructure rules for the venues used in its competitions. Its Stadium Infrastructure Regulations grade grounds into categories. The rules cover areas such as seating, floodlighting, media facilities and the playing surface. A ground that falls short of the required level cannot stage the matches those rules apply to. That holds even if it hosts regular domestic football.

The Victoria Stadium is Gibraltar's main football ground. It sits beside Gibraltar International Airport, on a territory where flat land is scarce. It also stages the territory's domestic league matches.

Portugal provided the alternative. The Estádio Algarve stands between the cities of Faro and Loulé in the country's southern Algarve region. It was built as a host venue for Euro 2004, the European Championship that Portugal staged that year. UEFA accepted it for Gibraltar's qualifiers, and the team played its home fixtures there.

The arrangement meant Gibraltar's supporters had to leave the territory to watch a home match. Spain is the only country that shares a land border with Gibraltar. Portugal does not border it at all. The overland route to the Algarve therefore crosses Spain before reaching the Portuguese border.

For Gibraltar, a home qualifier meant a trip through one country to play in another.

In a recent development, israel played its home UEFA Nations League matches in Hungary in autumn 2024. The fixtures moved because UEFA matches could not be played safely in Israel during the conflict.

UEFA organizes the Nations League and sets the conditions for its matches. A national association cannot choose any venue it likes for a competitive fixture. The governing body has to accept that a site is safe for players, officials and spectators. When a country cannot meet that test, the match is staged elsewhere.

Israel belongs to UEFA, the governing body for European football, rather than to Asia's confederation. Its national team therefore enters UEFA competitions, including the Nations League. Hungary is also a UEFA member.

Moving the fixtures to Hungary kept them inside UEFA's own membership. The matches stayed under the same competition rules, at a venue that still had to meet UEFA's standards for the Nations League.

Industry observers note that the Nations League is UEFA's competition for national teams. It is played during international windows outside the major tournaments. Group results decide standings, as well as promotion and relegation between leagues. A home game in the competition is a competitive fixture, not a friendly. It cannot be dropped from the schedule without affecting the group table.

Sources indicate that the matches in Hungary kept their status as Israel's home fixtures in the group. The venue moved, but the fixture's designation did not. Israel's squad traveled to another country to play matches it was formally hosting. Its opponents also traveled to Hungary instead of making the trip to Israel.

Sources indicate that the cause sets Israel's case apart from relocations driven by stadium standards or licensing rules. The condition of Israel's grounds was not the reason for the move. The question was whether UEFA matches could be held safely in the country at all during the conflict. A stadium upgrade could not settle that question. The answer depended on security conditions in the country, not on construction work or an inspection.

Recent findings suggest that iraq played its home football internationals outside the country for years. FIFA had restricted Iraq from hosting competitive internationals because of security conditions.

Those fixtures moved to other countries. Qatar, Jordan and Iran were among the places where Iraq lined up as the home side.

The restriction came from FIFA, football's world governing body, rather than from Iraq's own federation. It applied to competitive internationals, the matches that count toward qualification and tournament standings.

The grounds for the restriction were security conditions inside Iraq. That made the issue one of safety, not a decision Iraqi football officials could reverse on their own.

The hosts differed in their relationship to Iraq. Jordan and Iran share land borders with Iraq. Qatar has no border with Iraq and lies farther down the Persian Gulf.

Recent findings suggest that the restrictions did not end in a single ruling. FIFA lifted them in stages.

Seattle-based Constellation Space is rolling out its flagship software platform, which uses machine learning to streamline operations for fleets of satellites and the ground networks that serve them.

“We build models in-house for things like weather, attenuation, signal jamming, demand … and synthesize all of that to help operators understand what their ground contact proposal looks like in the future, and how to optimize their fleets,” CEO Kamran Majid told GeekWire.

In a recent development, the Constellation Platform is tailor-made for a growing number of satellite constellations in low Earth orbit. Keeping track of thousands of satellites — and the best opportunities for downlinking data from each of those satellites — is becoming an increasingly complicated task.

Constellation Space, which was founded last year, draws upon Majid’s experience as a NASA engineering intern and as a software engineer working on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network.

Recent findings suggest that “At Starlink, I saw firsthand how manual mission-control processes break down as constellations scale,” he stated. “I started Constellation to help smaller teams get ahead of link failures instead of spending their time rebuilding pass plans and recovering from outages.”.

Majid’s fellow co-founders include chief technology officer Raaid Kabir, a veteran of Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture, and Omeed Tehrani and Laith Altarabishi, who were previously software engineers at Capital One. “We’re a team of six people right now,” Majid remarked.

It has been revealed that one year into its existence, Constellation Space has already gained traction. Several months ago, the startup said it raised $7.5 million in a seed round backed by Y Combinator, Nvidia, OpenAI, Samsung Next and other investors.

Industry observers note that majid remarked an early version of the Constellation Platform has attracted more than 10 customers, including Amazon Web Services. It’s also used by more than 20 academic institutions. “Our annual contract value this year is $2.25 million,” he said.

Industry observers note that the platform combines forecasts for factors affecting satellite transmissions — including space situational awareness, weather conditions, signal-to-noise ratios, signal jamming and bandwidth demand — to predict how many gigabytes of data can be transmitted during a given pass. Operators can then use that data to optimize transmission settings and schedules.

According to recent reports, its machine-learning model is pre-trained on data from a global network of sensors. Once it’s deployed, the model adapts to each fleet’s specific hardware and ground stations. Constellation Space says satellite operators can boost downlinked data per pass by as much as 36%.

Majid stated the journey from SpaceX to startup has been “really interesting.”.

According to recent reports, “The mindset is very similar,” he said. “I was previously an engineer. Now I’m finding myself in more of a business role. The mindset is just ‘first-principles thinking’ about everything. Eliminate all the requirements that don’t make sense before you even start to think about solving the problem. Those core tenets have stayed as we’ve progressed as a venture, and I think that’s been really notable to our success so far.”.

Setting up the startup in the Seattle area, where more than half of the world’s satellites are built, has also been interesting.

Industry observers note that “We are a Y Combinator company, so we were in San Francisco for a couple of months, and there was a lot of pressure from the community in SF to have everyone be in San Francisco. We definitely felt that a little bit,” Majid said.

Sources indicate that “But operating in the satellite sector of the space industry, Seattle is becoming more and more of a hub for the space industry in general,” he remarked. “Space companies are either completely moving here, opening up headquarters here, or just branching out here. It’s that, mixed in with Seattle just being known as a tech hub — and also, we all love Seattle.”.

Food delivery startup Wonder is moving closer to becoming a publicly traded firm after confidentially filing for an initial public offering (IPO). The company declared the filing on Thursday, marking a major milestone following years of fundraising, acquisitions, and expansion.

Wonder has yet to reveal how many shares it aims to make available or the expected price range.

Sources indicate that founded in 2018 by entrepreneur Marc Lore, Wonder has evolved from a food delivery concept into a broader food technology business. Its model goes beyond traditional delivery apps, with the company operating food hall-style locations where customers can order meals from multiple restaurant brands through a single platform. The company handles everything from meal preparation to delivery, pickup, and dine-in service.

Lore, who previously founded Jet.com and Diapers.com, has made no secret of his plans to take Wonder public. Those ambitions gained further attention in July, when the firm confirmed it had raised more than $650 million in a funding round that valued it at around $9 billion. Investors include Accel, GV, AllianceBernstein, and ARK Invest.

Meanwhile, Wonder has been busy expanding its footprint and strengthening its business through acquisitions. The tech giant has outlined ambitious growth looks, including a major push into Texas, where it aims to open more than 100 locations by the end of 2027.

Additionally, Wonder has acquired meal-kit tech giant Blue Apron, restaurant delivery platform Grubhub, media company Tastemade, and kitchen robotics company Spyce. The latter acquisition gives Wonder access to automation technology that could help streamline food preparation and improve how food is served.

Wonder is also branching out with Wonder Create, its platform focused on letting food entrepreneurs and social media influencers develop upcoming food concepts, restaurant brands, and menu items. The platform leverages AI to design and launch restaurant brands in less than a minute.

Another notable move is its $425 million partnership with DoorDash to expand its campus dining business, which operates at 450 colleges and universities and other locations.

Sources indicate that despite its growth, a move into the public markets will bring new challenges. Wonder is operating in an increasingly competitive food delivery landscape, going up against established names such as DoorDash and Uber Eats.

#92. How MLB's qualifying offer works, from salary formula to pick compensation

How MLB's qualifying offer works, from salary formula to pick compensation

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read | Sumber: https://qz.com/mlb-qualifying-offer-explained

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The MLB qualifying offer ties a one-year salary to draft pick compensation, and these 10 explainers cover who gets it, what it pays and what happens when players decline.
  • Industry observers note that A club about to lose a free agent can turn his departure into draft pick compensation.
  • A club collects compensation only if the player declines and signs with another team.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The MLB qualifying offer ties a one-year salary to draft pick compensation, and these 10 explainers cover who gets it, what it pays and what happens when players decline.

Industry observers note that A club about to lose a free agent can turn his departure into draft pick compensation. The price of that option is the risk that he accepts a one-year salary instead. For the 2023-24 offseason, that salary was $20.325 million. The mechanism behind the trade-off is the MLB qualifying offer, a one-year contract a team can extend to its own impending free agent.

The offer cuts both ways. A club collects compensation only if the player declines and signs with another team. If he accepts, the club owes him the one-year salary. A player who declines gives up a guaranteed salary to test the open market. He also enters that market carrying a cost for any rival club that signs him.

Recent findings suggest that the system dates to the 2012 collective bargaining agreement between the league and its players. It replaced the older Type A and Type B classifications, which relied on player rankings. The salary is not negotiated player by player. It is pegged to the average salary of the 125 highest-paid players in the majors and recalculated every offseason. That formula ties the offer to the top of the market rather than to any one player's performance.

A player generally must spend the full season with the same club to be eligible. A player traded midseason is not eligible. A player can also receive an offer only once in his career. When a player declines and signs elsewhere, the signing club gives up draft picks and, in some cases, international bonus pool space. The exact cost depends on whether the clubs involved receive revenue-sharing money or pay the luxury tax. The size of the contract also matters.

Those costs have shaped individual free agencies. Kyle Lohse, a free agent after 2012, remained unsigned into spring training 2013. The draft pick cost attached to him was a factor. Stephen Drew and Kendrys Morales each turned down the 2013 offer of $14.1 million. Both signed in June 2014, after the draft, when the pick compensation no longer applied. Drew went to the Red Sox, and Morales went to the Twins.

The 10 slides below cover the offer piece by piece, from its definition and salary formula to eligibility, acceptance, departure and the compensation rules.

The MLB qualifying offer is a one-year contract that a team may extend to one of its own players who is about to become a free agent. The player then chooses between two paths: accept the deal and stay, or decline it and test the open market.

The offer is optional. A club decides player by player whether to make it. Nothing requires a team to extend one to any departing free agent.

According to recent reports, the arrangement exists to give clubs something back when a player leaves. If the player turns the offer down and then signs with a different team, his former club receives draft pick compensation.

That conditional link sits at the center of the system. Declining alone does not trigger anything for the original club. Compensation depends on whether the player goes on to sign with another team, not on the rejection itself.

For the player, the offer is a fallback and a decision point at once. Accepting locks in a one-year salary with his current club. Declining keeps every other option open. It also attaches a cost in draft selections to any other team that signs him.

In a recent development, for the team, the calculation runs the other way. Making the offer creates a path to compensation if the player walks. It also carries the possibility that he states yes. In that case, the club is committed to a one-year salary it chose to put on the table.

The qualifying offer arrived with the 2012 collective bargaining agreement. It took the place of an older approach to free agent compensation that sorted players into Type A and Type B classes based on rankings.

According to recent reports, the newer system ties compensation to a team's decision to make an offer, rather than to where a player sat in a ranking. A player becomes subject to compensation because his club offered him the one-year deal and he turned it down.

The qualifying offer salary equals the average salary of MLB's 125 highest-paid players. The league recalculates that average every offseason.

The player receiving the offer has no effect on the amount. A team cannot lower it for a modestly paid player or raise it for a star. Every qualifying offer made in a given offseason carries the same one-year salary.

In a recent development, the figure is also the same for every club. A team with a small payroll and a team with a large one face an identical number. That single salary takes up a bigger share of a smaller budget. The same offer can therefore be a heavier commitment for one club than for another.

That makes the offer a fixed price rather than a negotiated contract. A club considering one is not bargaining over terms. It is deciding whether the player is worth that single figure for one more season.

A fixed price also means a club has to be prepared to pay all of it. A player who accepts receives the full amount, whatever he earned the year before.

Sources indicate that the benchmark draws on the highest salaries in the sport. When the largest contracts rise, the average rises with them. When pay at the top levels off, the figure follows.

According to recent reports, because it is an average across 125 salaries, no single contract sets the figure. One record-setting deal shifts the average by only a fraction of that deal's size. Broad movement across many top contracts is what moves the number.

The yearly recalculation means the price can change from one winter to the next. A club weighing an offer in one offseason may face a different figure than a club weighing a similar player a year earlier.

For a player, the formula provides a known number. He can compare that guaranteed one-year salary with the offers he expects from other clubs before he responds.

Industry observers note that A qualifying offer can go only to a club's own impending free agent. That player generally must have spent the entire season with the same club. A player who changes teams in a midseason trade is not eligible to receive one.

Sources indicate that both conditions have to be met. The first is contract status. The offer is meant for a player whose deal is ending and who is about to reach the open market. A player still under contract for the following season falls outside the system, no matter how long he has been with his club.

According to recent reports, the second condition is tenure. The rule generally ties eligibility to a full season with one organization. The club extending the offer has to be the club the player spent the whole year with.

It has been revealed that A midseason trade breaks that link. A pending free agent who is dealt during the season cannot receive a qualifying offer from his new team. His old team cannot make one either. He is no longer its own free agent when the offseason arrives.

According to recent reports, that limit carries over to trades of pending free agents. A club that acquires one during the season gets his play for the rest of that year. It does not gain the option of making him a qualifying offer once the season ends. The club that trades him away loses that option as well.

According to recent reports, eligibility also decides whether draft pick compensation is possible. Compensation goes only to a club whose offer was declined and whose player then signed with another team. A player who was never eligible for an offer carries no such cost. The club that signs him does not forfeit draft selections under this mechanism.

In a recent development, eligibility does not oblige a team to act. A club may extend the offer to an eligible player. It may also let him leave without one, in which case no draft pick compensation follows.

Sources indicate that A Major League Baseball player can receive a qualifying offer only once in his career. After a club makes him that one-year offer, no team can make him another, whether he accepted it or turned it down.

According to recent reports, the limit follows the player, not the club that made the offer. It does not reset when he changes teams. A club that signs him later cannot extend a fresh offer to a player who has already had one.

Sources indicate that the limit shapes his later free agency. Draft pick compensation for a departing free agent flows only through a declined qualifying offer. A player who can no longer receive one carries no pick cost the next time he hits the open market.

A club that wants to sign him at that point does not give up draft picks or international bonus pool space to do it. His former club, in turn, cannot collect compensation when he leaves.

Sources indicate that the rule applies to players who accept. An accepted offer is a one-year contract. The player can return to free agency a season later. When he does, his club cannot matter a second offer.

According to recent reports, joc Pederson and Martin Perez accepted offers in the 2022 offseason, as did Hyun-Jin Ryu in 2019 and Brandon Belt in 2021. Each of those acceptances used up that player's single offer.

According to recent reports, the same limit covers players who decline. Stephen Drew and Kendrys Morales both turned their offers down. Having received one, neither could be given another later in his career.

Recent findings suggest that the limit also holds as the offer's value climbs. A player who received an offer at an earlier, lower amount cannot be tagged again when the figure is higher.

For a player, the compensation attached to his name is a one-time event. For a club, making the offer is a single chance to tie draft pick compensation to that player's departure.

Sources indicate that the MLB qualifying offer was worth $13.3 million in 2012, the year the system began under that year's collective bargaining agreement. By the 2023-24 offseason, the figure had climbed to $20.325 million.

Recent findings suggest that two more figures mark points along the way. The offer was $14.1 million in 2013. For the 2022-23 offseason, it was $19.65 million.

Sources indicate that those four numbers are snapshots rather than a full year-by-year record. Two sit at the start of the system, in its first two years. The other two come from back-to-back offseasons much later. Read in order, each figure is higher than the one before it.

Industry observers note that the direction follows from how the number is set. The offer is an average of top salaries, so it moves when that group of salaries moves. Bigger contracts at the high end of the market push the next offer up. A quiet offseason for top-end deals would hold the figure down. The number reflects where elite pay stood in a given offseason. It is not a reward tied to any single player.

Recent findings suggest that the same sum applied to every club that made a qualifying offer in a given offseason. A team with a modest payroll faced the same one-year figure as a team with a large one. That fixed figure takes up a bigger share of a smaller payroll than of a larger one.

Recent findings suggest that A higher number changes what is at stake on both sides. It means a larger guaranteed salary for any player who accepts. It also means a larger one-year bill for the club that made the offer.

In a recent development, that raises the bar for extending an offer. A club has to be willing to pay the full figure for one season if the player says yes. A player weighing the offer compares that one-year sum with what he expects to find on the open market. The higher the figure, the more the guaranteed side of that comparison is worth.

Industry observers note that A player who accepts the qualifying offer signs a one-year contract with his current club at that offseason's set salary. He skips the open market, and the club keeps him for one more season instead of collecting draft pick compensation.

Industry observers note that joc Pederson and Martin Perez both took that route in the 2022 offseason. Each accepted $19.65 million, the qualifying offer figure for the 2022-23 offseason. Two players signed at an identical salary in the same winter because the offer carries one price for everyone who receives it that year.

It has been revealed that hyun-Jin Ryu accepted a qualifying offer worth $17.8 million in 2019. Brandon Belt accepted $18.4 million in 2021. Both figures sit below the $19.65 million that Pederson and Perez took. The amount a player accepts depends on the year he receives the offer, not on his own salary history.

It has been revealed that acceptance also changes what happens on the club side. Draft pick compensation exists only when a player declines and then signs with another team. Once a player accepts, that path closes. His club receives no extra draft selection. No rival club forfeits picks or international bonus pool space to sign him.

What the club gets instead is another season of the player's services at a fixed, known price. The deal covers one year only, with no multiyear commitment attached to the offer itself.

It has been revealed that for the player, accepting means trading the uncertainty of free agency for a guaranteed salary. He gives up the chance to test what other clubs would pay him. In return, he avoids a market where any signing team would have to give up draft picks to land him.

According to recent reports, the choice also carries a career-long consequence. A player can receive a qualifying offer only once in his career, and a player who accepts has used that one offer. When his one-year deal ends, his club cannot attach a second qualifying offer to him. He reaches his next free agency without that draft pick cost following him.

Recent findings suggest that A player who turns down the qualifying offer becomes a free agent on the open market. His former club receives draft pick compensation only if he signs with a different team.

The decline alone earns the original club nothing. Compensation depends entirely on where the player lands. If no other club signs him, no picks change hands.

Industry observers note that turning down the offer means walking away from a guaranteed one-year salary. In exchange, the player can negotiate terms with any club in the league.

That single trigger shapes the calculation for the club that made the offer. Extending it places a price on the player's departure. The club collects that price only when a rival team decides to sign him.

The decline also travels with the player. Any team weighing a contract with him has to account for what it would give up to sign him. The size of that cost varies from club to club.

It has been revealed that each side makes its own trade-off. The player exchanges a guaranteed salary for access to the open market. The original club exchanges its hold on the player for the possibility of draft picks. The signing club gives up some of its draft capital to add him.

According to recent reports, when a player turns down a qualifying offer and signs with a fresh team, that new team gives up draft picks. In some cases it also surrenders international bonus pool space. The size of that cost depends on whether the clubs involved receive revenue sharing or pay the luxury tax, and on how large the contract is.

According to recent reports, the forfeiture is one half of an exchange. The club that made the offer receives draft pick compensation, but only if the player signs with a different organization. If he never signs elsewhere, no picks move in either direction.

Recent findings suggest that three variables shape the exchange. The first is whether a club is a revenue-sharing recipient. The second is whether a club is a luxury-tax payer. Both questions apply to each club in the transaction — the team that loses the player and the team that signs him. The third variable is the size of the contract the player signs.

Those factors mean the price of signing a player who declined a qualifying offer is not uniform across MLB. Two clubs pursuing the same free agent can face different forfeitures based on their financial standing. The compensation that flows back to the team that lost him also depends on that club's own status.

None of the three variables is a direct measure of the player's performance. Two describe the finances of the clubs involved. The third reflects the deal he signs.

The possible loss of international bonus pool space means the penalty for some signings reaches beyond the draft. A single free-agent signing can draw down two separate resources at once.

For a front office, the cost of a free agent tied to a declined offer has two parts. One is the contract itself. The other is the picks, and in some cases the bonus pool space, that the club gives up to sign him. The size of that contract can also change the second part.

Kyle Lohse, Stephen Drew and Kendrys Morales are three examples of how draft pick compensation can weigh on a free agent's market. All three stayed unsigned for long stretches while pick compensation was attached to them.

It has been revealed that lohse reached free agency after the 2012 season. He remained unsigned into spring training in 2013. The draft picks a new club would have had to surrender to sign him were a factor in that wait.

According to recent reports, drew and Morales went through a similar wait. Both declined the 2013 qualifying offer of $14.1 million and entered the open market.

Both players signed in June 2014. By then the draft had already taken place. The pick compensation tied to each of them no longer applied. A club could add either player without forfeiting a draft selection.

Industry observers note that drew signed with the Boston Red Sox. Morales signed with the Minnesota Twins.

According to recent reports, in all three cases, the cost sat with the club doing the signing. Any team that wanted Lohse, Drew or Morales before the draft would have given up draft selections to get him. Their former clubs stood to collect compensation only if each player signed somewhere else.

According to recent reports, that cost fell on the buyer, but it still shaped each player's options. A club weighing a contract for one of them had to count the picks it would lose alongside the salary it would pay. For Lohse, that added cost was a factor in a wait that stretched into spring training.

In a recent development, the Drew and Morales signings show the other side of that calculation. Once the draft passed, the compensation attached to them ended, and the extra cost to a signing club went with it.

Recent findings suggest that the cases also show the risk a player takes by saying no. Declining means giving up a guaranteed one-year salary for an uncertain market. Drew and Morales each passed on $14.1 million and then spent months without a contract.

Sources indicate that the 2012 collective bargaining agreement replaced MLB's old Type A and Type B free agent classes with the qualifying offer. Compensation stopped hinging on where a player ranked and started hinging on a one-year salary offer he could accept or decline.

Recent findings suggest that under the earlier system, a player's class came from his place in player rankings. Compensation followed from that classification. The qualifying offer took rankings out of the equation.

It has been revealed that in their place, the 2012 agreement put two decisions. The club makes one, and the player makes the other.

Recent findings suggest that the club decides first whether to extend a one-year contract to its own impending free agent. A club that makes no offer has no claim to compensation if that player leaves. Under the new structure, compensation starts with an action the club takes, not with a label attached to the player.

The player then chooses between that guaranteed one-year salary and a search for a deal on the open market. His answer, not his ranking, determines whether compensation comes into play at all.

Sources indicate that the offer is not tailored to the individual. In a given offseason, every club extending one offers the same amount. A league-wide salary formula sets that figure, not the player's own record. Two players with very different track records face the same number.

In a recent development, that uniform price turns the question of a player's value into a test both sides answer. A club weighing an offer has to decide whether the player is worth that salary for one season. A player weighing it has to decide whether the open market will pay him more than that.

That design puts a price on the club's choice. A team that extends the offer must be ready to pay the full one-year salary if the player accepts. If he declines, that salary commitment falls away.

The framework built in 2012 remained in place through the 2023-24 offseason.

#93. ‘We’re still here’: Technology Access Foundation keeps opening doors for students of color, 30 years later
