‘We’re still here’: Technology Access Foundation keeps opening doors for students of color, 30 years later

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/were-still-here-technology-access-foundation-keeps-opening-doors-for-students-of-color-30-years-later/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:11 amNovember 12, 2026 at 11:17 am.
  • Industry observers note that editor’s note: Microsoft, which underwrites GeekWire’s Impact Series, is a longtime TAF supporter.
  • Back in the fall of 2002, then-Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer wrapped up a luncheon speech at Seattle’s Rainier Club by asking a question that few people in the room expected — least of all the college freshman he directed it to.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:11 amNovember 12, 2026 at 11:17 am.

Industry observers note that editor’s note: Microsoft, which underwrites GeekWire’s Impact Series, is a longtime TAF supporter. The company was not involved in this story.

Back in the fall of 2002, then-Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer wrapped up a luncheon speech at Seattle’s Rainier Club by asking a question that few people in the room expected — least of all the college freshman he directed it to.

“So you want an internship this summer?” he asked Miya McClain, as she remembers it.

She was Miya Sneed then, 18 and homesick at Mills College in Oakland, Calif. She had come home to speak for Technology Access Foundation, the Seattle nonprofit where she had gone from knowing nothing about computers to building software and leading a team of student interns. Earlier in the luncheon program, she had shown the crowd a scheduling system she built for TAF.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft had planned the offer in advance and already had her resume, but she had no idea what was coming. A Seattle Times photographer caught the look of shock on her face, and the photo ran the next day on the front of the newspaper’s business section.

That internship, the first of two, led to a full-time job at Microsoft after college. She spent eight years there before moving into product leadership roles at Nordstrom, Cisco and Smartsheet. Today McClain is senior vice president of product management at SumerSports, a sports analytics firm.

“Most of my jobs came through connections with TAF,” she noted, crediting the organization for repeatedly “opening doors I didn’t even know could be opened.”.

That’s the path Trish Millines Dziko had in mind when she left Microsoft 30 years ago to start TAF with her partner, Jill Hull Dziko: teach kids of color to work with technology, and get them hired by tech companies.

But about eight years in, she saw a problem. TAF’s interns were thriving, she mentioned, but many couldn’t get into college computer science or engineering courses because their high schools had already steered them into lower-level math and science.

To change that, TAF would need to reach students by sixth grade, inside the schools.

So TAF went into public education. The organization, which marked its 30th anniversary Oct. 1, now co-manages a public middle and high school in Federal Way, Wash., and coaches teachers in other public schools.

Industry observers note that “No matter what our kids do, we teach them to use STEM skills. They have to critically think. They have to solve problems. … They have to communicate. They have to lead.”.

Executive director, Technology Access Foundation.

Working with entire schools, rather than kids who signed up for a tech program, changed the goal, too. The focus now is on skills students can use in any field, whether or not it’s tech.

It has been revealed that students learn science, technology, engineering and math through projects that combine subjects and put classroom lessons to use. In 2020, for example, two students at TAF’s Federal Way school turned a gardening robot into a model 3D printer using a cake-frosting syringe, a threaded rod and a motor, as GeekWire reported at the time.

“What we want to make sure is, no matter what our kids do, we teach them to use STEM skills,” Millines Dziko mentioned. “They have to critically think. They have to solve problems. … They have to communicate. They have to lead.”.

It has been revealed that the shift has cost TAF money. The organization has missed out on larger funding opportunities, Millines Dziko remarked, because it isn’t focused solely on tech and isn’t growing as fast as some funders would like. In the early 2010s, as education philanthropy flowed to charter schools, TAF couldn’t raise enough to open the additional schools it had planned.

“But we stuck with what was true, and what works for our kids,” she mentioned, “and we’re still here.”.

Millines Dziko grew up in Latest Jersey, raised by a single mother who cleaned floors for a living. She told the Seattle P-I in 1995 that she believed she’d been placed in a lower-level math class because of her race. She took summer-school classes to work her way into honors.

Recent findings suggest that she studied computer science at Monmouth College on a basketball scholarship and began working at Microsoft in 1988 as the first tester on SQL Server. “She was always a force to be reckoned with,” mentioned Bob Muglia, the longtime Microsoft executive who hired her, speaking with GeekWire at the organization’s 30th anniversary party in October. His foundation now supports TAF.

It has been revealed that she later moved into a diversity role and took over Microsoft’s high school internship program, making it technical and filling it almost entirely with Seattle kids of color. When she pushed the organization to reach students earlier, she said, “the attitude was, it’s not broken, so let’s not fix it.”.

Then her partner, Jill Hull Dziko, a social worker in Seattle Public Schools’ behavior-disorder classrooms, brought seven or eight middle schoolers to campus. They were rowdy on the shuttle ride over and went silent when they walked into a room of high school interns testing a fresh handheld computer.

Industry observers note that on the way back, Millines Dziko recalled, they were saying, “I want to be an engineer. I want to do what they did.”.

She left Microsoft in August 1996 and put $150,000 of her own money into TAF. If she didn’t help others, she told the P-I the next year, her late mother “would want me to have my butt kicked.”.

In a recent development, TAF set up in a Columbia City storefront next to a Taco del Mar. When they first opened the door, she mentioned, they could see the basement through the subfloor, and the staff wired the network themselves. The first students started after-school classes in 1997, training for paid summer internships.

McClain joined the second class as she entered ninth grade, along with her older sister. Millines Dziko taught them to take apart a computer and write their first programs. “She’s encouraging, but she’s also very strict,” McClain remarked. “We all got jobs that summer, so obviously she taught us something.”.

In 2000, TAF started a program for younger students called TechStart. At the anniversary party in October, Sherry Williams, TAF’s executive director of operations, who joined in 1997 as its fourth employee, told the crowd about a young girl who was afraid of math. The girl’s mother brought her every afternoon, and the girl kept working at it.

One day she walked in wearing a T-shirt that stated “I love math.”.

“Although her school wasn’t serving her, in our after-school program, she was being served,” Williams noted. “And she knew she could do anything after that.”.

Sources indicate that TAF opened a public school, TAF Academy, with Federal Way Public Schools in 2008. Mike Miles, one of its first ninth-graders, went reluctantly. The school looked way too small, he told the Federal Way Mirror the following year. “I didn’t want to have six kids in my class, but my parents made me go anyway.”.

He was ahead in math, and the latest school couldn’t offer the class he needed, so he spent his first year in the back of the room teaching himself from a textbook.

Sources indicate that the next year, TAF arranged for him to take math at another public school down the street. Looking back as a parent, he said in a recent interview, he appreciates that the school was willing to “swallow your pride a little” and acknowledge that it couldn’t give him what he needed. He got the math education there, and where he is today, he said, is “better than what I ever could have expected.”.

Miles, now 32, graduated in 2012 with TAF Academy’s first class, earned a business degree at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and leads data teams at a cybersecurity startup in the Washington, D.C., area.

He remembers sitting in a circle in social studies, discussing the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin, an unarmed Black teenager in Florida, and learning to keep disagreements from turning into “a shouting match,” a skill he relies on in his work now.

According to recent reports, federal Way wasn’t the original strategy. TAF spent two years designing a school for Seattle Public Schools, and in 2006 it proposed one for Rainier Beach High School, first as a replacement for the school and then as an academy inside the building.

Industry observers note that many students and teachers saw it as a takeover. Teachers worried the academy would drain resources from the existing school, and families objected that the district had discussed the proposal for a year without telling them. At a packed community meeting that November, there was shouting, and the PTSA president walked out with dozens of students, The Seattle Times reported.

“It was just the dumbest and the most frustrating thing I had ever been through,” Millines Dziko said in a recent interview. “I said we’re done, no more.”.

Federal Way Superintendent Tom Murphy read about it, called her and came up to Seattle to meet. After a couple of hours, she remarked, he told her, “You belong in Federal Way.” TAF is now working with its fifth superintendent there, she said.

The lowest point, she noted, came around 2012, when TAF had to lay off staff for the second time. Education philanthropy was pouring into charter schools, a planned expansion into Renton had stalled for lack of money, she said, and TAF had just moved into a new building.

She recalled seeing reports that only a small share of major philanthropic funding went to nonprofits led by people of color, and she started asking herself a question. “Is me being a leader of this organization gonna hold us back from getting funding? Would it be better if we had someone who was white to lead the organization?”.

In a recent development, she talked it over with Williams and Zithri Saleem, two of her top leaders, and “we almost went down that road,” she stated. But she reconsidered. “That’s not the answer either,” she said. Instead, TAF had to “get out there and show them,” and find other people interested in its work.

Seattle came back around after Denise Juneau became superintendent. In 2020, the school board approved a TAF partnership at Washington Middle School in the Central District. Three years later, facing a budget shortfall, the district cut it, as GeekWire reported at the time. “It’s solely about money,” Millines Dziko told The Seattle Times then.

Asked whether she could see herself working with Seattle Public Schools again, she mentioned, “No.” The district has “way too many problems,” she said, and dealing with them “takes our energy away from places where we could be having impact.”.

In 2024, TAF was among the nonprofits chosen in MacKenzie Scott’s open call, after a process that included peer review. TAF expected $1 million and got $2 million. “It wasn’t the money; it was the belief in our work,” Millines Dziko mentioned.

TAF used $500,000 for operating needs it had been saving for and put the rest in a certificate of deposit, she remarked.

It has been revealed that TAF reported about $4 million in revenue and $5 million in expenses in its Form 990 for the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2025, and ended the year with about $11.4 million in net assets. Millines Dziko remarked the organization’s annual budget is now close to $7 million, and its fundraising team raises about 93% of it, mostly through grants.

It has been revealed that TAF Academy had been recognized for test-score gains. It was named a School of Distinction in 2012 for improvement in middle-school reading and math. In 2016, the district cited three consecutive years of recognition as one reason for merging it with Saghalie Middle School. The combined school, TAF@Saghalie, opened in 2017, and TAF co-manages it with the district.

In a recent development, TAF@Saghalie’s four-year graduation rate for the class of 2025 was above 88.5%, compared with 82.6% statewide, according to state data. On state tests in 2024-25, 17% of the school’s low-income students who took the tests in grades 6–8 and 10 met the English language arts standard and 11% met the math standard, compared with 30% and 15% for low-income students in the same grades across Federal Way Public Schools.

According to recent reports, millines Dziko argues that standardized tests don’t measure what matters. They assume every student had a teacher who covered everything on the exam, she said, and “they demean kids,” charting their academic course as early as third grade.

TAF trains teachers to track each student’s growth and is building its own way to document it. Teachers score students from 1 to 4 against standards, backed by photos of projects and samples of student work. The data lives in the modern version of SQL Server, the Microsoft database Millines Dziko was hired to test in 1988.

The system is in the third year of a pilot. Only selected teachers are participating, and TAF is still working out how much time teachers can spend documenting students’ work while teaching, she said. TAF is bringing in an evaluator from the University of Washington Bothell to review the pilot, she said.

Recent findings suggest that millines Dziko’s goal is for every district in the country to use it, and for standardized tests to “go out the window,” with the money states spend on them going to teacher training instead. “I believe it will,” she said.

Miles liked the project-based learning but mentioned he found gaps in his preparation when he got to college. “I took physics at TAF Academy, took physics in college, and I was not prepared,” he said. What he got in return, he said, was “a different way of thinking.”.

TAF looked like a program for teaching technical skills, he said, but “they taught kids how to be people.” He tries to pass that on to his son, he said, including putting others first and using his gifts to help others.

TransformED, TAF’s teacher-coaching program, places a full-time coach in a partner school for five years. It works with five schools now and looks to add 10 more over five years, at about $200,000 per school per year, Millines Dziko noted. In September, TAF hired a former Atlanta principal, Donya Loyd Kemp, to lead it, as GeekWire reported.

Millines Dziko is wary of the rush to bring AI into classrooms. Students can use it to find sources, she noted, but then they have to investigate those sources themselves. “It should be used as a tool to gather quickly, so I can now use most of my time doing the thinking.”.

Millines Dziko said the region’s tech companies should invest in public schools as a way to attract and keep families here, not just with donated products and the occasional volunteer day. “That’s performative,” she said.

In a recent development, what she wants are lasting relationships, like the ones TAF has with smaller companies that come back to its schools every year to give students real problems to solve. As for the significant tech companies, “I need them to be more about pouring into instead of extracting out of,” she mentioned.

It has been revealed that millines Dziko turns 70 in July. For the past year and a half, she remarked, Williams and Joshua Halsey, TAF’s executive director of education, have taken on more of the leadership, freeing her to spend more time raising money and building relationships.

She doesn’t expect to stop working, she said, predicting that she’ll never retire.

At the 30th anniversary party, she hugged about three-quarters of the room, by her count. Looking around at her former students, many with kids of their own, it hit her.

“This is 30 years, man, and look at y’all,” she said, recalling the moment later. “Y’all are good.”.

According to recent reports, microsoft is working across Washington to help build a future-ready state where innovation creates economic opportunity and resilient communities benefit from the AI economy. From housing and transportation to education, nonprofit support and AI skills, we’re investing in the people and partnerships that help our home state thrive.

#94. NeuralSat raises $3.2M to bring high-speed data connectivity and compute to space

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words)
General

NeuralSat raises $3.2M to bring high-speed data connectivity and compute to space

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/13/neuralsat-raises-3-2m-to-bring-high-speed-data-connectivity-and-compute-to-space/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • German startup NeuralSat GmbH unveiled Thursday that it has raised €2.9 million, about $3.2 million, in pre-seed funding to develop a 72-satellite data-relay processing network aimed at speeding up the flow of data from space.
  • According to recent reports, capnamic and Bayern Kapital co-led the round.
  • In a recent development, founded in early 2026, NeuralSat’s satellite constellation will allow operators to offload computing and communications.

German startup NeuralSat GmbH unveiled Thursday that it has raised €2.9 million, about $3.2 million, in pre-seed funding to develop a 72-satellite data-relay processing network aimed at speeding up the flow of data from space.

According to recent reports, capnamic and Bayern Kapital co-led the round. Other investors participating in the round included ZOHO.VC, Robin Capital, BAB – Die Förderbank für Bremen und Bremerhaven, Mission E and KIEMIS Holding.

In a recent development, founded in early 2026, NeuralSat’s satellite constellation will allow operators to offload computing and communications. According to the company, its network will deliver up to 50 gigabits per second via optical and high-frequency radio links.

The network will support real-time edge processing, hosted workloads for commercial and defense clients and provide for time-critical missions like Earth observation and signals intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that “We believe the next major evolution in space will… come from connecting satellites to shared infrastructure that enables them to communicate, access computing resources, and operate together,” Chief Executive Mohd Bilal stated in a statement. “Just as the internet transformed how computers interact on Earth, we intend to transform how intelligence is connected and delivered in space.”.

The tech giant said the funding will help it accelerate aims to launch its first in-orbit demonstration node, planned for October 2027. After that, NeuralSat plans to begin rolling out commercial operational satellites.

The race to develop and build better connectivity and compute capabilities in space is on. Canadian startup Kepler Communications Inc. launched its first commercial space data relay service in January, allowing resilient data transfer and onboard computing, with a next-gen optical relay network declared in August. Skyloom, acquired by quantum computing firm IonQ Inc. in early 2026, deployed 84 optical terminals and a relay architecture in low Earth orbit.

In a recent development, space is not the optimal place to run processors because heat dissipation becomes a major issue with no air to carry it away. But space technology firms have developed solutions to radiate it from giant sails and other surfaces. Space-based compute may not replace terrestrial data centers, but it can enable edge compute given payload weight restrictions for orbital launch.

Starcloud Inc., formerly known as Lumen Orbit, raised $250 million in August at a $2.3 billion valuation. The company has already tested an Nvidia H100 graphics processing unit in orbit in late 2025, proving that it can scale to multi-satellite AI “data centers.” The company is now collaborating with Nvidia Corp. on upcoming space-grade chips.

In a recent development, currently, data relay and compute processing in space reduce the need for other satellites to send data to Earth to complete workloads. Talking to a nearby satellite for edge compute can shave significant time off data transfers. Sending data down to Earth can take a round trip of four to more than 30 milliseconds; satellite-to-satellite is slightly faster, at three to 30 milliseconds.

According to recent reports, the real boost comes from relaying between satellites rather than routing long distances on the ground to a data center and back, often via optical cable ground networks, which add additional lag. Over long distances across the globe, inter-satellite links are around 30% to 50% faster than sending signals down to Earth for processing.

Companies such as NeuralSat hope to use the advantage of being right there, near the data production, to provide processing capabilities, or swift relay to a satellite closer geographically to terrestrial data center processing to reduce delays.

#96. Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1082 words)
AI & Tech

Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Sumber: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/05/axiom-math-wants-to-keep-ai-slop-out-of-mathematics/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It feels like AI is cracking a new math problem every week.
  • It has been revealed that axiom Math is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground.
  • Industry observers note that on Wednesday, the manufacturer confirmed it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans.

It feels like AI is cracking a new math problem every week. Last month, OpenAI released 719 manuscriptsclaiming solutions to some of the field’s hardest problems. But even the computer checks meant to confirm those results can slip. After years of AI slop, it’s fair to wonder whether math is next.

It has been revealed that axiom Math is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground. The $1.6 billion startup wants to build a verified foundation that AI agents can rely on to write software and, eventually, do science.

Industry observers note that on Wednesday, the manufacturer confirmed it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans. Mathematicians often hold Stacks in rare regard — Columbia mathematician Peter Woit has claimed there’s “nothing else really comparable,” comparing the project to “the famous Bourbaki books,” a series that rebuilt math from its foundations in the 20th century.

Woit’s Columbia colleague Johan de Jong started the Stacks Project in 2005 as an open source reference. Mathematicians have contributed to it ever since, building out results from college-level algebra all the way up to the field’s most advanced ideas across algebra, geometry, and number theory.

The organization’s fleet of AI agents translates the library’s roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code.

Formalizing math is a way of making sure the structure underneath it is sound. Mathematicians rewrite the proof as code in a programming language called Lean, and a program called a proof assistant checks the code line by line. If the proof passes, mathematicians can trust that it’s logically sound.

Engineers use the same idea, called formal verification, to confirm their chip designs work, while researchers in France have used it to catch bugs in software that calculates family benefits.

For a library like the Stacks Project, checking each theorem is only part of the job. The theorems and definitions in Stacks are interconnected, and each one builds on the ones before it. Like a family tree, many results in Stacks trace back to the ones that came before it.

That interconnectedness made Axiom unsure the project would work at first. The team had to keep every connection intact across about 16 million lines of Lean code.

“Things that are big and things that are delicate in life just don’t go together,” Axiom CEO Carina Hong told TechCrunch. “[Stacks] is a collection of mathematical results that is the foundation of mathematics. You want [theorems] to be consistent and not, like, paradoxical. You want the definitions to not fight with each other.”.

The 25-year-old CEO dropped out of a Stanford math PhD program and founded the tech giant in March 2025. In March, Axiom raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures.

“We were not sure if vibe coding would be able to preserve the beauty of Stacks,” Hong said.

To pull off the project, the team gave its agents a loose structure and let them run in parallel. “With Stacks, we imposed a hierarchy … [but] it was not, like, a complete hierarchy of dictating what every single agent was doing,” stated Ashvin Swaminathan, a member of Axiom’s technical staff. “The agents were finding tasks for themselves and identified things that they could work on in parallel.”.

Axiom also trained its own models to be good at math, an approach Hong said most other verification startups haven’t taken. At first, the team relied on one of its in-house Lean experts to teach the agents a human sense of taste. Over time, Hong said, the agents have picked up taste on their own.

The result fills one of the biggest gaps in formalized math. “When you look at what has been formalized in mathematics, there’s this huge black hole. And that black hole covers algebraic geometry,” Swaminathan stated.

Until now, researchers who wanted to check new work in algebraic geometry with Lean had little to build on, Swaminathan mentioned. “Well, now they do.”.

According to recent reports, axiom argues that each verified result becomes a building block, so future proofs can lean on checked math instead of starting from scratch. Terence Tao, the UCLA mathematician and Fields Medal winner, has made the general case more simply: “The more formalized proofs you have, the more formalized proofs you can make.”.

It has been revealed that mathematicians aren’t Axiom’s only intended audience. Developers have long struggled to guarantee that their code is free of bugs and security holes. That problem grows as AI agents write more of the world’s code.

Axiom is betting that the software of the future will need to rest on verified foundations, the way Stacks now does.

“We believe that mathematics is the domain where you start building these things and that it’s a transferable skill,” Swaminathan mentioned. “Agents can read our code, understand it, and build new infrastructure on top of it. Our Lean formalization is now the substrate that agents can build upon.”.

The way Axiom’s agents built Stacks, working in parallel and picking their own tasks, is how Hong expects much of AI’s future work to happen. AI agents, she argues, will need a well-built, reusable body of knowledge to keep from producing slop.

“You want [agents] to have a reusable library for them to build on and keep pushing the frontier,” Hong mentioned. “If you slop drop in a way that’s bad engineering choices in the beginning, then it’s very hard for them to grow that boundary.”.

Hong is confident enough in that approach to problem a dare. “I openly challenge all the coding companies to work on formalization at this scale.”.

Seattle’s Allen Institute helps create a ‘Rosetta Stone’ for brain cells to unlock clues to disease

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/seattles-allen-institute-helps-create-a-rosetta-stone-for-brain-cells-to-unlock-clues-to-disease/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 11, 2026 at 5:15 pm.
  • According to recent reports, A coalition of 56 institutions across nine countries is publishing groundbreaking research today on the basal ganglia — a group of brain structures that help control movement, emotions, motivation and habits.
  • The scientist have produced a biological Rosetta Stone that creates a shared system for naming and describing cells in the basal ganglia across species.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 11, 2026 at 5:15 pm.

According to recent reports, A coalition of 56 institutions across nine countries is publishing groundbreaking research today on the basal ganglia — a group of brain structures that help control movement, emotions, motivation and habits. The region is linked to psychiatric and degenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and Parkinson’s disease.

The scientist have produced a biological Rosetta Stone that creates a shared system for naming and describing cells in the basal ganglia across species. The goal is to help researchers compare findings, collaborate and accelerate their understanding of this essential brain region.

“This is groundwork that is necessary to really make progress,” remarked Michael Hawrylycz, principal investigator with the Seattle-based Allen Institute who helped organize the consortium.

The project, called the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, or BICAN, produced a basal ganglia atlas that is publicly available for basic researchers, clinicians and others to use.

According to recent reports, the research is being presented in a package of 26 articles in a special issue of the journal Cell. The data comes from humans, macaques, marmoset and mice. One of the benefits of comparing the basal ganglia between species is understanding which components are uniquely human, providing potential insights into neurological diseases.

Despite the critical and wide-ranging roles, the basal ganglia is relatively small — it’s about 2% of the brain with a volume roughly the size of a large gumball.

In a recent development, for the project, the researchers pulled information from 25.5 million brain cells, including 21 million human cells. They used a variety of techniques to tease out insights, including RNA sequencing to identify gene activity from single cells in precise locations; epigenomic studies revealing where genes are switched on or off; and measurements of electrical activity combined with cell shape and genetic information.

Sources indicate that it’s a lot of data to stitch together and make sense of, Hawrylycz noted. “AI is a perfect tool” for the job, he said, because it excels at finding patterns.

The findings could help guide future treatments, but the work remains basic research rather than clinical research, Hawrylycz said.

The latest research is the first major installment of the third phase of a brain-mapping effort that began in 2014. The first phase demonstrated that scientists could analyze individual cells on a large scale. The second produced an atlas of the mouse brain.

BICAN aims to create a standardized atlas describing cells throughout the brains of humans and other primates. Hawrylycz said the work is expected to take another two or three years.

#98. From interim CEO to Form 8-K: 10 steps boards take after a sudden CEO exit

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23 min read (4543 words)
Business & Policy

From interim CEO to Form 8-K: 10 steps boards take after a sudden CEO exit

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read | Sumber: https://qz.com/ceo-succession-after-sudden-exit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • How companies replace a CEO after a sudden exit, from naming an interim chief executive to running a board search and filing the required disclosures.
  • Industry observers note that A sudden CEO exit tests a board's preparation more than its judgment.
  • The stakes reach well beyond the boardroom.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How companies replace a CEO after a sudden exit, from naming an interim chief executive to running a board search and filing the required disclosures.

Industry observers note that A sudden CEO exit tests a board's preparation more than its judgment. When a chief executive resigns without warning, dies, falls seriously ill or is dismissed, directors rarely have time to deliberate from scratch. The decisions they make in the first days are shaped by work they did, or failed to do, long before.

The stakes reach well beyond the boardroom. Employees want to know who is in charge and whether their projects will survive. Investors want evidence that the company has a blueprint and that strategy will not drift. Customers and suppliers watch for signs of disruption. For a U.S. public company, regulators also expect prompt disclosure of the change.

Recent findings suggest that understanding how companies replace a CEO after a sudden exit means looking at several moving parts at once. Boards must put an accountable leader in place rapidly. They must decide whether that person is a placeholder or a contender for the permanent job. They also need a process for finding a successor that staff and shareholders find credible.

The tools available to directors are well established. Many boards keep an emergency succession plan alongside their longer-term CEO succession planning. They can promote a sitting executive or ask a director to step into an executive role. They can also bring in an outside search firm to build a slate of candidates. Each route carries tradeoffs between continuity and change.

Recent findings suggest that the legal and financial side matters too. A departing chief executive usually leaves behind an employment agreement, equity awards and possibly severance terms that the board must review. The interim leader and the eventual successor each need a pay package. Public companies must also manage what they say, when they say it and to whom.

Industry observers note that the 10 slides that follow cover a selection of common steps boards take during an emergency CEO succession. They are not a complete or ranked list, and the order is not fixed. In practice, many of these steps run in parallel during the first weeks of a chief executive transition. Each slide explains one step, why boards use it and what it involves.

Sources indicate that when a chief executive leaves without warning, the board's first move is usually to name an interim CEO. That appointment gives employees, investors and customers one accountable leader while the search for a permanent successor begins.

A manufacturer cannot run for long without someone holding the chief executive's authority. Contracts need signatures and budgets need approval. Managers need a person who can settle disputes and make final calls. Payroll, regulatory obligations and customer commitments do not pause for a leadership change. Naming an interim closes that gap and makes clear who is in charge.

Recent findings suggest that speed matters outside the firm as well. Investors, lenders, customers and suppliers watch a leadership change closely. An announcement that pairs the departure with a named replacement highlights that the board has acted. A long silence between the two can invite speculation about why the previous CEO left.

Interim chief executives usually come from one of two places: the board or the senior management team. A director tends to know the firm's strategy, finances and governance history. A senior executive brings day-to-day knowledge of operations, staff and customers. The board weighs which of those strengths the business needs most in the moment.

The interim holds the CEO's authority, but the board usually sets the terms of the role through a formal resolution. Those terms cover whom the interim reports to and how long the arrangement is expected to last. Some boards also require their own approval for transactions above a set size.

Some interims state from the start that they will not seek the permanent role. That clarity can let other executives focus on the transition instead of on competing for the top job. Other interims stay open to the position. In those cases, the board may evaluate the interim alongside outside and internal candidates in the formal search.

According to recent reports, the title varies from organization to company. Some boards use "interim CEO," while others prefer "acting CEO." A few split the job temporarily between two senior executives as co-CEOs. That structure requires the board to spell out which parts of the business each executive oversees and how they resolve disagreements.

Many boards keep a confidential emergency succession plan that names who takes charge if the chief executive leaves without notice. Putting that plan into action lets directors carry out a decision they made in calm conditions, rather than improvising one in a crisis.

Sources indicate that an emergency plan usually answers a short list of practical questions. It names the person or people who can step in on short notice. That is often a senior executive or a sitting director. The plan may also say who convenes the board, who speaks for the firm and which outside advisers get called first.

Industry observers note that this document differs from long-term CEO succession planning. A long-term plan develops candidates over years and prepares for an orderly retirement. An emergency plan deals with a narrower problem: who runs the tech giant tomorrow.

Sources indicate that the person named for an emergency is not always the board's preferred permanent successor. Keeping the two roles separate lets the board fill the gap without locking in a long-term choice. It also leaves directors room to run a fuller search later.

Recent findings suggest that some prepares distinguish between kinds of sudden exit. A dismissal for cause may bring legal review and an internal investigation. A death or illness raises questions of privacy and of care for the executive's family.

According to recent reports, confidentiality is part of the design. Boards generally keep the proposal private to avoid signaling who is in line for the top job. A leaked name can unsettle other executives or create expectations the board never meant to set.

A blueprint works only if it stays current. Executives change roles, get promoted or leave the organization. A name on the plan can go stale as a result. Boards review and update these looks periodically, often through the full board or its governance or nominating committee. Directors may also confirm that the named stand-in is still willing and able to serve.

The absence of a initiative carries its own cost. Without one, directors must debate who leads while employees, customers and lenders wait for answers. That debate can stretch from hours into days. It also leaves room for internal rivalries to surface during the transition.

According to recent reports, after a sudden CEO exit, boards commonly set up a small committee of directors to run the search for a permanent successor. The committee manages the process day to day and brings a recommendation back to the full board, which keeps the final vote.

A full board is too large, and meets too rarely, to run a search on its own. A smaller group can schedule interviews promptly and review candidates in detail. It can also keep sensitive information within a tight circle. Some boards hand the job to an existing nominating and governance committee. Others create an ad hoc committee for this search alone and dissolve it once a upcoming chief executive is in place.

In a recent development, independent directors usually make up the committee. These are directors who are not firm employees and have no material business ties to the company. A lead independent director or a non-executive chair often leads the group. That person typically serves as the main contact for candidates, advisers and the rest of the board.

In a recent development, membership comes with a conflict rule. A director who wants to be considered for the CEO job generally steps off the committee. The same applies to an interim chief executive who may compete for the permanent role. Keeping candidates off the committee separates the people doing the judging from the people being judged. It also strengthens the board's ability to defend its choice later.

One of the committee's first tasks is to write a candidate profile. This document sets out the experience, skills and leadership qualities the next CEO needs. It reflects the company's strategy, its current challenges and the circumstances of the departure. A profile agreed early gives the committee a fixed standard for comparing candidates.

Recent findings suggest that the committee then sets the process and the timetable. It decides how candidates will be sourced, who interviews them and in what order. It also oversees reference and background checks on finalists. Those checks carry extra weight after an abrupt exit tied to misconduct.

Industry observers note that confidentiality shapes the committee's work. Candidate names, interview notes and deliberations stay inside the committee and its advisers. A leak can cost the company a candidate who is employed elsewhere.

In a recent development, the committee reports to the full board at regular intervals throughout the search. Its decision rights stop short of the appointment itself. It recommends a finalist, and the full board votes to name the latest CEO.

According to recent reports, promoting a sitting executive, such as the chief operating officer or chief financial officer, is a common way for a board to fill a sudden CEO vacancy. An insider already knows the business, the people and the numbers. That shortens the time before the company has a working leader.

According to recent reports, the appeal starts with familiarity. A COO typically oversees day-to-day operations and already manages many of the teams that report up to the chief executive. A CFO knows the balance sheet, the lenders and the investor base. Either one can step into the top job without a long orientation period.

Sources indicate that existing relationships also count. Customers, suppliers, lenders and major shareholders often already deal with the internal candidate. That prior contact can make the leadership change easier to explain to each of them. Employees may read an internal appointment as a sign that the company's direction is not about to be overturned.

Industry observers note that an insider also brings a track record the board has watched directly. Directors have usually seen the executive present at board meetings, defend budgets and respond to problems. That direct view removes some of the guesswork that comes with a candidate the board has met only in interviews.

The tradeoff is change. An executive who helped build the current strategy may be less inclined to question it. If the exit followed poor results or misconduct, a board may judge that an insider is too close to the problem.

Industry observers note that promotion also creates a second vacancy. If the COO becomes chief executive, someone still has to run operations. Companies often fill that seat with an acting appointment from the next management layer. Others split the duties among existing leaders for a period. A manufacturer that promotes its CFO must keep financial reporting and internal controls running without a gap. A public company also faces periodic filing deadlines that do not pause for a leadership change.

In a recent development, readiness is the last test. Running one function is different from running the whole manufacturer. A COO may have limited experience facing investors. A CFO may have little exposure to product development or sales. Boards weigh those gaps before deciding. Some pair the upcoming chief executive with an experienced chair or outside adviser. Others set out a defined development blueprint covering the areas where the executive has less experience.

Industry observers note that A board sometimes asks its chair or another director to take on a temporary executive role after a sudden CEO exit. The appeal is speed and familiarity. The cost is that the person meant to supervise management now helps run it.

Directors who step in already know the company's strategy, finances and open risks from board meetings. They have usually worked with the senior team and the largest investors. That background lets them take charge without the orientation an outside hire would need. It also gives the board a leader whose judgment it has already seen up close.

Industry observers note that the arrangement takes two main forms. In one, the chair becomes executive chair and takes on operating duties alongside the remaining executives. The CEO seat then stays vacant or goes to an internal officer. In the other, the chair or another director is named interim CEO outright. Both forms place a board member inside management, and both are meant to be temporary.

It has been revealed that the tension is built into the board's role. Directors hire, oversee, evaluate and, when necessary, remove the chief executive. A director serving as interim leader ends up overseeing their own work. Questions about performance, pay and strategy become harder for the board to examine at arm's length.

Recent findings suggest that boards use several safeguards to manage that conflict. A common step is naming a lead independent director, or strengthening the role if one exists. That director runs executive sessions of the non-management directors and acts as a check on the interim leader. Under NYSE and Nasdaq $NDAQ listing standards, audit committee members must be independent. A director who takes on paid executive duties generally steps off the audit committee and often the compensation committee as well.

In a recent development, time limits are another safeguard. Boards often set a defined term or tie the role to the end of the permanent search. A stated end point tells employees and investors that the arrangement is a bridge, not a fresh leadership structure. It also keeps a split role from becoming the default.

Recent findings suggest that the board also has to settle whether the director in the executive seat is a candidate for the permanent job. Boards often decide that early. A director who is a contender generally steps away from the search committee's deliberations. A director who is not can say so publicly. That statement tells internal candidates the search is open.

Once a permanent CEO arrives, the director typically returns to a non-executive role. Some boards keep the director on as executive chair for a set period to support the handoff. The board then revisits committee assignments and independence determinations. The specifics depend on the company's bylaws, governance guidelines and listing requirements.

Boards often retain an executive search firm to find and vet candidates for a permanent chief executive. Spencer Stuart, Russell Reynolds Associates, Heidrick & Struggles and Korn Ferry are among the firms that take on this kind of board-level assignment.

The firm works for the board, not for management. It typically reports to the committee of directors that oversees the search. That reporting line matters after a sudden exit, when an interim leader may also be a contender for the permanent job.

In a recent development, A search usually begins with a role specification. The firm and the directors agree on what the next CEO needs to deliver. That brief draws on the company's strategy, its financial position and the circumstances of the previous leader's departure. The resulting document shapes which industries, functions and backgrounds the firm targets.

The firm then maps the market. Consultants identify executives who fit the profile, including sitting CEOs, division heads at larger companies and leaders at competitors. Many of those people are not looking to move. The first approach is therefore typically discreet and framed as a conversation rather than a job offer.

Confidentiality runs in both directions. Candidates employed elsewhere often cannot afford to have their interest become public. The hiring company, for its part, may not want rivals or its own employees to learn who is under consideration before the board decides.

In a recent development, assessment goes beyond the résumé. Search firms conduct structured interviews and check references. They also examine how a candidate performed in situations similar to the one the firm now faces. Some boards ask the firm to evaluate internal candidates as well. That gives directors a common yardstick for comparing insiders and outsiders.

CEO searches are generally run on a retained basis. Under that model, the firm is paid for conducting the search rather than only when a candidate is hired. Fee terms are set in each engagement letter and vary by firm and assignment.

It has been revealed that boards also ask about conflicts. Search firms commonly observe off-limits arrangements that restrict them from recruiting executives out of their own current clients. A large firm's client list can therefore narrow the pool of executives it is able to approach.

Industry observers note that the firm's output is a short list of finalists, not a decision. Directors interview the candidates, often over several rounds, and the full board votes on the appointment. The board, not the search firm, remains accountable for the final choice.

Industry observers note that the choice between an internal and an external CEO candidate turns on one question: does the company need continuity or a change in direction? No fixed rule settles it. Boards weigh each sudden exit on its own circumstances.

Industry observers note that the reason for the departure shapes the answer. A CEO who leaves because of illness or death may leave behind a strategy the board still supports. In that case, a leader who already knows the strategy can carry it forward with less disruption.

A dismissal tied to misconduct or weak results points the other way. If the board has lost confidence in the direction of the business, an insider may look too close to the decisions that caused the problem. Directors then have to judge whether a familiar face can credibly signal a break with the past.

Internal candidates come with a known record. Directors have usually watched them present to the board, manage budgets and lead teams. They already understand the tech giant's products, customers and culture. That familiarity lowers the risk of a poor fit. It can also limit fresh thinking.

It has been revealed that external candidates offer a different set of tradeoffs. An outsider arrives without loyalty to past strategy or to particular executives. That independence can make it easier to restructure, exit a business line or reset relationships with investors.

The cost is a learning curve. A chief executive hired from outside has to learn the organization, its people and its informal ways of working. Until that happens, acting with confidence on major decisions is harder.

Culture adds another layer to the comparison. A company with a strong internal culture may resist a leader who does not share it. A company whose culture contributed to the exit may need someone willing to challenge it.

It has been revealed that the depth of the internal bench also narrows or widens the field. If no executive is ready for the top role, the debate moves swiftly toward outside candidates. If several insiders are credible, the board can compare them directly against an external slate rather than choosing one pool at the outset.

Timing is another variable. An insider can usually step into the permanent role faster. A wider external search can take longer. That extends the period the manufacturer spends under interim leadership.

A U.S. public company generally must report a CEO departure, and the appointment of an interim or permanent replacement, on SEC Form 8-K under Item 5.02. The standard filing deadline is four business days after the triggering event.

Form 8-K is the Securities and Exchange Commission's current report. Companies file it to tell investors about significant events that occur between quarterly and annual reports. Item 5.02 governs the departure and appointment of directors and certain senior officers. The principal executive officer, usually the CEO, falls within it.

Recent findings suggest that A typical filing states who is leaving, when the change takes effect and who is taking charge. For a newly appointed officer, the disclosure includes background such as age and business experience. It also describes any material compensation arrangement tied to the appointment.

Recent findings suggest that the four-day window is a deadline, not a waiting period. Companies often announce the news by press release on the same day and attach that release to the 8-K as an exhibit. A quick announcement shortens the stretch in which rumors circulate without an official account.

Industry observers note that regulation Fair Disclosure, known as Reg FD, shapes how the news goes out. The rule bars a public company from selectively sharing material nonpublic information with analysts or certain investors ahead of the general public. A sudden change at the top can be material. That pushes companies toward one broad public announcement rather than a round of private calls.

Foreign companies listed in the U.S. as foreign private issuers follow a different route. They generally furnish reports on Form 6-K rather than Form 8-K. Companies without SEC reporting obligations file no 8-K at all. Their boards still decide how and when to inform lenders, investors and staff.

Recent findings suggest that inside the organization, timing is a practical problem. Employees who learn about a leadership change from a headline may question whether anyone is in control. Boards and communications teams therefore tend to schedule an all-staff message close to the public announcement.

In a recent development, that message usually names the person now in charge and explains what happens next. It often confirms that the board has started a search, without committing to a date. Companies generally avoid speculating about the reasons for an exit, especially while lawyers are still reviewing the circumstances.

Recent findings suggest that customers, suppliers and lenders form a third audience. Sales teams and account managers may need prepared language for their contacts. The board may also need to check whether any financing or commercial agreements require formal notice of a leadership change.

According to recent reports, after a sudden CEO exit, the board reviews the departing executive's employment agreement to settle severance, equity awards, clawback rights and any non-compete. It also sets pay for the interim leader and, later, for the permanent successor.

Sources indicate that the compensation committee usually leads this work, often with outside legal counsel. Its first task is to establish what the contract actually states. Employment agreements differ from company to company. The signed documents set the baseline, and departing from them usually means negotiating newly introduced terms with the former executive.

It has been revealed that the reason for the departure shapes almost every term. Chief executive agreements commonly treat a termination "for cause" differently from one "without cause." A resignation for "good reason," as the contract defines it, often carries the same benefits as a dismissal without cause. Death and disability usually have their own provisions. A board that labels an exit incorrectly can invite a legal dispute with the former executive.

According to recent reports, equity awards are often the largest piece of value at stake. Unvested stock options and restricted shares may be forfeited, continue to vest or vest immediately. The outcome depends on the equity proposal and the individual award agreements. Performance-based awards can carry separate rules tied to whether targets are met after the executive leaves.

Clawback provisions let a organization recover pay that should not have been awarded. In the U.S., stock exchange listing standards adopted under SEC Rule 10D-1 require a clawback policy. That policy must cover erroneously awarded incentive pay after an accounting restatement. Some company policies reach further and cover misconduct.

It has been revealed that restrictive covenants come next. These can include non-compete, non-solicitation and confidentiality clauses. Whether a non-compete can be enforced depends on the jurisdiction. The board's lawyers assess that question for each case.

Industry observers note that many departures end in a negotiated separation agreement. In exchange for severance, the former CEO typically signs a release of legal claims against the organization. The agreement may also cover a short transition period, a consulting arrangement or a mutual non-disparagement clause.

In a recent development, the committee then turns to the interim leader. An executive who steps up temporarily may receive added cash pay, a one-time equity grant or both. Those terms reflect the extra duties and the uncertainty of a temporary role. The permanent successor's package is negotiated later, as part of the search itself.

Industry observers note that public companies also face scrutiny of the payout. U.S. proxy statements describe the potential payments named executive officers would receive on termination. Shareholders can compare that disclosure with what the departing CEO actually receives.

During a CEO transition, an interim leader usually keeps strategy steady, holds the senior team together and leaves major long-term bets for the permanent chief executive. Retention arrangements for key executives are a common tool for limiting departures while the search runs.

Industry observers note that A sudden exit leaves a gap at the top, and the people just below it often feel the uncertainty first. Senior executives may wonder whether the next CEO will keep them, reshape their roles or bring in a upcoming team. Some may hear from recruiters or competitors during this period. Losing several leaders at once would add to the disruption the board is trying to contain.

The interim CEO's job is partly to answer that uncertainty. An interim leader often meets early with each member of the executive team to clarify reporting lines and decision rights. Those conversations confirm which projects continue and who owns them. That clarity lets managers keep running their units rather than wait for direction.

Retention pay is another lever. A board may offer selected executives cash bonuses or additional equity. These awards pay out only if the person stays through the transition or for a set period after it. The terms vary by company and by individual. The aim is to give critical leaders a concrete reason to stay until the new CEO is in place.

On strategy, interim leaders typically focus on carrying out the existing plan. They tend to defer decisions that would bind the next CEO for years. Examples include large acquisitions, major restructurings or a shift in the firm's core direction. Routine operations, approved budgets and customer commitments continue. Postponing the biggest choices preserves options for whoever takes the permanent role.

Industry observers note that that caution has limits. A business facing a crisis, a regulatory deadline or a fast-moving competitor cannot simply pause. In those cases the board and the interim leader decide which time-sensitive matters must move forward. The board often stays more involved than usual while those decisions are made.

The final stage is the handoff. Once the permanent CEO is named, the interim leader typically briefs the successor on open issues, pending decisions and the state of the executive team. An interim drawn from management may return to a previous role or leave the tech giant. An interim drawn from the board may go back to serving as a director. The new chief executive then sets the longer-term direction. That includes any changes to the leadership team or strategy that the transition period left open.

Sovereign or not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide

  • BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin.
  • Sovereignty is everywhere right now, and most people still can’t agree on what it means and, just as importantly, what it all means to them.
  • This week theCUBE Research releases its latest market report, Sovereign or Not?

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin.

Sovereignty is everywhere right now, and most people still can’t agree on what it means and, just as importantly, what it all means to them.

This week theCUBE Research releases its latest market report, Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide. In this Breaking Analysis, we’re joined by its author, Amit Eyal Govrin, lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and CEO of Agentcy Labs, to talk about why he wrote it, what sovereignty is and what it isn’t, and what surprised him most in the findings.

It has been revealed that the full scores are in the report. Read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide https://siliconangle.com/sovereign-or-not.

Dave: As someone who’s been leading the thought leadership in this domain, how did you come up with the inspiration to research this topic and write the report?

It has been revealed that amit: To understand the how, it helps to understand the why. I’ve been thinking about this subject for a while now. It hasn’t always been called “sovereignty,” but the tenets have always been the same.

Sources indicate that it all started around four years ago, as I’ve been a builder in this space for that long. First with Kubiya, one of the industry’s first agentic implementations, deploying agents in enterprise production environments as early as September 2023, before agents were even an industry term.

Sources indicate that we were deploying as a software-as-a-service organization, and many of those concerns were legitimate. As a software company, we got to keep our intellectual property and license it out. If we were successful, we would create dependency, which effectively meant customers lost control of their crown jewels.

It has been revealed that when we started Agentcy Labs earlier this year, customers familiar with our work approached us, and many of these points crystallized for us. What they told us: We’re relieved you are no longer at Kubiya. It’s not that we ever doubted your technology or the value it brings. Quite the opposite. That was what they were afraid of. Kubiya creates a dependency, adoption balloons, and they lose control of their costs. Or a vendor changes the meter on them because of shareholder pressure or regulatory controls.

What clicked for us is that their resistance was never about Kubiya or our technology. It was about the loss of control of their alpha. Namely, the Agentic Operating System, the key driver of their artificial intelligence transformation, which falls under our technological pillar.

It doesn’t matter if the vendor is a startup, an AI lab or a hyperscaler. No enterprise can afford to mortgage its entire business on an external dependency on such a key matter. It’s far too strategic not to own outright.

That finding forced us to rethink the model behind software, dig deeper into sovereignty as an problem of control, and help the industry define it in a more standardized way.

According to recent reports, dave: So control is the heart of it. But when most people hear sovereignty, they think about where the data sits. Is that the wrong way to look at it?

Recent findings suggest that amit: Sovereignty goes well beyond territory, which is often the most misunderstood aspect. People hear sovereignty and immediately revert to the sovereign state: government initiatives, national security, on-premises air-gapped environments. That can be true in some cases. But by and large, our sovereignty discussions involve enterprises and regulated industries that have sovereignty as a core tenet of their AI initiatives.

According to recent reports, it goes beyond buzzwords and sovereign-washing claims. Think back to the explosive Alex Karp interview on CNBC claiming enterprises are losing their alpha to frontier labs. I largely agree with that claim, by the way. Only he finished his pitch by offering customers to move it over to Palantir. In other words: Stop mortgaging your alpha to Anthropic and OpenAI, come rent it from us.

That interview was my trigger point to take up arms and educate the industry on sovereignty: what it is, what it isn’t, and most importantly, what you, as a buyer of AI, can do about it.

Sources indicate that dave: And you’ve been out in the field with buyers ever since. What did those conversations teach you, and how did that shape the framework?

Amit: Since then, we’ve been included in dozens of engagements with enterprises, governments and policymakers around the world, from Washington to Brussels, New Delhi, Sydney and even Riyadh. We are in the room when sovereignty discussions happen. That helped us shape our view, tease out the concerns, and focus on what really matters and why. From those discussions came the 5 Pillars of Sovereignty framework. We use it today to assess all vendor relationships, policy and regulation, and geopolitical events.

Recent findings suggest that dave: Which brings us to the report. You started with the hyperscalers. Walk us through how you approached it.

Amit: In our first edition, Sovereign or Not? The Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide, we take the buyer’s lens and assess each hyperscaler by its sovereignty posture.

Hint: By definition, working with any hyperscaler means ceding a good portion of control over your Operational, Technological, Legal and Financial pillars. Oftentimes that’s the reality in the real world.

My view: Sovereignty is not a purity test. It’s perfectly acceptable to go with a hyperscaler, as long as it’s a known dependency you priced in as an acceptable risk. If that’s the case, let us guide you through these considerations to the best path forward for your organization.

According to recent reports, dave: OK, let’s get to the part everyone wants to know. Who scored what, and why?

Amit: We looked at seven hyperscalers and 40 of their offerings, from the point of view of buyers in five regions: the U.S., Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the rest, including the Middle East and Africa. Everything is scored out of 5.

The short version: The most sovereign product a hyperscaler sells is the one the hyperscaler itself can’t reach.

Sources indicate that on these tests, sovereignty often runs inverse to how a hyperscaler is built. A shared global control plane and services the vendor runs for the customer make a cloud easy to adopt, but every layer the vendor runs is a layer the buyer does not control. Amazon Web Services and Google built their platforms around that abstraction, which becomes a hindrance once a buyer needs to run the stack without them. The grades measure how much control a buyer can take back, not the quality of the cloud.

It has been revealed that who came out on top, who came in last, and by how much, is in the report. And every score is backed by a source. Don’t like your grade? Publish the document and we’ll re-score it.

Dave: What surprised you most when you went through the findings?

Amit: None of the hyperscalers has a practical solution for the U.S. CLOUD Act, and that alone has created a real legal clawback on non-U.S. companies.

In plain English: The U.S. government can ask an American cloud company for data it controls, no matter which country the data sits in. A sovereign cloud in Brandenburg, run by a German subsidiary, doesn’t change the answer. It’s still owned by an American company.

The vendors aren’t hiding it. AWS told us as much on the record. Microsoft’s own lawyer in France told the French Senate he couldn’t guarantee French data would never reach U.S. authorities. That’s honesty, and we don’t penalize honesty. It’s the law, and it applies to every American cloud the same way.

European privacy law notes you can’t just hand that data over. So a European firm can end up stuck between two governments, breaking one law to obey the other. That’s the clawback.

The fixes buyers are being sold, like keeping data local, holding your own encryption keys, or a contract promise to fight requests, don’t change who the government can go to.

Dave: So what’s a non-U.S. buyer supposed to do about that?

Amit: There’s no perfect answer today, only partial ones.

Going with a hyperscaler is fine, as long as you know the risk and priced it in. What’s not fine is believing a data center in Brandenburg, on its own merits, solved your sovereignty problem.

In a recent development, dave: And this is just the first of several. Where do you go from here?

According to recent reports, amit: This is the first of a series: neoclouds, OEMs, telcos and specialized sovereign initiatives, wherever you happen to be, whether you’re a U.S., EU, Latin American, APAC or Middle Eastern buyer. Every edition covers the 5 Pillars, plus security, regulation and exit costs. Readers will be surprised by how deep we got, including quotes from the hyperscalers themselves and surveys of actual buyers. I truly think this will be valuable to everyone listening and reading.

Dave: That’s phenomenal, Amit. This is a cutting-edge report on a truly important and timely subject. If previously you were building on the frontier, you’re now squarely on the frontier of research. The scores, the vendor answers and the buyer data are all in the full report.

Sources indicate that read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide.
