Fly-E Group, Inc. Announces Second Quarter and First Half of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Results

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read | Sumber: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/fly-e-group-inc-announces-second-quarter-and-first-half-of-fiscal-year-2027-financial-results-302939337.html

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fly-E Group, Inc.
  • Second quarter of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Summary.
  • Zhou (Andy) Ou, Chief Executive Officer of Fly-E, commented, "During the second quarter, our operational network stabilized following the retail restructuring, with our top-line revenue holding steady sequentially.

NEW YORK, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fly-E Group, Inc. (Nasdaq: FLYE) ("Fly-E" or the "Manufacturer"), an electric vehicle company engaged in designing, installing, selling, and renting smart electric motorcycles, electric bikes, and electric scooters, today confirmed its unaudited financial results for the second quarter and first half of fiscal year 2027 ended September 30, 2026.

Second quarter of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Summary.

Mr. Zhou (Andy) Ou, Chief Executive Officer of Fly-E, commented, "During the second quarter, our operational network stabilized following the retail restructuring, with our top-line revenue holding steady sequentially. Our wholesale revenues grew 21.4% year-over-year and accounted for a significantly higher proportion of our total revenue. This evolving revenue mix, combined with promotional pricing in our retail business, naturally influenced our overall margin profile for the period. Meanwhile, we continued to control store-level costs and address corporate matters carefully to strengthen the Manufacturer's foundation for the future. By maintaining our operational network and disciplined cost management, we are dedicated to preserving business stability while positioning Fly-E to explore strategic opportunities for long-term growth.".

Second quarter of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Results.

In a recent development, net revenues were $2.6 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 33.7% from $3.9 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily driven by a lower sales volume of 7,392 units in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to 18,564 in the same period last year, resulting from the reduction in our direct retail store count to four stores as of September 30, 2026, compared to 11 stores as of September 30, 2025.

Cost of revenues was $2.4 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 18.8% from $2.9 million in the same period last year, primarily aligning with lower sales volume driven by the downsizing of our retail store network.

Gross profit was $0.2 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to $1.0 million in the same period last year. Gross margin was 8.1% in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to 25.0% in the same period last year. The decrease in gross margin was primarily attributable to a structural mix shift from direct retail toward lower-priced wholesale channels, further impacted by competitive retail pricing and inventory clearance discounts.

Total operating expenses were $1.8 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 9.8% compared to $2.0 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily attributable to store-level operational savings, which were partially offset by increases in expected credit losses and professional fees.

Net loss was $1.7 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to $1.8 million in the same period last year.

Basic and Diluted Earnings (Losses) per Share.

Basic and diluted losses per share were $1.07 in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to $2.18 in the same period last year.

EBITDA was negative $1.3 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to negative EBITDA of $1.0 million in the same period last year.

First Half of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Results.

Net revenues were $5.3 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 42.2% from $9.2 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily driven by a significant reduction in direct retail store counts, resulting in a lower sales volume of 14,950 units in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to 29,012 in the same period last year.

Cost of revenues was $4.8 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 19.5% from $6.0 million in the same period last year, primarily reflecting lower sales volume following the downsizing of our retail store network.

Recent findings suggest that gross profit was $0.5 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to $3.2 million in the same period last year. Gross margin was 9.5% in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to 35.1% in the same period last year. The decrease in gross margin was primarily attributable to the greater revenue percentage of wholesale channels at lower-priced wholesale pricing, as well as promotional retail pricing adjustment and inventory clearance discounts.

Total operating expenses were $5.7 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 2.2% compared to $5.8 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily attributable to operational cost savings from retail store reductions, which were offset by increases in expected credit losses and software development fees.

Net loss was $5.6 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to $3.8 million in the same period last year.

Basic and Diluted Earnings (Losses) per Share.

Basic and diluted losses per share were $3.48 in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to $6.58 in the same period last year.

EBITDA was negative $4.7 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to negative EBITDA of $2.2 million in the same period last year.

As of September 30, 2026, the Company had cash of $0.5 million, compared to $0.3 million as of March 31, 2026.

Fly-E Group, Inc. is an electric vehicle organization that is principally engaged in designing, installing, selling, and renting smart electric motorcycles, electric bikes, and electric scooters under the brand "Fly E-Bike." The Company's commitment is to encourage people to incorporate eco-friendly transportation into their active lifestyles, ultimately contributing towards building a more environmentally friendly future. For more information, please visit the Company's website: https://investors.flyebike.com.

To supplement our financial information presented in accordance with the generally accepted accounting principles in the United States (the "U.S. GAAP"), management periodically uses certain "non-GAAP financial measures," as such term is defined under the rules of the SEC, to clarify and enhance understanding of past performance and prospects for the future. Generally, a non-GAAP financial measure is a numerical measure of a company's operating performance, financial position or cash flows that excludes or includes amounts that are included in or excluded from the most directly comparable measure calculated and presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP. For example, non-GAAP measures may exclude the impact of certain items such as acquisitions, divestitures, gains, losses and impairments, or items outside of management's control. Management believes that the following non-GAAP financial measure provides investors and analysts useful insight into our financial position and operating performance. Any non-GAAP measure provided should be viewed in addition to, and not as an alternative to, the most directly comparable measure determined in accordance with U.S. GAAP. Further, the calculation of these non-GAAP financial measures may differ from the calculation of similarly titled financial measures presented by other companies and therefore may not be comparable among companies.

In a recent development, we use EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) to evaluate our operating performance. We believe EBITDA provides additional insight into our underlying, ongoing operating performance and facilitates year-to-year comparisons by excluding the earnings impact of interest, tax, depreciation and amortization and that presenting EBITDA is more representative of our operational performance and may be more useful for investors.

We reconcile our non-GAAP financial measure to our net income, which is our most directly comparable financial measure calculated and presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP. EBITDA includes adjustments for provision for income taxes, as applicable, interest income and expense, depreciation, and amortization. EBITDA does not represent and should not be considered an alternative to net income as determined by U.S. GAAP, and our calculations thereof may not be comparable to those reported by other companies. We believe EBITDA is an important measure of operating performance and provides useful information to investors because it highlights trends in our business that may not otherwise be apparent when relying solely on U.S. GAAP measures and because it eliminates items that have less bearing on our operating performance. EBITDA, as presented herein, is a supplemental measure of our performance that is not required by, or presented in accordance with, U.S. GAAP. We use non-GAAP financial measures as supplements to our U.S. GAAP results in order to provide a more complete understanding of the factors and trends affecting our business. EBITDA is a measure of operating performance that is not defined by U.S. GAAP and should not be considered a substitute for net (loss) income as determined in accordance with U.S. GAAP.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 5:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 5:51 am.

DeltaGen, an AI startup that got its start in Seattle before moving to San Francisco this year, has been acquired by Worker.ai, a latest small-business software manufacturer backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev.

Worker, which rolled out Thursday, acquired all of DeltaGen for an undisclosed price that included a substantial cash component and equity in Worker, DeltaGen co-founder and CEO Rene Bystron told GeekWire.

Bystron joins Worker as co-founder and COO, and nine other DeltaGen employees are coming with him, including co-founders Michal Studnicka and Matus Ondreicka.

Worker, led by co-founder and CEO John Roberts, a former private equity operator based in Raleigh, N.C., is building software that lets small businesses hand off recurring work to AI agents. DeltaGen’s voice technology captures decisions made in conversations and turns them into assigned tasks.

Roberts had been a DeltaGen customer before Worker needed voice technology, Bystron noted. “We could have raised another round and kept building independently, but this gave us the capital and experience to move faster with people we trusted,” he said.

It has been revealed that released in 2024, DeltaGen raised a $1.2 million pre-seed round in early 2025 to build generative AI tools for financial professionals, with a focus on streamlining mergers and acquisitions. The organization relocated from Seattle to San Francisco earlier this year.

“I still love Seattle and miss it like crazy,” said Bystron, who is keeping his apartment in Belltown. “But being closer to the AI founders, customers and investors in San Francisco makes a real difference at this stage. It also didn’t help that Washington has been chipping away at its tax advantage.”.

Timashev, who co-founded data backup giant Veeam, is backing Worker to help small businesses such as manufacturers, service companies and family businesses grow.

According to recent reports, “AI can now give small businesses more capacity without asking already stretched owners to work longer days,” he remarked in a statement. “Worker is my bet on that shift.” The size of his investment was not disclosed.

DeltaGen’s current product is an AI voice platform, which will continue as it’s integrated into Worker. DeltaGen’s AI voice platform will continue as it’s integrated into Worker, which is opening access gradually through a waitlist.

#102. Zipline hits $21.5B valuation as Walmart expands bet on drone delivery

Zipline hits $21.5B valuation as Walmart expands bet on drone delivery

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/05/zipline-hits-21-5b-valuation-as-walmart-expands-bet-on-drone-delivery/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Zipline has raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart, a pair of deals that have raised the autonomous drone delivery and logistics startup’s profile and valuation.
  • Zipline and Walmart reached a fresh multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States.
  • It has been revealed that on the fundraising side, Zipline’s $1.5 billion raise was led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, with participation from Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Tech giant, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P.

Zipline has raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart, a pair of deals that have raised the autonomous drone delivery and logistics startup’s profile and valuation.

Zipline and Walmart reached a fresh multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. The two companies have had a drone delivery agreement since 2021, but this deal is a significant jump from the 21 active drone delivery sites they have together today.

It has been revealed that on the fundraising side, Zipline’s $1.5 billion raise was led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, with participation from Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Tech giant, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest, and Salesforce Ventures. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion.

The manufacturer, which has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software, said it looks to use the funds to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and hire more workers to build out a nationwide drone delivery network.

Founded in 2014, Zipline got its start in Africa, where it used its autonomous drones to deliver blood in Rwanda, and later expanded to Ghana and Nigeria. The California-based firm began its first operations in the U.S. in 2020, ferrying medical equipment and supplies to Novant Health in North Carolina. The following year, it struck a deal with Walmart.

It has been revealed that but it was in 2022 that Zipline’s business really started to take off in the United States. Zipline received its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration that year, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the organization to complete long-range commercial drone deliveries. It has locked in a number of partnerships since then, including with Uber earlier this year.

It has been revealed that zipline now uses its drones to deliver food, retail, agricultural, and health products in five African countries, several cities in the United States, and Japan. Zipline’s home delivery service uses Zipline’s Platform 2 drones, which are designed to carry up to eight pounds and travel to customers within a 10-mile radius. Its larger Platform 1 drones are used for long-range deliveries for enterprise, business, and government that can cover 120 miles round trip.

The firm said Thursday that its share of delivery revenue grew from 10.8% to 34.9% between March and October of this year. This latest funding aims to push that metric even higher.

Arm Holdings does not manufacture a single chip, yet its technology runs inside processors designed by Apple $AAPL, Qualcomm $QCOM, Nvidia $NVDA and Samsung. The manufacturer, based in Cambridge, U.K., sells something less tangible than silicon. It licenses the rules a processor follows and, in many cases, ready-made blueprints for the processor cores themselves. Partner companies turn those designs into finished chips. Contract manufacturers such as TSMC $TSM then fabricate them.

That division of labor lets a company with no factories of its own shape the design of chips that other companies build and sell. Arm leaves the expensive work of building and running fabrication plants to others.

Understanding how Arm chip licensing works starts with two kinds of payment. A firm that wants to use Arm technology generally pays an upfront license fee. It then pays a royalty on each chip it ships. Arm earns money when a partner signs on and again when that partner's products reach customers.

According to recent reports, the rights a company buys vary. Some companies license ready-made core designs and build their chips around them. Others, such as Apple, hold an architecture license that lets them design their own cores to Arm's instruction set. The choice affects how much control a company has over its chip's design. It also sat at the center of a legal dispute between Arm and Qualcomm.

The business has changed hands and leaders in recent years. In September 2020, Nvidia agreed to buy Arm from SoftBank for $40 billion. Jensen Huang, Nvidia's co-founder and CEO, led the organization at the time. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission sued to block the purchase in December 2021. U.K. and EU regulators had also raised concerns. Nvidia abandoned the deal in February 2022. That same month, Rene Haas became Arm's CEO, succeeding Simon Segars. Under Haas, Arm listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ in September 2023, and SoftBank kept a majority stake.

Industry observers note that the 10 slides that follow cover a selection of the pieces that make up the Arm licensing model. They explain what an instruction set architecture is, how the company began and which license types chipmakers choose. They also look at how RISC-V and x86 compete with Arm. Each slide covers one part of what Arm does and can be read on its own.

Arm does not manufacture semiconductors. The manufacturer, based in Cambridge, U.K., creates processor designs and sets the rules those processors follow. It then sells other companies the right to use that work.

It has been revealed that arm owns no chip factories. What it produces is intellectual property — detailed specifications and circuit designs that exist as digital files rather than as physical silicon. A customer receives those files, not a box of finished parts.

Other companies design the chips that carry Arm technology. Apple $AAPL, Qualcomm $QCOM, Nvidia $NVDA and Samsung are among the companies that build chips on Arm's foundation. Each one takes Arm's work as a starting point and turns it into a product of its own.

It has been revealed that A finished processor for a phone or laptop usually contains far more than Arm's contribution. Chip designers combine Arm-based processor cores with their own graphics units, memory controllers and other circuits on a single piece of silicon. The industry calls that combined design a system-on-chip. The Arm portion handles general computing tasks. The rest of the chip reflects each company's own engineering.

It has been revealed that manufacturing is a separate step, handled by yet another manufacturer. When a chip designer finishes its layout, it sends the design to a foundry for fabrication. TSMC $TSM, short for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., is a contract foundry that fabricates chips for other companies. Its customers include many of the same companies that license Arm technology.

Companies that design chips but outsource production are described as fabless. Qualcomm and Nvidia work this way. Arm sits one layer further back in the chain. It supplies the designs that those chip companies start from.

Industry observers note that the three-way split lets each tech giant specialize. Arm concentrates on processor design. Chip companies concentrate on complete products. Foundries concentrate on production technology. A single Arm design can appear in chips from many different companies at the same time.

Arm's revenue comes from that same chain. The company collects money from the businesses that use its technology, not from selling hardware. Its income therefore depends on what its partners design, build and ship.

Arm started in 1990 as Advanced RISC Machines Ltd, a joint venture formed by Acorn Computers, Apple $AAPL and VLSI Technology. The company grew out of processor work at Acorn, a British computer maker. Its name was later shortened to Arm.

Industry observers note that acorn was based in Cambridge, U.K. It was best known for the BBC Micro, a home computer used widely in British schools during the 1980s. For its next generation of machines, Acorn designed its own processor instead of buying one from another supplier. Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber led that design work. The first chip, the ARM1, ran its first code in 1985.

Recent findings suggest that at that stage, the letters ARM stood for Acorn RISC Machine. Acorn used the chip family in its Archimedes computers, launched in 1987. Its simple design also meant the chip drew relatively little power. That trait later suited battery-powered devices.

The 1990 spinout changed who the processor was for. The design moved out of Acorn and into a separate company that could supply it to others. Each of the three founders brought something different. Acorn contributed the processor design and the engineers behind it. Apple was a prospective customer for the chips. VLSI Technology, a U.S. chip company, brought manufacturing capability.

It has been revealed that apple's interest centered on the Newton, its handheld personal digital assistant. The Newton MessagePad, released in 1993, ran on an ARM processor. The device never sold in large numbers. It still gave the young organization an early commercial product in the market.

Robin Saxby became the manufacturer's first chief executive. Under his leadership, the company licensed its designs to other firms instead of building and selling chips itself. In 1998, it listed its shares in London and on Nasdaq $NDAQ.

That period as a listed company ended in 2016. SoftBank, the Japanese technology investor, acquired Arm that year for about £24 billion, or roughly $32 billion. The deal took Arm private.

The Arm instruction set architecture is the list of basic commands an Arm processor understands and carries out. It acts as the shared language between software and hardware. Any program meant to run on an Arm chip must first be translated into those commands.

Industry observers note that an instruction set architecture is usually shortened to ISA. It defines operations such as adding two numbers, loading data from memory or jumping to another part of a program. It also sets out the registers a processor exposes and how memory is addressed.

According to recent reports, the ISA is a specification, not a physical circuit. Two chips can look very different inside and still run the same software, as long as both follow the same ISA.

According to recent reports, this separation explains why compilers matter. A compiler converts code written in a language such as C or Rust into machine instructions for one specific ISA. A program compiled for Arm will not run natively on an x86 processor from Intel $INTC or AMD $AMD. The reverse is also true. Developers either recompile their code for each architecture or rely on translation software.

Sources indicate that the Arm architecture follows RISC, short for reduced instruction set computing. The RISC approach favors a small set of simple instructions that each do one job. Arm is also a load/store design. Arithmetic happens on values held in registers, and separate instructions move data to and from memory.

According to recent reports, the x86 family follows the complex instruction set computing, or CISC, approach. Some of its instructions combine a memory access and a calculation in a single step. Its instructions also vary in length.

Arm's 64-bit era began with Armv8, which introduced the AArch64 execution state. AArch64 instructions are a fixed 32 bits long. A fixed size makes them simpler for a processor to decode. AArch64 also provides 31 general-purpose registers. Armv8 kept a separate 32-bit state, called AArch32, so older software could still run on many chips.

Armv9 was confirmed in 2021 as the next major version of the architecture. It includes Scalable Vector Extension 2, known as SVE2. This feature lets a single instruction work on many pieces of data at once. That style of processing is used in machine learning, image handling and signal processing.

It has been revealed that each new version builds on the previous one rather than replacing it. Software written for earlier 64-bit Arm chips generally continues to run on newer ones.

According to recent reports, arm earns money in two stages. A company pays an upfront license fee to gain access to Arm's designs, and then it pays a royalty on each chip it ships that uses that technology.

Recent findings suggest that the license fee comes first. A chip firm pays it when it signs an agreement, long before any product reaches a customer. The fee buys the right to use Arm's intellectual property. That property can be the instruction set itself or a finished processor core design. With it, the licensee can start building a chip around Arm technology.

Industry observers note that the royalty comes later. It applies to each unit the licensee sells once its chip is in production. A processor in a smartphone, a microcontroller in a household appliance and a server chip in a data center can each generate a royalty for Arm.

Sources indicate that that timing creates a gap between a deal and the money it produces. Designing a chip, verifying it and moving it into manufacturing at a foundry takes time. An agreement signed today may not produce royalty income until the resulting chip ships. That can be years later.

In a recent development, the gap runs the other way at the end of a product's life. A chip design can stay in production for years after launch. Every unit shipped during that time adds to the royalty stream. An older license can keep paying Arm long after the original fee was collected.

It has been revealed that the two streams track different things. License fees reflect how many companies are starting latest projects with Arm. Royalties reflect how many chips those companies actually sell. A licensee that ships chips in large volumes generates more royalty income than one that ships few.

According to recent reports, this structure ties Arm's income to its partners' sales. When companies such as Apple $AAPL, Qualcomm $QCOM, Samsung and Nvidia $NVDA ship more Arm-based processors, Arm collects more in royalties. When demand for those products slows, royalty income slows too.

The specific fees and royalty terms are set in contracts negotiated between Arm and each licensee. The basic two-part model applies whether a tech giant licenses a ready-made core or designs its own cores to Arm's instruction set.

According to recent reports, an Arm architecture license gives a firm the right to design its own processor cores from scratch, as long as those cores run Arm's instruction set. Apple $AAPL and Qualcomm $QCOM are two of the best-known companies that use this route to build custom CPU designs.

Fewer companies take this path than license Arm's ready-made cores. Many Arm customers do not design cores at all. They license finished core designs from Arm and place them inside their chips. An architecture licensee takes on that engineering work itself. It decides how the core is organized internally, how it processes instructions and how it balances speed against power use.

Compatibility is the part that does not change. A custom core built under this license must execute the same Arm instructions as any other Arm processor. Software compiled for Arm can therefore run on it. The licensee gains control over the hardware design without giving up access to the wider pool of Arm software.

According to recent reports, apple is one example. Its M1 chip, confirmed in November 2020, used Apple-designed cores built to Arm's instruction set. The M1 began Apple's shift away from Intel $INTC processors in its Mac computers. The custom approach lets Apple shape its chips around its own devices and operating systems.

In a recent development, qualcomm is another. Its newer custom CPU designs trace back to Nuvia, a chip startup that Qualcomm acquired. Nuvia held its own architecture license with Arm before that deal.

Recent findings suggest that those designs became the subject of a court fight. Arm sued Qualcomm in 2022 in a dispute over which license terms applied to the Nuvia-based designs after the acquisition. A jury in Delaware returned a verdict in December 2024 that went mainly in Qualcomm's favor.

It has been revealed that the case put the terms of an architecture license in public view. It demonstrated that the specific wording of such a license, including which company holds it, can decide who may use a design after a change in ownership.

Industry observers note that the custom route also carries practical trade-offs. Designing a competitive CPU core requires large engineering teams and years of development. The companies that take this path are generally those that want processors tuned closely to their own products rather than a design shared with competitors.

Sources indicate that A core license gives a chip tech giant a finished processor design from Arm that it can place directly into its own chip. Arm sells these ready-made cores in families aimed at different markets. They include Cortex-A for phones, Cortex-M for microcontrollers and Neoverse for servers and data centers.

According to recent reports, the licensee does not have to design a processor core from scratch. It takes Arm's completed core and builds a larger chip around it. That chip can also include graphics processors, memory controllers, wireless modems and other circuits the company designs or sources elsewhere.

Sources indicate that cortex-A is the family built for application processors. These are the chips that run full operating systems, such as Android on a smartphone or tablet. Phone chips often combine several Cortex-A cores of different sizes on one piece of silicon. Larger cores take on demanding work. Smaller cores handle lighter tasks and use less power.

Cortex-M targets microcontrollers. These are small, low-power chips that control a single device or a narrow set of tasks. They show up in appliances, sensors, wearables and industrial equipment. They typically run simple firmware or a small real-time operating system. That is far lighter than the software found on a phone or laptop.

In a recent development, arm also sells Cortex-R cores for real-time systems. These are used where a chip must respond within strict time limits, such as in automotive systems and storage controllers.

Neoverse is Arm's line for servers, cloud computing and networking infrastructure. It is meant for chips that sit in data centers rather than in consumer devices. Amazon $AMZN's Graviton processors, which power servers in Amazon Web Services, are one example. Amazon designs the Graviton chips itself but builds them around Neoverse designs.

Industry observers note that A ready-made core removes a large engineering task from a licensee's project. Creating an original processor core requires a specialized engineering team and extensive testing. Licensing a finished core lets a firm focus its effort on the surrounding circuits instead.

The trade-off is control over the core. A manufacturer using a standard Arm core gets the same core design that its competitors can license. It can still set its product apart through the other components on its chip, its software and its manufacturing choices. Companies that want to change the internal design of the core itself take a different route, through an architecture license.

Arm Flexible Access, introduced in 2019, lets a manufacturer try out a wide range of Arm designs before signing a full license for any of them. Compute Subsystems take a different approach to a related problem: they bundle several Arm designs into one pre-integrated package that a chip team can build around.

Both programs aim to lower the cost and effort of building an Arm-based chip. Under the traditional model, a firm negotiates a license for a specific design and pays for it before engineering work goes far. For a large chipmaker, that is routine. For a startup, a university lab or a small device maker, it can mean committing money before knowing which design fits.

Flexible Access changes the order of those steps. A participant gets access to a portfolio of Arm intellectual property, along with tools and design support. Engineers can evaluate cores, run simulations and build prototypes using several options side by side. The company pays a license fee only for the designs it decides to take into production. Royalties still apply once finished chips ship.

The program is built for companies that have not yet settled on a processor. A maker of connected sensors, for example, might compare several microcontroller-class cores before choosing one. Under a conventional arrangement, each of those comparisons could require its own license negotiation.

Recent findings suggest that compute Subsystems address a later stage of the design process. A modern processor is more than its CPU cores. The cores have to connect to each other, to memory and to other parts of the chip. Integrating and verifying those pieces takes significant engineering time.

A Compute Subsystem packages Arm cores with surrounding components that Arm has already integrated and tested together. A licensee starts from that working foundation instead of assembling the pieces itself. The aim is to cut the integration and verification work a chip team would otherwise do on its own.

According to recent reports, the trade-off is control. A firm that builds on a pre-integrated bundle accepts more of Arm's design choices. A company that assembles individual cores, or designs its own under an architecture license, keeps more room to differentiate its chip.

Nvidia $NVDA's $40 billion agreement to buy Arm from SoftBank, announced in September 2020, was abandoned in February 2022 after regulators in the U.S., U.K. and EU objected. Their central worry was that one chipmaker would own the designs its rivals license.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it as CEO since then. The organization built its business on graphics processors. Those chips later became widely used hardware for training AI models. Buying Arm would have added a widely licensed CPU architecture to a company already known for GPUs.

Recent findings suggest that softBank had owned Arm since 2016. SoftBank does not design or sell chips. Under the proposed deal, Arm would have moved to an owner that designs and sells chips in large volumes. That change sat at the center of the regulatory fight.

Sources indicate that arm's model depends on licensing the same technology to many companies, including firms that compete with one another. Several of those licensees also compete with Nvidia. The deal raised the question of whether Arm could stay neutral under an owner with its own chip products to sell.

It has been revealed that in December 2021, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission sued to block the acquisition. The agency's complaint argued that the merger would give Nvidia control over computing technology and designs that its rivals rely on. The lawsuit meant the deal faced a court process in the U.S. on top of reviews in other jurisdictions.

Industry observers note that regulators in the U.K. and the EU had also raised concerns. Arm's headquarters in Cambridge, U.K., placed the deal under British review. With objections on several fronts, the companies walked away from the agreement. That came about 17 months after the deal was announced.

Industry observers note that the collapse did not end Nvidia's use of Arm technology. Nvidia remains an Arm licensee. Its Grace CPU, designed for data centers, is built on Arm designs. Nvidia kept access to the architecture through the same licensing route that other chip designers use, rather than through ownership of Arm itself.

Industry observers note that rene Haas has run Arm as chief executive since February 2022, when he succeeded Simon Segars. Under Haas, Arm listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ on September 14, 2023, under the ticker ARM, with shares priced at $51.

Sources indicate that haas was promoted from inside the organization. Before becoming CEO, he led Arm's IP products group. IP stands for intellectual property. At Arm, that term covers the processor designs and instruction set rights the company licenses to chipmakers. The group Haas ran was responsible for the products Arm sells to its customers.

Recent findings suggest that earlier in his career, Haas worked at Nvidia $NVDA. Jensen Huang co-founded that firm and serves as its CEO. Nvidia is one of the chip designers that license Arm technology.

Sources indicate that haas took charge in the same month that Nvidia abandoned its agreement to buy Arm from SoftBank. With that sale off the table, SoftBank, which had acquired Arm in 2016, remained the owner. The Nasdaq listing followed in September 2023.

Sources indicate that that listing was an initial public offering. In an IPO, a privately held firm sells shares to outside investors. Those shares then trade on a stock exchange. The $51 figure was the offering price, set before trading began. Once trading opened, the share price was set by buyers and sellers on the market.

Sources indicate that softBank kept a majority stake after the offering. Holding more than half the shares means SoftBank owns more of Arm than all other shareholders combined. Public investors gained a piece of the company, but control stayed with SoftBank.

It has been revealed that the ticker ARM is the short code investors use to buy and sell the stock on Nasdaq. Nasdaq is a U.S. exchange based in New York. Arm's shares trade there even though the company's headquarters are in Cambridge, U.K.

Industry observers note that the listing changed who owns Arm. It did not change the licensing business at the center of the firm. A public listing does add a daily share price. That price gives investors a running measure of how they value the business Haas oversees.

Arm faces competition from two architectures that sit at opposite ends of the licensing spectrum. RISC-V is an open instruction set that companies can use without paying license fees. x86, at the other end, is a closed architecture made by Intel $INTC and AMD $AMD.

Sources indicate that RISC-V began as a project at the University of California, Berkeley. Like Arm, it follows the reduced instruction set computing approach, which relies on a small set of simple instructions. The difference lies in ownership. The RISC-V specification is published openly. Any manufacturer can design a processor that implements it without signing a license with an architecture owner.

Sources indicate that that openness offers a direct alternative to the Arm licensing model. Arm charges companies for the right to use its instruction set and designs. A chipmaker that builds on RISC-V does not pay an architecture owner for the instruction set itself.

Industry observers note that free access to the specification does not mean free chips. A organization choosing RISC-V still has to design its own processor cores or obtain finished designs from another supplier. It also has to make sure compilers, operating systems and applications run properly on the result. That engineering work carries real cost. It is also part of what Arm sells when it offers ready-made designs.

Sources indicate that x86 presents a different kind of competition. Intel created the architecture, and Intel and AMD are its principal makers. The two companies design and sell their own x86 processors. They do not license designs to a wide pool of customers the way Arm does. Decades of desktop, laptop and server software were written for x86. That installed base keeps the architecture entrenched in PCs and in many data centers.

Arm's position against both rivals rests less on any single chip than on its ecosystem. Operating systems, development tools and applications have been compiled for Arm over many years. Software is built for a specific instruction set. A large library of programs that already runs on Arm makes switching away more costly for device makers.

The same principle works against Arm where x86 holds the advantage. Moving PC or server software to Arm requires recompiling it or running it through translation. The contest among these three architectures turns largely on which software already runs where. It also turns on what it costs a chip designer to change.

In a recent development, the Microsoft 365 outage has shown how email dependencies can interrupt business processes even when other functions remain available. Infotech's research note, Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs, covers recovery validation, potential security coverage gaps, and continuity measures for prolonged cloud outages.

ARLINGTON, Va., Nov. 13, 2026 /CNW/ -- In response to the Microsoft 365 outage that began on November 12, Infotech, a global research and API-driven advisory firm, is recommending that CIOs verify the recovery of business-critical workflows, integrations, and security controls before declaring normal operations restored. The firm's newly introduced research note, Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs, also advises organizations to document service disruptions and preserve evidence for potential service level agreement claims.

Recent findings suggest that the outage began Thursday afternoon with Exchange Online mailbox access failures in the Americas and affected functions in Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender. Thursday night, servers that had returned to service failed again under load, and Microsoft added capacity and began rolling back a recent network change. According to the note's midday ET enhancement on November 13, availability was improving, but intermittent problems persisted, and Microsoft had not given a restoration time. At that point, Microsoft had reported no evidence of malicious activity, and the root cause was still under investigation.

According to recent reports, "CIOs need a clear basis for telling the business it can return to normal operations," says Kate Wood, AVP of Research Development at Infotech. "That means knowing which critical processes have been tested, where security coverage still needs checking, and which teams must continue using workarounds. Executive updates should make those outstanding challenges visible so that business teams can initiative their next steps.".

The examples summarized in Infotech's note show contingency aims holding where a manual route existed and stalling where email was the only channel. According to news reports, disruptions included delays to patient referrals and court communications, while some organizations maintained critical operations using other systems or manual procedures. Core Teams messaging and meetings and direct SharePoint file access also remained largely operational, reinforcing the need to assess the specific functions and dependencies supporting each business process.

Recommended Actions for Microsoft 365 Response and RecoveryInfotech advises CIOs to focus on maintaining operations and documenting impacts. IT teams should log unresolved issues and failed workarounds throughout recovery, giving executives a clear view of operating status and creating a record to guide improvements to continuity plans.

The firm's Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs research note groups its recommendations as follows:.

For longer-term readiness, Infotech emphasizes testing continuity procedures against prolonged outages affecting multiple cloud services. Organizations should identify where reliance on a single cloud environment creates shared points of failure and establish independent continuity options where the business impact justifies them.

Additional resources include the firm's Develop a Business Continuity Proposal, Create a Right-Sized Disaster Recovery Plan, and IT Communications Research Center.

#105. AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors

AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/ai-voice-company-wellsaid-retools-for-agents-while-keeping-its-commitment-to-human-actors/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene.
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:56 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 3:19 pm.
  • WellSaid, the AI voice manufacturer that spun out of Seattle’s Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, is reinventing itself for the era of AI agents.

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:56 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 3:19 pm.

WellSaid, the AI voice manufacturer that spun out of Seattle’s Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, is reinventing itself for the era of AI agents.

The tech giant this week launched WellSaid Producer, which connects its voiceover direction tools directly to AI assistants such as Claude and Microsoft Copilot.

Instead of logging into WellSaid’s app, corporate users can ask the AI assistant for a voiceover to accompany a training or marketing video, for example. The assistant then sends the script to WellSaid, which generates the audio using its licensed voices.

It’s part of a broader overhaul and refocusing of WellSaid’s business. The manufacturer has spent the past two years moving away from individual people to focus on businesses. It now has about 30 employees, down from more than 70 in late 2024.

Along the way, WellSaid has turned profitable, CEO Benjamin Dorr told GeekWire.

In a recent development, “We’ve been calling this adventure Act II, so I guess Producer is Scene I,” Dorr remarked. Extending the metaphor, he acknowledged that “the cast is a lot smaller,” and noted that many of the company’s leaders are new, recruited from his own network.

It has been revealed that dorr joined WellSaid as CFO in 2024 and became CEO in spring 2025. He was previously chief operating officer of Cordial, a San Diego marketing software company, and earlier worked in tech investing and banking at The Carlyle Group, Morgan Stanley and Citi.

He succeeded Brian Cook, the former Nintex CEO who led WellSaid for about 16 months. Co-founder Matt Hocking, who was CEO until early 2024, remains on WellSaid’s board and is now chief product officer at Type, an AI startup for creative writers.

Dorr’s leadership team includes three executives who also worked at Cordial and joined WellSaid since last fall: Natalia Holts, senior vice president of finance and accounting; Jeni Bishop, vice president of marketing; and Bryan Keefer, vice president of product.

Chris Johnson, the chief product and technology officer, and co-founder Mixail Petrochuk, the chief technology officer, remain from the earlier leadership team.

The tech giant is maintaining its longstanding practice of building its AI voices from recordings of professional voice actors, who are paid royalties when businesses use their voices to narrate training courses, marketing and other videos.

WellSaid drew widespread attention in 2023 when it created a spot-on synthetic version of former NPR “Planet Money” host Robert Smith’s voice, with his permission, as part of a special series by the popular radio show and podcast.

Recent findings suggest that its customers include nearly half of the Fortune 100, according to WellSaid. The company’s licensing approach stands out in a sector that remains a wild west, with models trained on audio scraped from the internet and tools used to fake the voices of public figures.

“We view [Model Context Protocol], and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago.”.

How it works: Producer uses Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a standard way for AI assistants to connect to other software. It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Atlassian’s Rovo, and Dorr noted AI agents that work on their own will be able to use it by the end of the year.

Recent findings suggest that companies using WellSaid Producer can set up style guides so brand names, acronyms and technical terms are pronounced the same way in every file. When a product name or script changes, Producer can upgrade every affected voiceover in one pass, and each finished file carries a record of its license.

WellSaid also indicates it’s the first voiceover platform to generate audio natively at 48 kHz, the standard for film and video. WellSaid will continue to offer its Studio app for customers who want to work there directly.

Sources indicate that producer is sold as a platform, with customers committing to buy credits for minutes of finished, licensed audio. WellSaid’s licenses today are mostly one-time buyouts, but Dorr said the manufacturer wants to price more like the traditional voiceover industry, where an ad voiceover is priced by its length, reach and how long it runs.

The strategy: Dorr said voiceover is just one step in a larger production process, and many creative tools now include basic AI speech that is sometimes good enough. He sees AI agents letting companies combine specialized tools from vendors they trust, instead of settling for one all-in-one app.

“We view MCP, and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago,” he stated.

Voice actors: Actors’ revenue share rates won’t change when their voices are used through AI assistants, Dorr mentioned. One of his first moves as CEO was to open the manufacturer’s stock option pool to its top 20 voice actors, and WellSaid is building a voice actor advisory board, with more details expected to be released in December. Dorr said WellSaid plans to add custom royalty structures, “potentially all the way up to union rate cards.”.

According to recent reports, customers will also be able to use voice models from other companies alongside WellSaid’s own, for features its models lack, such as one voice speaking several languages. The voices still come from WellSaid’s actors under its licensing terms. “We’re not moving from our position on commercial licensing,” Dorr said.

According to recent reports, the business: WellSaid has about 1,000 business customers, and its top 25 customers each spend more than $100,000 a year, Dorr mentioned. Moving away from individual owners “did flatten our growth compared to a lot of AI companies growing at astronomical rates,” he said.

By comparison, rival ElevenLabs, which has offered voice generation through Claude since 2025, was valued at $22 billion in a recent employee tender offer.

According to recent reports, wellSaid raised venture debt from Multiplier Capital in March but didn’t disclose the amount. Its most recent disclosed equity funding was a $10 million Series A round in 2021 that valued the tech giant at $65 million, according to PitchBook.

Dorr noted debt was a better fit than equity for a “modestly growing and, now, profitable manufacturer,” at a time when investors’ growth expectations “have become extreme.” He said WellSaid will consider other financing in 2027 “if our ambitions outstrip our ability to reinvest.”.

#106. Aina’s smart ring has a screen, a joystick, and a mic so you can talk to AI agents

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words)

Aina’s smart ring has a screen, a joystick, and a mic so you can talk to AI agents

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/05/ainas-smart-ring-has-a-screen-a-joystick-and-a-mic-so-you-can-talk-to-ai-agents/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hardware startup Aina released a smart ring today that features a screen, a joystick, and a mic so that you can talk to your agents and take notes.
  • The startup, which raised $5.5 million in July, is positioning the ring as a controller of sorts for both AI and non-AI apps.
  • The company previously made Mirage, a three-key controller that let you invoke buttons based on the app on your Mac’s screen.

Hardware startup Aina released a smart ring today that features a screen, a joystick, and a mic so that you can talk to your agents and take notes. The $399 ring has a speaker so you can take calls using it as well.

The startup, which raised $5.5 million in July, is positioning the ring as a controller of sorts for both AI and non-AI apps.

The company previously made Mirage, a three-key controller that let you invoke buttons based on the app on your Mac’s screen. For instance, if you were on a Google Meet call, you could map keys to camera on/off, mic mute/unmute, or to leave the meeting.

Aina has baked in lessons from that device to create the fresh ring, which it’s simply calling “AI ring.” Using its mic, you can take notes, send a prompt to agents, set reminders, and dictate notes on your Mac using Wispr Flow or the startup’s own dictation engine.

In a recent development, now, there are already smart rings in the market that do similar things, like the Pebble Index 01, Sandbar Stream, Oasis, and Natura, which is probably why Aina has added more controls and functionality to stand out. Its ring comes with a speaker so that you can take calls, and there is a screen, which lets you see notifications from your phone or which apps you are controlling.

For navigation, there is a joystick, and it also supports gestures, so that it can trigger different actions based on what’s on your Mac or phone’s screen. The ring also lets you control music or even smart home devices like Apple TV.

I have used the ring for a few days, and it feels like a smartwatch in a ring format, with more controls. I can get notifications and reply to them. It surfaces my meetings; I can call Uber if I want to get a ride home.

Sources indicate that it’s easier to use Apple TV’s remote itself, but the Aina ring proved useful the couple times I couldn’t find the remote. Granted, a lot of the software and features are still being fleshed out, so it’s hard to figure out where such a device ring might sit in my daily usage, but it is squarely aimed at folks who are surrounded by digital devices and AI applications.

“Phones and laptop screens were designed for an age of browsing where you think about opening apps. For interacting with proactive agents, we need a better interface, and that is what we had in mind while designing Aina,” Apoorv Shankar, Aina’s founder, told TechCrunch over a call.

It has been revealed that companies are trying to cater to programmers and AI enthusiasts with specialized hardware that could help them harness different agents. This includes OpenAI’s experimental keyboard and Rabbit trying to position itself as a controller. The hope with such hardware is that enough people will have multiple agents running to invest in specific gadgets to keep tabs on them.

Industry observers note that aina’s ring goes on preorder starting Thursday at early-bird pricing of $399, and the company looks to start shipping the device in January 2027. Once the early-bird period ends, the ring will cost $499.

#107. How GTA Online makes money: free updates, Shark Cards and 10 moments

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18 min read (3557 words)
General

How GTA Online makes money: free updates, Shark Cards and 10 moments

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read | Sumber: https://qz.com/how-gta-online-makes-money

💡 Key Takeaways
  • How GTA Online makes money comes down to Shark Cards, free updates and console and PC re-releases, traced here through 10 moments from 2013 to 2022.
  • GTA Online gives away its new content and sells the currency players spend inside it.
  • That arrangement explains how GTA Online makes money.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How GTA Online makes money comes down to Shark Cards, free updates and console and PC re-releases, traced here through 10 moments from 2013 to 2022.

GTA Online gives away its new content and sells the currency players spend inside it. New missions, vehicles, properties and game modes arrive as free updates. Many of the biggest items in those updates carry steep prices. Players pay those prices in GTA$, an in-game currency they can either earn through play or buy with real money.

That arrangement explains how GTA Online makes money. It turned a multiplayer mode into a business built on content that players never pay for directly. Each new update gives players something else to spend on. Each purchase helps fund the next round of free updates.

Sources indicate that the mode came from Rockstar Games, the studio that developed Grand Theft Auto V, and Take-Two Interactive $TTWO, its publisher and parent manufacturer. GTA V went on sale Sept. 17, 2013. Take-Two reported that the game passed $1 billion in sales within its first three days. That figure covers GTA V as a whole, not GTA Online on its own. The online mode opened on Oct. 1, two weeks later, inside a game that had already reached a large audience.

In a recent development, the start was rough. Connection failures and characters that would not save marked the first weeks. Rockstar gave affected players GTA$500,000 as an apology. From there the model took shape one piece at a time. Shark Cards, added in the weeks after launch, gave players a direct way to buy GTA$. Heists, businesses and a casino added new things to do and new things to buy. Releases on newer consoles and PC kept bringing fresh players into the same online world.

The 10 slides that follow are a selection of those moments and mechanisms, arranged in chronological order. They run from the October 2013 launch to the March 2022 release on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR|S. That release arrived alongside a latest subscription called GTA+. These slides are not a ranking, and they are not the complete story. Each one covers a specific revision, release or business decision in the mode's history.

GTA Online opened on Oct. 1, 2013, two weeks after Grand Theft Auto V went on sale on Sept. 17. The online mode was not sold separately. It arrived as part of a game that players had already bought.

According to recent reports, rockstar Games developed both the story campaign and the online mode. Rockstar North, the studio's team in Edinburgh, Scotland, led the work. Take-Two Interactive $TTWO published GTA V and is Rockstar's parent firm.

GTA V first went on sale for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. GTA Online opened on those same two consoles. On those consoles, a single session held up to 16 players.

The story campaign follows three playable leads: Michael, Franklin and Trevor. Their story plays out in Los Santos, a fictional city modeled on Los Angeles, and in the countryside of Blaine County. GTA Online uses the same map. Players build their own character instead of controlling the three story leads.

Industry observers note that that shared setting tied the two halves of the package together. Players who spent the first two weeks in the campaign already knew the streets, the vehicles and the layout of the city. The multiplayer side did not have to introduce a new world.

Some faces carried over as well. Characters from the campaign, including Lamar Davis and Lester Crest, hand out jobs to online players. Those jobs sit alongside races, deathmatches and other modes that pit players against each other or put them on the same team.

Sources indicate that progress in the online mode runs on two tracks. Reputation points, known as RP, raise a character's rank and unlock weapons, clothing and activities. GTA$, the in-game currency, pays for cars, apartments and gear. Completing jobs earns both.

The release order also shaped how the mode found its audience. GTA Online did not need to attract buyers on its own. Its potential player base was everyone who already owned GTA V on PlayStation 3 or Xbox 360.

GTA Online launched in October 2013 with serious connection failures and lost character saves. Rockstar Games answered by giving affected players GTA$500,000 in in-game currency as an apology.

It has been revealed that the trouble began on day one. GTA Online went live on Oct. 1, 2013, on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. Those were the same consoles Grand Theft Auto V had reached two weeks earlier. Players opened the online mode from inside GTA V and did not buy it separately. Many could not connect at all. Others got in, only to find the game had failed to save the characters they had built.

According to recent reports, lost saves struck at the core of the mode. GTA Online characters are created by players and are separate from Michael, Franklin and Trevor, the three protagonists of the GTA V story mode. Each one is a persistent character who earns money, buys property and climbs in rank over time. A failed save erased that progress. A player who lost a character in the first week had to start again from the beginning.

Rockstar released patches over the following weeks to address the connection and save problems. The compensation was part of that recovery. Instead of cash refunds, the studio paid players in GTA$, the fictional currency used throughout GTA Online. GTA$ exists only inside the game and cannot be exchanged back into real money.

It has been revealed that the payment fit the way the mode works. Players spend GTA$ on cars, weapons, apartments and other items in Los Santos, the game's fictional version of Los Angeles. Apartments also serve as a base, with garage space for the cars a player collects. A payment of GTA$500,000 gave affected players a head start on those purchases.

Recent findings suggest that the broken start did not end GTA Online. The mode recovered from its October 2013 failures and kept its players. Rockstar went on to support it with new content for years.

It has been revealed that shark Cards let GTA Online players spend real money to receive GTA$, the in-game currency. That currency buys the cars, weapons, apartments and clothing sold inside the game. The cards form the direct link between GTA Online's virtual economy and real-world revenue.

Sources indicate that rockstar Games added Shark Cards in the weeks after GTA Online opened on Oct. 1, 2013. The online mode came included with Grand Theft Auto V at no extra charge. The cards gave Rockstar a way to earn money from players after the initial game sale.

Sources indicate that the cards are sold in tiers named after sharks, including Red Shark, Great White Shark and Megalodon. Larger tiers deliver more GTA$ for a higher price. Megalodon takes its name from an extinct prehistoric shark and sits at the top of the range.

The purchase itself is simple. A player picks a card, pays in real currency and sees the GTA$ added to their in-game balance. Cards can be bought through a platform's digital storefront or through the store menu inside the game.

The GTA$ is then spent at in-game shops and on the game's fictional websites. Legendary Motorsport, the in-game site for high-end cars, is one example. Property and vehicle purchases go through these same menus whether the money was earned or bought.

Shark Cards do not unlock a separate catalog. GTA$ bought with a card is the same currency players earn by completing jobs, missions and races. A player who never spends real money can reach the same items by playing longer.

Sources indicate that that earn-or-buy choice defines how the cards work. Players with limited time can skip hours of repeated jobs. Players with more time can earn the same currency without paying.

It has been revealed that take-Two Interactive $TTWO, Rockstar's publisher and parent firm, reports this kind of ongoing in-game spending under a category it calls recurrent consumer spending. The cards turned GTA Online into a product that could keep earning money long after a player bought the base game.

The Heists update arrived in GTA Online on March 10, 2015, about a year and a half after the mode opened. It added cooperative, multi-stage robberies that a crew plans and carries out together. Each stage feeds into a final job.

Heists were not upcoming to the Grand Theft Auto series. The single-player campaign of Grand Theft Auto V is built around them, with its three protagonists planning and pulling off large scores. Online players waited until 2015 for a version of that structure designed for groups.

It has been revealed that the patch shipped with five heists: The Fleeca Job, The Prison Break, The Humane Labs Raid, Series A Funding and The Pacific Standard Job. Each one follows the same basic pattern. A crew completes a set of setup missions, then attempts a finale that carries the main payout. Setup missions range from stealing vehicles to collecting equipment the finale depends on.

Recent findings suggest that most of the heists call for four players. The Fleeca Job, the first in the sequence, needs only two. Lester Crest, a character from the story mode, offers the jobs.

Planning happens on a board inside a high-end apartment. A player has to own one of these properties to host a heist. Apartments are bought with GTA$. The host also pays the setup costs before any missions begin.

It has been revealed that that host acts as heist leader. The leader assigns players to roles and decides what share of the final payout each crew member receives. Roles change from one job to the next. One player might fly or drive while another hacks a security system or provides cover.

In a recent development, the upgrade came out on PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, PlayStation 4 and Xbox One at the same time. It gave every console version of the online mode the same new long-form content on the same day. Grand Theft Auto V had not yet reached PC at that point.

Rockstar Games releases newly introduced GTA Online content as free updates instead of selling it as paid expansions. Revenue comes afterward, when players spend GTA$ on the vehicles, weapons, properties and other items those updates introduce.

In a recent development, that arrangement differs from a paid add-on. A player downloads an update at no cost and gets access to its new missions and activities. Many of the items inside it carry an in-game price tag, though. To own them, the player needs enough GTA$ in the bank.

It has been revealed that there are two ways to get that money. Players can earn GTA$ by completing missions, races and other jobs inside the game. They can also buy it with real money through Shark Cards, the currency packs Rockstar sells for GTA Online. Both routes lead to the same GTA$ balance.

This structure links each content release to Shark Card sales. A newly introduced car or property gives players a specific GTA$ target. A player short of that total can keep earning through jobs or buy the difference with real money. The revision costs nothing, but what it unlocks can lead to a real-money purchase.

Industry observers note that free updates also keep the online player base together. Paid expansions divide players into those who bought the add-on and those who did not. When every player receives the same content, newly introduced missions and items reach the whole audience at once. A new vehicle or activity is open to everyone who plays GTA Online, not only to buyers of a specific pack.

Rockstar used the paid model with its previous game. Grand Theft Auto IV received two paid episodic expansions in 2009, The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony. GTA Online took a different path, offering its additions as downloads with no separate charge.

It has been revealed that the approach has carried through the mode's major releases. Large cooperative missions, property and business updates and later content drops all arrived without a purchase price of their own. Each one added newly introduced items with GTA$ prices attached.

Three GTA Online updates pushed players toward buying property and running criminal businesses inside the game. They were Executives and Other Criminals in 2015, Gunrunning in 2017 and After Hours in 2018.

Each update added expensive properties and businesses. Players paid for them with GTA$, the currency used throughout the mode. The updates themselves came free. The price sat inside the game rather than at the point of release.

Before these releases, a GTA Online player mostly took on jobs and finished them. The business updates added ownership to the mode. A player now had property to buy and an operation to run.

Executives and Other Criminals came first. As its name signals, the update cast the player as the head of a criminal enterprise. The player was no longer only a lone operator picking up work.

Gunrunning followed in 2017. Its theme was arms dealing. It carried the ownership idea into a second line of illegal work.

It has been revealed that after Hours arrived in 2018 and became known as the nightclub patch. Its new content revolved around a nightclub that players could own. That made it the third business type in the series, after the criminal enterprise and the arms trade.

Price links the three releases. Each one put a large GTA$ cost on the property or business at its center. Those costs gave players a concrete target for the currency. A player saving for a business had a specific item in mind, not just a growing balance.

It has been revealed that the updates also built on one another. Each arrived as a newly introduced business type rather than a replacement for the last one. A player who bought into an earlier business did not lose it when the next enhancement arrived. Each release instead added another option to spend GTA$ on.

From 2015 to 2018, owning an in-game business became a recurring theme of new GTA Online content rather than the subject of one release.

Grand Theft Auto V and GTA Online were re-released for PlayStation 4 and Xbox One in November 2014, then for PC on April 14, 2015. Each fresh version brought another group of players into the same online mode.

According to recent reports, the console re-release came about 14 months after the original game went on sale. The PC version followed roughly 19 months after that first launch.

According to recent reports, none of these releases created a separate online game. Players on the upcoming platforms entered the same GTA Online that had opened in October 2013. They joined its missions, its in-game economy and its GTA$ currency.

Recent findings suggest that that meant newcomers did not arrive at a blank start. By November 2014, the mode had been running for more than a year. Its missions, prices and GTA$ economy were already in place when the new versions went on sale.

That structure ties each re-release to the mode's revenue model. GTA Online earns money when players use real money to buy GTA$ through Shark Cards. Those cards were already on sale when the latest versions arrived. A new platform adds more people who can make those purchases. Rockstar Games did not have to build a new multiplayer game to reach them.

The PC release also followed a major content drop. The Heists update came out on March 10, 2015. The PC version arrived about five weeks later. PC players joined with the cooperative heist missions already live. They could plan and carry out those multi-stage missions with other players from their first weeks. The newest content and the newest platform reached players within weeks of each other.

Sources indicate that rockstar Games developed each version, and Take-Two Interactive $TTWO published them. The same online mode carried on across every format. Players on every system bought the same GTA$ and spent it on the same kinds of in-game items. Each release widened its audience without changing how it made money.

The Diamond Casino & Resort enhancement arrived in GTA Online in July 2019. It added an in-game casino that served two roles: a social space where players could gather, and a fresh source of content inside the mode.

In a recent development, rockstar Games, which develops GTA Online, released the enhancement nearly six years after the multiplayer mode opened on Oct. 1, 2013. Take-Two Interactive $TTWO publishes the game and is Rockstar's parent company.

Many earlier updates centered on missions, properties and businesses. The casino offered a different kind of content. It was not another job to finish or another business to manage. It was a destination inside the game world where players could meet and spend time together.

The update also sits at a specific point in the mode's timeline. It came the year after After Hours, the 2018 nightclub update. It arrived before the Cayo Perico Heist, which followed in December 2020.

In a recent development, like other GTA Online content, the casino reached players as a free upgrade to the existing mode. It was not sold as a separately priced expansion.

The Cayo Perico Heist rolled out in GTA Online on Dec. 15, 2020. It was set on a private island, and players could complete it alone or with a group.

Sources indicate that that solo option broke from how GTA Online heists had worked before. The Heists update of 2015 was built around a crew. Its missions were cooperative jobs that players planned and carried out together. Cayo Perico made those other players optional rather than required.

According to recent reports, the change removed a practical hurdle for players without a regular crew. A heist no longer depended on finding teammates, matching schedules or waiting for others to join. Players who preferred tech giant could still bring a group along.

The design widened the audience for a major piece of content. A crew-only heist served players who already had organized groups. A heist one person could finish was open to anyone who logged in to the mode.

Recent findings suggest that the private island also gave GTA Online a newly introduced setting for a heist. Earlier updates had expanded the mode with businesses, properties and a casino. Cayo Perico added a destination of its own.

Recent findings suggest that the release date shows how long the mode had stayed active. The heist arrived more than seven years after GTA Online opened on Oct. 1, 2013. It came about five years and nine months after the original Heists update of March 10, 2015. It followed the Diamond Casino & Resort update of July 2019 by about 17 months.

Those gaps point to a mode that kept growing rather than being replaced. Rockstar Games added a fresh heist to the same online world that had opened in 2013, instead of moving players to a new game.

Cayo Perico reached players the same way as other GTA Online content. Rockstar Games delivered it as a free enhancement. Players did not buy the heist as a separate expansion. Like other GTA Online activities, the heist paid out in GTA$, giving solo players a way to earn the currency through play.

GTA V and GTA Online arrived on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR|S on March 15, 2022. Rockstar Games paired the release with two changes to how players could get into the online mode and pay for it. The first was a standalone GTA Online download on PlayStation 5. The second was a subscription called GTA+.

Industry observers note that the release moved GTA Online onto a newer generation of home consoles than the PS4 and Xbox One versions of November 2014. The mode had opened on Oct. 1, 2013, so the new versions came about eight and a half years into its life. Rockstar Games developed the game, and Take-Two Interactive $TTWO publishes it.

The standalone version split the multiplayer mode off from the GTA V story campaign. On PS5, a player could download GTA Online by itself instead of buying the full game. For the first three months after release, that download was free.

According to recent reports, the free entry point fit a game that earns its money from spending after the download. Every upcoming player joins the same online world, where GTA$ pays for vehicles, properties and businesses. Players can earn that currency through play or buy it with real money through Shark Cards. Under that model, the revenue comes from what players buy once they arrive, not from the download itself.

Sources indicate that rockstar introduced GTA+ the same month. It is a paid subscription service for GTA Online that bills players on a recurring basis. It added another way to pay, alongside buying the game and buying Shark Cards.

Both changes kept the core of the model intact. New content stays free to play, and spending happens inside the game. The standalone download widened the way in, and GTA+ added a recurring way to pay once there.

#108. Industry News: Leaving VMware starts as a cost decision, but day-two operations decide whether it works

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words)
