Industry News: Leaving VMware starts as a cost decision, but day-two operations decide whether it works

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/13/data-management-layer-eases-vmware-exit-kubernetes-teams-kubeconna/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprises leaving legacy hypervisors are finding that moving virtual machines is only half the job, and that a portable data management layer often decides whether a Kubernetes migration succeeds.
  • According to recent reports, that shift is playing out at Mouser Electronics Inc., one of the world’s largest electronic components distributors.
  • It has been revealed that “It doesn’t matter if we’re running containers or VMs, we’re running it on the same foundation, which really works well,” Waller said.

Enterprises leaving legacy hypervisors are finding that moving virtual machines is only half the job, and that a portable data management layer often decides whether a Kubernetes migration succeeds. Rising license costs are pushing teams to run containers and VMs on one platform.

According to recent reports, that shift is playing out at Mouser Electronics Inc., one of the world’s largest electronic components distributors. After running Red Hat Inc.’s OpenShift for containers for five to six years, the manufacturer is now building a production OpenShift Virtualization cluster to move workloads off Broadcom Inc.’s VMware, according to Ronald Waller (pictured, left), systems engineer at Mouser.

It has been revealed that “It doesn’t matter if we’re running containers or VMs, we’re running it on the same foundation, which really works well,” Waller said. “Because we can manage those things with the same tool sets and same skill sets.”.

It has been revealed that waller and Jon Owings (right), assistant vice president of global technical presales, cloud and data services, at Portworx by Everpure, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how the data management layer helps run VMs and containers on OpenShift. (* Disclosure below.).

According to recent reports, kubernetes already serves as a common control plane for containerized AI workloads, and pulling VMs onto it extends that standard to older applications. Everpure Inc., which rebranded from Pure Storage Inc. this year as part of a data-centric pivot, positions Portworx as the matching abstraction for storage.

It has been revealed that “Kubernetes provides that ubiquitous control plane for all of them, and that’s what customers are asking us for,” Owings said. “The one thing that was missing was the same thing but for data.”.

The learning curve for VMware administrators moving to Kubernetes is steep, and Waller has climbed it over the last year. Storage turned out to be the easy part when he built Mouser’s proof-of-concept cluster, he explained.

“I asked the storage guy what I needed from him, and he handed me a user ID and an API key. I went to Portworx Central. I configured my spec for the operator and the storage cluster, created my secret, and boom, Portworx Enterprise did everything else on the backend,” Waller stated. “I didn’t even have to think about it.”.

Portworx keeps building for that use case. It made data management native to OpenShift in May and unveiled new AI and VM capabilities at KubeCon. For teams following Mouser’s path, Owings sees the exit from a legacy hypervisor as a chance to rethink day-two operations on a data management layer that travels across clouds and Kubernetes distributions.

“What can we change that we didn’t like about the last 15 years? … Were we dependent on a vendor? Were we dependent on shell scripts or PowerShell?” Owings noted. “We have this great opportunity to do something new, and Kubernetes has that open API that allows you to be creative.”.

A YC startup is putting $1M behind 5 unsolved materials science problems for AI

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/05/a-yc-startup-is-putting-1m-behind-five-unsolved-materials-science-problems-for-ai/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Discovered Materials, a months-old San Francisco startup using AI models to find new substances for building advanced chips, announced a million-dollar challenge for AI models to solve five critical problems in materials science.
  • While frontier AI models have solved a remarkable series of outstanding mathematics problems and made progress in the life sciences, they have yet to truly plumb the complex physics in advanced materials.
  • Recent findings suggest that “It’s more difficult to specify problems clearly in materials science because it’s not like math, where you have a very specific definition and can get to a yes or no,” said Advaith Sridhar, a co-founder of Discovered Materials, which was part of Y Combinator’s spring 2026 batch.

Discovered Materials, a months-old San Francisco startup using AI models to find new substances for building advanced chips, announced a million-dollar challenge for AI models to solve five critical problems in materials science.

While frontier AI models have solved a remarkable series of outstanding mathematics problems and made progress in the life sciences, they have yet to truly plumb the complex physics in advanced materials.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s more difficult to specify problems clearly in materials science because it’s not like math, where you have a very specific definition and can get to a yes or no,” said Advaith Sridhar, a co-founder of Discovered Materials, which was part of Y Combinator’s spring 2026 batch. “We came to this discussion [wondering], what are the grand challenges in this field? How do we know AI is making progress?”.

Though materials science doesn’t have an equivalent of the Millennium Prize Problems, Discovered Materials recruited an advisory group of academics at leading global universities to spell out five open problems. The company is offering a pool of prizes, worth $1 million in total, for solutions to the problems.

“Across materials science, there are phenomena we observe but cannot explain,” Felipe Jornada, a Stanford professor who helped develop the challenges, said in a statement. “Explaining these phenomena would improve our understanding of physics, and the answers would directly shape how we build electronics, store energy, and manufacture the materials of the future.”.

In a recent development, before announcing the challenges, Discovered Materials turned frontier lab models loose on them, giving AI agents internet access and other resources to work autonomously for days. The models spent several days on each problem without making much headway. Still, it’s easy to imagine OpenAI or Anthropic attempting to one-shot them with significantly more compute or a newer model.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s not particularly a concern to us whether we find it, or someone else finds it, or a professor finds it, or the frontier labs find it,” Sridhar noted. “The reason we’re putting out these challenges is because we want them to serve as the goalposts. If you go and solve these challenges, we are deepening our understanding of materials and how things around us behave.”.

Tracking efforts to solve the problems will show “whether the models are climbing in this domain,” he added.

The challenge also reflects the changing nature of scientific inquiry as AI proves capable of uncovering insights and techniques human researchers didn’t anticipate. With solutions apparently easier to find than ever, the questions become more notable.

Industry observers note that “This is a latest way of thinking about science, where we come up with the verification and the challenges first, and then we let somebody come up with the ideas that explain the problem,” Sridhar remarked. “Knowing what are the right questions to ask is not trivial and very difficult in this domain, so this is where the professors have really helped us shape what are the right questions we should be asking.”.

Discovered Materials’ main focus is developing new materials for use in semiconductors; the startup partners with chip giants on research projects while also funding its own scientific efforts. When the firm unveiled its seed round in August, Sridhar told TechCrunch that he hoped the company would generate a useful material within a year.

“Those timelines have accelerated a little bit,” he indicates today. “I’m more confident now that we will be able to find these industrially useful materials in a timeline shorter than a year.”.

#110. Latest Update: Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (509 words)

Latest Update: Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/lila-bio-lands-3-65m-grant-to-fight-pulmonary-hypertension-with-ai-designed-proteins/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:31 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 2:31 pm.
  • Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension.
  • The condition causes high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:31 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 2:31 pm.

Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension.

The condition causes high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs. It forces the heart to work harder and can lead to heart failure.

The Small Business Innovation Research fast-track award supports Lila’s efforts to develop a protein-based treatment for pulmonary hypertension that could be given by injection a few times a year.

Recent findings suggest that “Most approved therapies only manage symptoms, such as vasodilators,” Lila CEO Jake Kraft remarked in a LinkedIn post, referring to drugs that widen blood vessels. “Lila Bio is pursuing clinically-validated, disease-modifying mechanisms that treat the underlying disease.”.

According to recent reports, the funding comes from the NIH’s National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is divided into two phases. The initial $605,981 will support early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates. The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will support further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients.

Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023. Both worked as postdoctoral fellows at UW’s Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. Lila raised $10 million in seed funding the year it was founded. Last year, it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop treatments for solid tumors.

It has been revealed that the startup uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins through two platforms. One supports the pulmonary hypertension project, creating long-acting injectable drugs designed to remain active in the body for weeks or months. The other focuses on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to deliver radioactive isotopes to tumors.

“We want to bring medicines to patients,” Kraft told GeekWire in an earlier interview. “We don’t want to just say we’ve designed a protein, but we actually want to be able to say we’ve saved lives.”.

Microsoft 365 Outage: CIOs Should Verify Recovery Across Workflows and Security Controls, Indicates Infotech

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Microsoft 365 outage has shown how email dependencies can interrupt business processes even when other functions remain available.
  • According to recent reports, ARLINGTON, Va., Nov.
  • The outage began Thursday afternoon with Exchange Online mailbox access failures in the Americas and affected functions in Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender.

The Microsoft 365 outage has shown how email dependencies can interrupt business processes even when other functions remain available. Infotech's research note, Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs, covers recovery validation, potential security coverage gaps, and continuity measures for prolonged cloud outages.

According to recent reports, ARLINGTON, Va., Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- In response to the Microsoft 365 outage that began on November 12, Infotech, a global research and API-driven advisory firm, is recommending that CIOs verify the recovery of business-critical workflows, integrations, and security controls before declaring normal operations restored. The firm's newly introduced research note, Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs, also advises organizations to document service disruptions and preserve evidence for potential service level agreement claims.

The outage began Thursday afternoon with Exchange Online mailbox access failures in the Americas and affected functions in Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender. Thursday night, servers that had returned to service failed again under load, and Microsoft added capacity and began rolling back a recent network change. According to the note's midday ET patch on November 13, availability was improving, but intermittent issues persisted, and Microsoft had not given a restoration time. At that point, Microsoft had reported no evidence of malicious activity, and the root cause was still under investigation.

"CIOs need a clear basis for telling the business it can return to normal operations," says Kate Wood, AVP of Research Development at Infotech. "That means knowing which critical processes have been tested, where security coverage still needs checking, and which teams must continue using workarounds. Executive updates should make those outstanding issues visible so that business teams can proposal their next steps.".

The examples summarized in Infotech's note show contingency intends holding where a manual route existed and stalling where email was the only channel. According to news reports, disruptions included delays to patient referrals and court communications, while some organizations maintained critical operations using other systems or manual procedures. Core Teams messaging and meetings and direct SharePoint file access also remained largely operational, reinforcing the need to assess the specific functions and dependencies supporting each business process.

Recommended Actions for Microsoft 365 Response and RecoveryInfotech advises CIOs to focus on maintaining operations and documenting impacts. IT teams should log unresolved issues and failed workarounds throughout recovery, giving executives a clear view of operating status and creating a record to guide improvements to continuity plans.

The firm's Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs research note groups its recommendations as follows:.

For longer-term readiness, Infotech emphasizes testing continuity procedures against prolonged outages affecting multiple cloud services. Organizations should identify where reliance on a single cloud environment creates shared points of failure and establish independent continuity options where the business impact justifies them.

Additional resources include the firm's Develop a Business Continuity Plan, Create a Right-Sized Disaster Recovery Plan, and IT Communications Research Center.

#112. 10 major tech outages of the 2020s, from Google to CrowdStrike to Cloudflare

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16 min read (3150 words)
AI & Tech

10 major tech outages of the 2020s, from Google to CrowdStrike to Cloudflare

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read | Sumber: https://qz.com/major-tech-outages-2020s

💡 Key Takeaways
  • These 10 major tech outages of the 2020s, from Google to CrowdStrike to Cloudflare, show how a single fault could disrupt flights, payments and everyday apps.
  • One routine change inside one company can stop planes from taking off, block card payments at checkout and silence messaging apps at once.
  • It has been revealed that this selection covers 10 outages, ordered by date from December 2020 to November 2025.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 major tech outages of the 2020s, from Google to CrowdStrike to Cloudflare, show how a single fault could disrupt flights, payments and everyday apps.

One routine change inside one company can stop planes from taking off, block card payments at checkout and silence messaging apps at once. That is a common thread running through the major tech outages of the 2020s. The failures in this list did not come from one dramatic attack on the internet. Several began with something ordinary: a quota setting, a configuration revision, a maintenance job or a software release.

It has been revealed that this selection covers 10 outages, ordered by date from December 2020 to November 2025. It is not a ranking. No single source measures these incidents against one another. Some hit consumer apps used for chat and video. Others reached airports, hospitals, banks and emergency phone lines.

The causes repeat. Google $GOOGL traced its December 2020 sign-in failure to an automated quota system. Meta $META noted a configuration change on its backbone routers took Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp offline in October 2021. The company also said it was not a malicious attack. Cloudflare said its November 2025 disruption came from an internal change rather than an attack. In the U.S., the Federal Aviation Administration's preliminary finding on its January 2023 Notice to Air Missions failure pointed to a damaged database file. Amazon $AMZN Web Services' post-event summary on its October 2025 cloud outage cited a DNS problem in its Northern Virginia region.

Sources indicate that another pattern is concentration. Several of these incidents started at one provider and spread to the services built on top of it. A software bug at Fastly, a content delivery network, knocked out sites including Reddit $RDDT and Gov.uk in 2021. A faulty CrowdStrike $CRWD patch in July 2024 crashed Windows machines at airlines, hospitals and banks. Microsoft $MSFT estimated that 8.5 million Windows devices were affected. Telecom failures followed a similar shape on a national scale. Rogers in Canada and Optus in Australia each had network failures that disrupted emergency calling.

Sources indicate that each slide that follows explains what failed, when it happened and what is known about its cause. Where a organization or agency published an incident report or public explanation, the slide names it and keeps to what that organization remarked.

Read together, the 10 cases span social and consumer apps, cloud platforms, content delivery networks, telecom carriers, security software and the U.S. flight-notice system.

On Dec. 14, 2020, Google $GOOGL's sign-in system failed for roughly 45 minutes, and Gmail, YouTube and Google Drive stopped working for users who were logged in. Google's incident report traced the failure to its automated quota system, which cut the capacity of its User ID Service.

The outage hit services that look separate to the people using them. Gmail handles email. YouTube streams video. Google Drive stores files. All three depend on Google confirming who the user is before anything else happens. When that check failed, the products built on top of it failed along with it.

Sources indicate that that check is called authentication. It is the step in which a service confirms an account's identity before granting access to it. Google runs one shared account system across its consumer products. A single Google account opens Gmail, YouTube, Drive and the company's other services. The design spares people from managing a separate login for each product. It also means a fault in the sign-in layer reaches every product that relies on it.

Sources indicate that the User ID Service is part of that sign-in layer. Once the automated quota system reduced its capacity, authentication requests arrived without enough resources to be processed. Requests that could not be verified went unanswered. The email, video and file services waiting on them stopped responding.

Recent findings suggest that quota systems are a standard tool in large computing operations. They divide capacity among internal services and cap how much any one of them can draw. That keeps a single service from consuming resources that others need. In this case, the automated system responsible for allocating resources was the component that took them away.

Recent findings suggest that the episode shows that a safeguard can become a single point of failure. The quota system governed a service that every signed-in product needed, so its error did not stay in one place. Email, video and file storage failed together during the same short window. Products that look independent shared one hidden dependency, and that dependency decided whether any of them worked.

On June 8, 2021, a software bug in Fastly's content delivery network knocked major websites offline, including Reddit $RDDT, The New York Times and the U.K. government's Gov.uk. The bug was triggered when a Fastly customer changed a configuration setting.

According to recent reports, A content delivery network, or CDN, is a distributed system of servers that stores copies of web content in many locations. When a reader requests a page, the CDN serves it from a server close to that reader instead of from the publisher's origin server. That setup makes pages load faster. It also absorbs traffic spikes that could overwhelm a single site.

Industry observers note that the same setup creates a dependency. Publishers that route their traffic through a CDN rely on it to deliver their pages at all. When the CDN fails, readers can lose access to a site even though the site's own servers keep running.

According to recent reports, that is the pattern this outage followed. The problem did not start inside Reddit, The Latest York Times or Gov.uk. It started at the shared provider that sat between those sites and their readers.

In a recent development, the change itself came from one customer, not from Fastly. CDN customers typically control the settings for their own content, such as which files are stored and for how long. In this case, one customer's adjustment exposed a flaw in Fastly's software. The effect reached sites far beyond that customer's own.

Fastly said 85% of its network was back to normal within 49 minutes. The tech giant then issued a fix for the bug.

The affected sites serve very different audiences. Gov.uk is the U.K. government's central website for public services such as tax, benefits and passports. Reddit hosts user-run discussion communities. The New York Times publishes news and opinion. A government portal, a discussion platform and a news publisher all went offline because they depended on the same provider.

Sources indicate that facebook $META, Instagram and WhatsApp went offline together for about six hours on Oct. 4, 2021. Meta traced the outage to a configuration change on its backbone routers.

Industry observers note that A backbone is the internal network that carries traffic between a company's data centers. Routers on that network direct data from one location to another. Meta stated the faulty change cut its data centers off from one another.

Recent findings suggest that the effect reached beyond the firm's own facilities. Meta stated the same change made its network unreachable from the wider internet. People who opened any of the three apps during the outage could not connect to the servers behind them.

The three services failed at once because they depended on the same manufacturer network. One change to that shared infrastructure took a social network, a photo-sharing app and a messaging service offline together.

Meta placed the cause inside its own operations. The organization said the outage was not a malicious attack. In its account, the trigger was a change it made to its own routers rather than an intrusion from outside.

In a recent development, rogers Communications lost wireless and internet service across Canada on July 8, 2022. The nationwide failure followed a maintenance update to the organization's core network. It disrupted debit payments and some emergency calling.

In a recent development, rogers is one of Canada's major telecommunications carriers. It sells mobile phone aims and home internet service. Businesses also depend on its network to move data. A failure at that scale reached well beyond people trying to place a call or load a web page.

Sources indicate that A carrier's core network is the central part of its system. It directs traffic between cell towers, home connections and the wider internet. A problem at that level can take down wireless and wired service at the same time. That is what happened in July 2022, when both failed together across the country.

Debit payments were among the most visible effects. Card terminals at checkouts need a working network connection to approve a transaction. With that connection gone, debit purchases at affected businesses could not go through.

Some emergency calling was also disrupted. For some people in Canada, the outage cut off a route to emergency services as well as everyday phone and internet use.

It has been revealed that service did not return all at once. Rogers' wireless and internet services came back over the following day.

The Federal Aviation Administration's Notice to Air Missions system failed on Jan. 11, 2023, and the failure led to a nationwide ground stop on departing domestic flights in the U.S. The FAA's preliminary finding pointed to a damaged database file.

It has been revealed that the outage did not take down a website or a messaging app. It held aircraft at airports across the country. The system that failed is one of the ways pilots learn about conditions that could affect a flight before departure.

A NOTAM alerts pilots and other flight personnel to conditions at an airport or along a route. Common examples include closed runways, temporary airspace restrictions and navigation aids that are out of service. Each notice is short and written with standard abbreviations. Flight crews and dispatchers review the relevant notices while planning a trip.

Recent findings suggest that NOTAMs are not only an American tool. The International Civil Aviation Organization sets the standards that member countries use to issue them.

Preflight review is a legal duty in the U.S. Federal Aviation Regulations require the pilot in command to become familiar with all available information concerning a flight before it begins. NOTAMs are one part of that information.

Recent findings suggest that the FAA changed the name of these notices in December 2021. They had been known as Notices to Airmen. The agency adopted the gender-neutral Notice to Air Missions and kept the NOTAM abbreviation.

A ground stop holds aircraft at their departure airports instead of letting them take off. Flights already in the air are outside its scope. The FAA uses ground stops at individual airports for reasons such as weather or congestion.

According to recent reports, the January 2023 order was different in scope. It applied to the whole country rather than a single airport. It was widely reported as the first nationwide halt of its kind since the September 2001 attacks.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft $MSFT 365 services, including Teams and Outlook, went down on Jan. 25, 2023, along with parts of the Azure cloud platform. Microsoft remarked a change to its wide-area network disrupted connectivity.

That explanation places the trigger in Microsoft's network rather than in any one app. A fault at the network level can affect every service whose traffic crosses that network. Workplace tools and cloud infrastructure went down on the same day.

A wide-area network, or WAN, links computers and data centers spread over long distances. A local network typically covers a single building or campus. For a cloud provider, the WAN connects its facilities to one another. It also connects them to the people and businesses using its services.

In a recent development, microsoft 365 is the company's subscription bundle of productivity software and online services. Teams is its workplace chat and video meeting app. Outlook is its email and calendar service.

According to recent reports, azure is Microsoft's cloud computing platform. Businesses use it to run their own software and store data. A disruption to Azure can reach the customers of companies that build on it, not only the people who use Microsoft's own apps.

Industry observers note that about 10 million Optus customers in Australia lost service on Nov. 8, 2023, in an outage that lasted roughly 12 hours. Optus attributed it to a software upgrade at one of its international peering networks.

According to recent reports, that account places the starting point outside Optus' own network, on a network connected to it. A peering network is a separate network that links directly with a carrier's network so the two can exchange traffic. Carriers use these direct connections to pass data to and from other parts of the internet.

Optus mentioned that after the upgrade, routing information exceeded preset safety limits on its core routers. Routing information is the data routers use to decide where traffic should go. A preset safety limit caps how much of that data a router will accept. Network operators set these limits in advance as a guard against overload.

Industry observers note that core routers sit at the center of a carrier's network. They carry traffic for the customer base as a whole rather than for a single neighborhood or cell tower. A problem at that layer can reach customers far from the point where it started.

Emergency calling was also affected. Failures in emergency calls were widely reported during the disruption. In Australia, emergency services are reached by dialing 000.

Those failures drew regulatory scrutiny of Optus.

On July 19, 2024, a defective content update to CrowdStrike $CRWD's Falcon sensor crashed computers running Microsoft $MSFT Windows. Microsoft estimated that 8.5 million Windows devices were affected.

Sources indicate that microsoft published that estimate in a blog post on its official site. It also put the number in context. The company mentioned the affected machines made up less than 1% of all Windows machines. That share still included computers at airlines, hospitals and banks.

In the airline industry, the effects reached passengers directly. Delta Air Lines canceled flights.

CrowdStrike is a cybersecurity organization, and Falcon is its endpoint security platform. An endpoint is an individual device, such as a laptop, desktop or server, that connects to a network. The Falcon sensor is the software installed on those devices. Organizations deploy tools like this to detect and block threats on each machine. Falcon also runs on macOS and Linux, but computers running those systems were not affected by this update.

It has been revealed that microsoft was not the source of the defect. The faulty update came from CrowdStrike, a separate company whose software runs on Windows. Security software typically receives frequent updates so it can respond to new threats. In July 2024, an update meant to help protect machines instead left them unable to run.

Unlike outages that leave a website or cloud service unreachable, this one stopped the computers themselves from running.

Recent findings suggest that amazon $AMZN Web Services suffered a major outage on Oct. 20, 2025, in its us-east-1 region in Northern Virginia. AWS's post-event summary traced the failure to a DNS problem affecting the endpoint for DynamoDB, its database service.

In a recent development, the disruption reached well beyond Amazon. Snapchat, Venmo and Fortnite were among the apps and services that reported problems. Each depends on infrastructure that AWS runs.

Sources indicate that DNS, short for Domain Name System, works like the internet's address book. It translates a name that software asks for into the numerical address of the machine that answers. An endpoint is the address a program contacts to reach a cloud service. When DNS cannot return a working address for that endpoint, software that calls the service cannot find it. That can happen even if the servers behind it are still running.

DynamoDB is a managed database that AWS runs on behalf of its customers. Applications use it to store and retrieve data without operating their own database servers. A lost connection to it can stop an app from loading accounts, records or settings.

According to recent reports, AWS's summary located the root of the problem in DynamoDB's own DNS management. It described a race condition. In software, a race condition occurs when two or more processes act on the same data at nearly the same time. The outcome then depends on which one finishes first. If the timing goes the wrong way, the system can end up in a state its designers did not intend.

Industry observers note that A cloud region is a cluster of data centers in one geographic area. Many unrelated companies build their products on the same regional services. A fault in one widely used component can therefore surface at a messaging app, a payments app and a video game at the same time. AWS lets customers spread workloads across several regions. That design can limit exposure to a failure in any one of them.

A database permissions change inside Cloudflare caused the firm's outage on Nov. 18, 2025. The change made a feature file used by its bot management system grow beyond its expected size. That oversized file crashed the software that routes traffic across Cloudflare's network. Sites including X $TWTR and OpenAI's ChatGPT were affected.

Recent findings suggest that cloudflare sits between many websites and the people trying to reach them. Customer sites route their incoming requests through its network, which provides services such as content delivery and protection against attacks. Visitor traffic passes through Cloudflare's systems before it reaches the site itself. A failure in that layer can make a working website unreachable.

According to recent reports, bot management is one of the Cloudflare products that operate inside that layer. It tries to separate automated traffic, such as scrapers and credential-stuffing bots, from requests made by people. The system depends on a feature file, a set of data the software consults when it evaluates incoming requests. On Nov. 18, that file became the point of failure.

The damage did not stay inside one Cloudflare product. The crash hit the component that moves requests through the network, not a single add-on feature. Websites that relied on Cloudflare to carry their traffic lost that path to their visitors. The fault sat inside Cloudflare's systems, not on those sites' own servers.

Industry observers note that cloudflare stated the outage was not an attack. The tech giant attributed it to an internal change of its own. The bot filtering at the center of the incident is itself one of the tools Cloudflare offers to screen out unwanted traffic.

Sources indicate that cloudflare later published a post-incident explanation. It traced the outage step by step, from the permissions change to the oversized file to the crash in the traffic-routing software. That sequence demonstrates how a change to database permissions reached all the way to the system that carries visitor requests.

  • Pei has teased an AI-first device for some time and the tech giant has also noted that it looks to release a pair of AI-linked smart glasses, as well as earbuds with AI integrations.

Nothing, the smartphone startup behind the distinctive Nothing Phone, is working on an AI product, but what it is remains unclear.

On Wednesday, CEO Carl Pei posted on X that the company’s first “AI-native product” ships in December. “It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no newly introduced screen, and it couldn’t have been an app,” Pei wrote.

Pei has teased an AI-first device for some time and the tech giant has also noted that it looks to release a pair of AI-linked smart glasses, as well as earbuds with AI integrations.

Recent findings suggest that pei’s description adds up to a screenless non-app that uses AI? He also calls it a “productivity tool.” Adding further mystique to the announcement, Pei seems to downplay any link to AI wearables.

In a recent development, “The whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life,” Pei wrote. “I admire the boldness, but I read this moment differently.”.

No firm release date has been announced, but Nothing fans should know soon enough what the company has in store for them.

Industry News: Rand Fishkin’s Seattle game studio serves up first trailer for ‘The Snackbar at the End of the World’

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/rand-fishkins-seattle-game-studio-serves-up-first-trailer-for-the-snackbar-at-the-end-of-the-world/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 11, 2026 at 11:21 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:21 am.
  • If the eventual release of “The Snackbar at the End of the World” is a full-on meal for video game fans, news this week of the game’s first trailer should at least suffice as an appetizer.
  • Sources indicate that seattle-based Snackbar Studio, co-founded by SparkToro founder Rand Fishkin and his wife, writer Geraldine DeRuiter, unveiled its debut title and Steam page on Tuesday.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 11, 2026 at 11:21 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:21 am.

If the eventual release of “The Snackbar at the End of the World” is a full-on meal for video game fans, news this week of the game’s first trailer should at least suffice as an appetizer.

Sources indicate that seattle-based Snackbar Studio, co-founded by SparkToro founder Rand Fishkin and his wife, writer Geraldine DeRuiter, unveiled its debut title and Steam page on Tuesday. The hand-drawn narrative adventure RPG puts players in the role of a chef trying to save a struggling family restaurant in a magical version of 1960s Italy.

Industry observers note that the studio now plans to launch the game late next year, after originally targeting the second half of 2026. Snackbar raised $2.15 million from 38 angel investors two years ago, and the project began four years ago, according to Fishkin. The team includes five co-founders (Fishkin, DeRuiter, game designer Nicolas Kraj, lead programmer Miriam Cabrera and art director Francesco Mazza) plus about 10 contractors.

Sources indicate that in the studio’s description on Steam, players forage for ingredients in the “forbidden wilds” outside town, battling explosive tomatoes, chaotic zucchini and vendetta-driven poultry. They then cook dishes back at the restaurant before a tyrannical mayor known as the Sindaco can shut it down. The game mixes combat and stealth with cooking mini-games based on real-world recipes.

The trailer is set to “’O surdato ’nnammurato,” a classic Neapolitan song performed by professional musicians recruited by the studio’s music director. Fishkin stated he and DeRuiter both cried the first time they heard it.

It has been revealed that fishkin is best known in Seattle tech circles as co-founder of SEO software tech giant Moz and audience research startup SparkToro, and he more recently debuted Alertmouse, a tool for tracking online mentions. DeRuiter, a writer and author, is Snackbar’s head writer.

In a LinkedIn post this week, Fishkin recalled telling DeRuiter during the COVID lockdown that he wanted to fulfill a childhood dream of making a video game. Her reply: “Don’t wait. Do it now. I’ll do it with you.”.

In the same post, he noted the game’s themes include found family and fighting fascism “even when there’s no hope you’ll win.” He called it a love letter to DeRuiter’s small family village in the mountains outside Naples, to that era of Italy, to video games, and to the many people both of their families have lost in recent years.

According to recent reports, moments like hearing that song come often in the work, Fishkin noted, such as when a new feature clicks or a new animation brings DeRuiter’s characters to life. He has always loved art without being good at any form of it. “I may not be able to create art, but I can enable it,” he said. “What a wonderful feeling.”.

It has been revealed that there have been lows, too. The team spent its initial 18 months on the project with a contract agency that didn’t work out, losing money with nothing to show for it. Fishkin is glad they kept going, “even when it felt financially irresponsible.”.

In a recent development, the game is entirely human-made, and Snackbar’s no-AI stance is firm. “Geraldine hates AI with the fury of a thousand suns,” Fishkin said. He once suggested, just once, that she use Google’s AI Mode to find a synonym, and she was mad at him for the rest of a six-hour flight home from Philadelphia. Even if players, the rest of the team and the games media were fine with AI (and they’re not), DeRuiter alone would make it a no-go, he said.

Recent findings suggest that still ahead are 10 to 12 months of finishing the game’s content, playtesting, bug fixing, marketing and launch prep. Fishkin called it daunting, but mentioned team members have done it many times before, “even though it’s our first rodeo.”.

It has been revealed that fishkin is still juggling Snackbar with SparkToro and Alertmouse, and describes his role at the studio as mostly oversight and management. SparkToro is growing again, and Alertmouse recently hit a big milestone in annual renewals with high retention. He and his Alertmouse co-founders are putting more money into the company to fund growth.

Balancing the three roles is a challenge, he said, but only rarely completely overwhelming. “Like this week.”.

#117. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure shakes AI industry’s foundations

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure shakes AI industry’s foundations

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read | Sumber: https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-ceo-jensen-huangs-abrupt-departure-shakes-ai-industrys-foundations/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof.
  • Industry observers note that honeypot or not, the Chinese executive/accused spy with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted an affair this week should have been a flashing red light to him.
  • According to recent reports, in the end, all that, and maybe more to come, was just too much for Nvidia’s board to bear despite the commanding position Huang (pictured) held not only at Nvidia but in the entire artificial intelligence industry.

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof.

Industry observers note that honeypot or not, the Chinese executive/accused spy with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted an affair this week should have been a flashing red light to him. So should fraternizing with one of your own VPs — and reportedly another employee too!

According to recent reports, in the end, all that, and maybe more to come, was just too much for Nvidia’s board to bear despite the commanding position Huang (pictured) held not only at Nvidia but in the entire artificial intelligence industry. Indeed, the speed with which he resigned — spectacularly stupid as his behavior was — still makes me wonder if there are other shoes to drop, especially on the legal or national security fronts. Market researcher SemiAnalysis thinks it came down to pressure from the U.S. intelligence community that’s very unhappy Nvidia chips have apparently been smuggled to China.

Huang was something of an AI puppet master, providing the chips and software to power the entire industry as well as seemingly unlimited cash to fund and backstop everyone from AI leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic to innumerable cloud compute providers worldwide. No single person inside or outside Nvidia seems likely to fill that role.

According to recent reports, however, Nvidia really is much more than Jensen Huang. Interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress helped craft the financial arrangements that in part put Nvidia at the center of AI — though for what it’s worth, Huang himself wasn’t a fan lately. Some of his direct reports such as high-performance computing chief Ian Buck seem quite capable of carrying on, if perhaps not with Huang’s panache. One tech giant is never one person, and shouldn’t be. I expect a less centralized Nvidia going forward, whoever’s at the top.

More than that, AI is much more than Jensen Huang, and it will continue to be going forward. It’s easy to forget that although Huang brilliantly helped create this fresh wave, AI and its enablers also are what made him a rock star. But that time is now over. Nvidia and certainly the AI industry shouldn’t be depending on one person to keep everything afloat anyway.

Sources indicate that the reverberations of his sudden and shocking departure will continue to echo for a long time to come across Nvidia, its investors watching hundreds of billions of market cap evaporate, legions of Jensen fanboys and the entire artificial intelligence ecosystem. A lot of people are hoping desperately that he didn’t just pop the AI bubble (though others are hoping he did). It seems unlikely this will be the pin, but we’re dealing with a lot of unlikely things in the past week or so, for better and worse, and this shock is clearly rattling the foundations.

Recent findings suggest that all that managed to overshadow what otherwise would be the big news this week: Anthropic went on the road to pitch its initial public offering. It’s hoping to raise more than $64 billion and keep the AI trade humming in Nvidia’s near-term absence. Looks like next Thursday is the big day.

According to recent reports, and it’s not the only good news in AI — that is, if the IPO is successful. After a difficult month on the stock front, uber neocloud CoreWeave provided a pleasant AI surprise with upside earnings and guidance, lifting its shares almost 25% Wednesday. AI chipmaker Cerebras’ shares rose almost 18% in late trading Thursday on positive guidance and a Microsoft deal. Cisco Systems said demand is strong for AI infrastructure, even if investors shrugged, and chipmaking equipment supplier Applied Materials said AI boosted demand as well.

Not everyone fared so well, though. Dutch neocloud Nebius saw its shares drop almost 17% Thursday as it lowered its outlook despite close to sevenfold revenue growth in the last quarter. The stock drop no doubt was partly because of Nvidia, which is, of course, an investor. CoreWeave –yes, another Nvidia investment — lost 7% Thursday.

Sources indicate that couple of really big outages out there: first, Microsoft Outlook, grounding a lot of office workers, then the whole damn U.S. air traffic control system, grounding thousands of flights.

Sources indicate that sovereignty is on many enterprise buyers’ lips these days, the notion that enterprises need a way to assert more control over their technology estates and protect their customers’ data. TheCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin just completed the first of a series of reports on how to approach sovereignty, this one focused on the hyperscale cloud providers.

According to recent reports, the software orchestrator Kubernetes has become boring, but as SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier said at this week’s KubeCon in Salt Lake City, that means it’s a success — with lessons for AI developers. “A lot of things that are happening in cloud-native that were involved in microservices in Kubernetes world are actually the same challenges in the AI world,” he noted.

It has been revealed that IBM has been working hard on quantum computing for a long time now, but at its Quantum Developer Conference in Chicago this week, it indicated significant progress, according to Dave Vellante. Its goal now is to show actual industry impact by 2028, a laudable goal that presents a lot of challenges, Dave wrote in his Special Breaking Analysis this week.

Next week the SC26 high-performance computing conference comes to Chicago, and theCUBE and theCUBE Research will be onsite with interviews and analysis. There’s also Microsoft Ignite in San Francisco. And earnings next week include… Nvidia! Bring the popcorn.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, most of it not salacious, along with analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:.

It has been revealed that breaking Analysis: Sovereign or not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide.

Breaking Analysis: AI cyber resilience and the trust gap.

Dario goes overboard with AI claims ahead of Anthropic’s IPO — the same guy who claims AI could also extinguish us. Somebody give him back his Xanax! Also, I really don’t think mental illness is a compute problem.

Gartner forecasts AI infrastructure spending to represent 59% of total global AI spending in 2027.

Gartner also forecasts AI will drive a net increase of 1.7M jobs by 2030 That one number hides a lot of job losses and especially job “transformations,” and not to throw shade on Gartner in particular, anyone betting on AI’s impact out in 2030 is barely more than guessing.

United Airlines is banning AI bots from booking flights, following Amazon and Walmart doing the same thing for shopping. Aren’t travel and shopping a prime use case for AI agents? But they’re still trying: OpenAI rolls out ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its ‘dots’ AI agents to make purchases for users.

Getting too close to Trump was a mistake, says Nick Clegg. Amen. We’ve already seen them trying to backpedal, starting with Palantir CEO Alex Karp, who had the audacity to call his company “progressive.” Dude, sit down.

#118. AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words)
AI & Tech

AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/aws-gives-developers-a-free-local-stand-in-for-its-cloud-built-from-scratch-by-ai-agents/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:52 am.
  • AWS states its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the firm is touting that as a selling point.
  • AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:52 am.

AWS states its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the firm is touting that as a selling point.

AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine. It’s built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. Developers and AI coding agents can use it to test code without a network connection and without paying for the real cloud.

In a recent development, the tool addresses a problem that coding agents such as Amazon’s Kiro and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made worse. Agents can write code faster than teams can test it against the real cloud. Agents check their work by running the code and reading the results, over and over, and doing that in the cloud adds delays and costs.

The emulator lets them run that loop on a developer’s own machine.

In an ironic or perhaps appropriate twist, AWS used AI agents to build the emulator. Agents also maintain it, testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find.

It has been revealed that “The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” wrote Matt Goldberg, the AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, in a blog post.

Goldberg compared his agents to himself as a kindergartner, too young to hold a crayon properly, who got yelled at by classmates for ruining a group drawing of dinosaurs. The problem wasn’t bad intent, he wrote, just a lack of competence. The answer, for agents, is clearly defined areas to fill in.

“I think agents also need coloring books,” he wrote.

The agents work from AWS’s public API models, which describe how each service should behave, and check their work against the real AWS cloud.

The agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. One writes “fidelity tests” — real-world scenarios such as creating a queue, sending a message and deleting the queue — and checks each against real AWS. A second runs those tests against the emulator and files challenges for failures, and a third fixes them, one agent per problem.

Recent findings suggest that every change passes through an automated gate where other agents check coding standards and security. Goldberg wrote that hundreds of agents now fix thousands of problems a day.

The project started as a weekend experiment, inspired by Anthropic’s demonstration earlier this year in which a team of Claude agents built a C compiler. Goldberg gave Kiro a three-step prompt and got a passable first version of Amazon SQS, AWS’s message queuing service, in 15 minutes.

By the end of the weekend, Goldberg wrote, Kiro had built a rough version of the rest of AWS, with obvious gaps, and his team started using it to test its software that Monday.

It has been revealed that swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI and emerging tech, tied the project to a lesson he described to GeekWire in June. He spent four nights babysitting Kiro as it tried to rebuild a replication engine he and Allan Vermeulen built by hand nearly 20 years ago.

Once he gave the agent a spec and a way to test its work, the job took about two hours.

“When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct,” Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on CTO Werner Vogels’ blog.

It’s the same idea behind Amazon’s recent move to rewrite its engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code.

The emulator has limits. Devin Pratt, an IDC analyst, told InfoWorld that it doesn’t yet simulate throttling, outages or differences in which services and features are available by region, and that it doesn’t sandbox the code it runs. The agents’ backlog of known gaps is public, in a GitHub folder called “things-that-do-not-work.”.

Other AWS emulators exist, most notably LocalStack, which this year put its free version behind an account requirement and limited it to noncommercial use. AWS released its emulator for free under CC0, a public domain dedication, with the full commit history on GitHub.

The company indicates it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

Industry observers note that BEIJING, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Yiren Digital Ltd. (NYSE: YRD) ("Yiren Digital" or the "Organization"), a leading company specializing in financial technology and artificial intelligence innovation across multiple industries in China and global markets, today confirmed that it received a letter dated October 20, 2026, from the Latest York Stock Exchange (the "NYSE") notifying the Company that it was not in compliance with the NYSE's continued listing standard under Section 802.01C of the NYSE Listed Company Manual (the "Price Criteria") for the average closing price of the Company's American depositary shares (the "ADSs") was below US$1.00 per ADS over a consecutive 30-trading-day period.

The Firm has six months following receipt of the notification (the "Cure Period") to regain compliance with the Price Criteria. The Company can regain compliance during the Cure Period if, on the last trading day of any calendar month during that period, its ADSs have both a closing price of at least US$1.00 per ADS and an average closing price of at least US$1.00 per ADS over the 30-trading-day period ending on that day. In the event that at the expiration of the Cure Period, both a $1.00 closing price and a $1.00 average closing price over the preceding 30 trading days are not attained, the NYSE will commence suspension and delisting procedures.

The notification does not immediately affect the Tech giant's business operations. The Company's ADSs will continue to be listed and traded on the NYSE subject to compliance with other applicable continued listing standards. The Company will continue to monitor the trading price of its ADSs and consider available measures to regain compliance.

Troy Hartless, who in September 2025 added president to his role as chief revenue officer, will return to serving solely as CRO.

HANGZHOU, China, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Greenland Technologies Holding Corporation (Nasdaq: GTEC) ("Greenland" or the "Company"), a technology developer and manufacturer of electric industrial vehicles and drivetrain systems for material handling machineries and vehicles, today revealed that the Company received a written notification (the "Notification Letter") from the Nasdaq Stock Market LLC ("Nasdaq") on November 10, 2026, notifying the Company that it is not in compliance with the minimum bid price requirement set forth in the Nasdaq Listing Rules for continued listing on the Nasdaq.

It has been revealed that nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2) requires listed securities to maintain a minimum bid price of US$1.00 per share, and Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A) provides that a failure to meet the minimum bid price requirement exists if the deficiency continues for a period of 30 consecutive business days. Based on the closing bid price of the Tech giant's Class A ordinary shares for the 30 consecutive business days from September 29, 2026 to November 9, 2026, the Company no longer meets the minimum bid price requirement.

In a recent development, the Notification Letter does not impact the Manufacturer's listing on the Nasdaq Capital Market at this time. In accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A), the Company has been provided 180 calendar days, or until May 10, 2027, to regain compliance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2). To regain compliance, the Company's Class A ordinary shares must have a closing bid price of at least US$1.00 for a minimum of 10 consecutive business days. In the event the Company does not regain compliance by May 10, 2027, the Company may be eligible for additional time to regain compliance or may face delisting.

Industry observers note that the Company's business operations are not affected by the receipt of the Notification Letter. The Company intends to monitor the closing bid price of its Class A ordinary shares and may, if appropriate, consider implementing available options, including, but not limited to, implementing a share consolidation, to regain compliance with the minimum bid price requirement under the Nasdaq Listing Rules.

#123. Seattle VC firm Ascend closes $17M fund to back ‘Third Act’ startups in physical AI and hardware

AI & Tech

Seattle VC firm Ascend closes $17M fund to back ‘Third Act’ startups in physical AI and hardware

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/seattle-vc-firm-ascend-closes-17m-fund-to-back-third-act-startups-in-physical-ai-and-hardware/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 7:15 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:30 am.
  • Venture firm Ascend has closed a $17 million third fund and landed its first institutional investor, in what founder Kirby Winfield calls the toughest fundraising market for small venture firms in 15 years.
  • In a recent development, the Seattle-based firm invests at the earliest stage, often writing the first check into a startup.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 7:15 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:30 am.

Venture firm Ascend has closed a $17 million third fund and landed its first institutional investor, in what founder Kirby Winfield calls the toughest fundraising market for small venture firms in 15 years.

In a recent development, the Seattle-based firm invests at the earliest stage, often writing the first check into a startup. It was the first investor in Overland AI, the maker of autonomous military vehicles, and an early backer of subsea geothermal startup Endurance Energy, among others.

Ascend Fund III will back more physical AI startups building robots, energy systems, defense technology and other ventures that blend software and hardware — part of a larger bet on what the Ascend team likes to call Seattle’s “Third Act.”.

Winfield said raising a third fund in this market highlights that Ascend has “arrived on the national stage,” along with Seattle’s rise as a hub for this new class of startups. He said the firm’s track record puts it in the same league as the country’s top seed investors.

“We are not just some nice guys in the corner of the country helping out our neighbors,” said Winfield, who works closely with Jen Haller, Ascend partner and chief of staff, and Nate Bek, a principal at the firm.

In a recent development, who’s backing the fund: The newly introduced institutional investor is FirstLook Partners, a firm that invests in smaller venture funds. Josh Porter, FirstLook’s co-founder and managing partner, stated the firm, which is “very bullish on the Seattle ecosystem,” looked at several startup markets outside San Francisco and New York and met many investors in Seattle, “but all roads kept leading back to Kirby.”.

Porter said Winfield has “lived the founder journey” and has “the operational chops to sit across the table from a founder and empathize with what they’re going through.”.

The rest of the fund comes from family offices, founders who have sold companies, and more than a dozen founders of Ascend portfolio companies.

Industry observers note that A tough market for small funds: Ascend’s raise comes as smaller venture firms struggle to bring in fresh money. Their investors, mostly wealthy individuals and family offices, are waiting longer for returns from earlier funds.

Just 211 newer venture firms closed at least one fund through the end of September, down from 927 in all of 2022, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. Established firms took a record 88.2% of the money raised by U.S. venture funds in the first nine months of the year, the report found. Porter remarked smaller firms have to show “a right to exist and a right to win deals.”.

Ascend launched its first fund in 2019 and ultimately raised $15 million. Its second fund closed at $25 million in 2023. The firm generally operates in the $15 million to $25 million range and writes the same size checks regardless of fund size, Winfield said.

“We think Kirby knows his place in the larger ecosystem, knows the value he brings to the table, and has sized his fund accordingly,” Porter said.

It has been revealed that the firm has already drawn about 60% of the money committed to Fund III. GeekWire first reported that the firm was raising the fund in April 2025, based on filings at the time. Endurance was one of the firm’s first investments from the newly introduced fund, in mid-2025.

Ascend’s track record: Winfield started Ascend after two decades in leadership roles at four startups. He described the first fund as a proof of concept that “stumbled into some unicorns,” including Fabric, an e-commerce software firm that was valued at $1.5 billion in 2022. Ascend was in its first round.

It has been revealed that with its second fund, Ascend moved away from consumer and marketplace investing to focus on enterprise AI and deep tech. Its most successful investments from that fund, according to Winfield, include Overland AI, Sabi, Yoodli and Zocks.

After Ascend’s first checks, its portfolio companies have gone on to raise more than $1.5 billion from investors including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer, Founders Fund, Khosla and Lightspeed, according to Ascend.

In a recent development, ascend’s second and third funds rank in the top 10% of funds of $50 million or less, based on current valuations of their portfolio companies, Winfield mentioned, citing figures Ascend shared with its investors at its annual meeting. The firm didn’t disclose specific returns or how much cash it has returned to its investors.

In a recent development, what Ascend looks for: The firm looks for ideas that seem too difficult, too boring, too confusing or too small for substantial multistage venture firms to evaluate. Ideally, Winfield mentioned, its founders are doing something that makes Series A investors “a little bit nervous.”.

According to recent reports, that’s why Ascend hasn’t made many more defense tech investments since backing Overland, he mentioned. Valuations for well-known founders in the sector have soared as more investors have piled in.

“The time to invest in defense tech was when nobody was investing in defense tech,” Winfield said.

Porter mentioned Ascend’s focus on Seattle and physical AI is “really the bet we made with Ascend,” adding that Endurance and Overland have the potential to become “generational, category-defining companies.”.

Fund III also backs AI software and infrastructure companies, including Seattle-area startup Govstream.ai, which uses AI to speed city permitting.

Seattle’s economic climate: Winfield is a champion of Seattle’s startup scene, known for Ascend’s annual Founders Bash party in the city and his ever-present ☔🔥☔ emojis on social media, symbolizing hot startups in rainy Seattle.

Ascend’s refreshed website and brand, rolled out with Fund III, nod to the firm’s Seattle roots with its longstanding Seattle Startup Toolkit and a Spotify playlist of Pacific Northwest indie rock and hip-hop.

Recent findings suggest that but Winfield has also been a vocal critic of state and local policies he sees as hostile to startups, including Washington’s newly introduced tax on income over $1 million, which takes effect in 2028 and survived a repeal vote last week. He worries the tax could eventually be extended to people earning $150,000 a year, which would make it harder for startups to recruit employees from places like Texas.

“The chilling effect that’s going to have on the ecosystem is real, and it’s happening,” he said.

About 60% of Ascend’s portfolio companies are based in Seattle, according to the firm.

Bek remarked hardware companies such as Endurance and Overland still have good reasons to be in Seattle, including testing on Lake Union and in Yakima, access to the sea and University of Washington talent. For Overland, he said, that also means proximity to Joint Base Lewis-McChord.

It has been revealed that combined with the region’s history in aerospace, defense and energy, Winfield noted, those advantages make Seattle one of the country’s key hubs for building physical products. He called it “El Segundo Northwest,” a reference to the Los Angeles-area city that has become a hub for defense and hardware startups.

As Winfield notes, Ascend isn’t the only early-stage firm chasing these companies. Pre-seed firms such as Cantos, Ironspring and Silent Ventures are backing similar founders, and some Seattle firms that historically focused on software are becoming more open to investing in hardware.

Ultimately, he noted, Seattle still benefits from a long legacy of technical founders, and Ascend is “betting that those folks are going to continue to create companies that are worth hundreds of billions of dollars.”.

#124. Agents idling while they wait on humans push Kubernetes to hand back unused resources

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (636 words)
General

Agents idling while they wait on humans push Kubernetes to hand back unused resources

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Sumber: https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/13/agentic-ai-workloads-push-kubernetes-return-idle-resources-kubeconna/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agentic AI workloads are handing Kubernetes an unexpected second act.
  • Past platform shifts, from physical servers to virtual machines and from virtual machines to containers, forced companies to wipe the slate clean and start over.
  • “Kubernetes now, 11, 12+ years in, has this whole latest life,” Allen stated.

Agentic AI workloads are handing Kubernetes an unexpected second act. The orchestrator once dismissed as reliable but boring is now at the center of how enterprises plan to run autonomous software.

Past platform shifts, from physical servers to virtual machines and from virtual machines to containers, forced companies to wipe the slate clean and start over. This shift is different because Kubernetes was built as a platform for building platforms, according to Bobby Allen (pictured), cloud therapist at Google Cloud LLC.

“Kubernetes now, 11, 12+ years in, has this whole latest life,” Allen stated. “You don’t need a new platform this time. … This shift doesn’t mean that you’ve got to retool and rebuild and replatform everything, and I think that could be comforting for folks to realize that they don’t have to start from scratch.”.

In a recent development, allen spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Kubernetes is recovering resources spent on idle agentic AI workloads. (* Disclosure below.).

It has been revealed that google is putting that view into practice. The company has donated Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, while engineering teams are tuning Kubernetes for agents rather than building a new stack.

In a recent development, “Google is doubling down on our commitment to not just open source but community-driven, collaborative, multiple-partner-involvement open source,” Allen said. “These concepts are foundational, but they’re important enough that we need to all contribute and shape these together.”.

Efficiency is a significant part of the motivation. Agents spend long stretches idle while they wait for human input, and the projects aim to give those resources back during the downtime, Allen explained.

In a recent development, “These are kind of different efforts that contribute to an open, flexible, transparent, collaborative way to make agentic workloads run better so that we can have these amazing outcomes but also be efficient with our resources,” Allen said. “We don’t want to have this sci-fi Star Trek moment where we’re stepping into the future and kill the planet.”.

#126. Latest Update: Seattle mayor lifts pause and will expand police surveillance cameras with fresh safeguards

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words)
General

Latest Update: Seattle mayor lifts pause and will expand police surveillance cameras with fresh safeguards

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Sumber: https://www.geekwire.com/2026/seattle-mayor-lifts-pause-and-will-expand-police-surveillance-cameras-with-new-safeguards/

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 1:10 pmNovember 10, 2026 at 1:28 pm.
  • Seattle will expand its police surveillance camera network to three more neighborhoods, Mayor Katie Wilson said Tuesday, ending a pause she put in place in March over privacy and civil liberties concerns.
  • In a recent development, the move comes a day after NYU’s Policing Project released an independent audit of the Seattle Police Department’s Real Time Crime Center (RTCC), which Wilson commissioned during the pause.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 1:10 pmNovember 10, 2026 at 1:28 pm.

Seattle will expand its police surveillance camera network to three more neighborhoods, Mayor Katie Wilson said Tuesday, ending a pause she put in place in March over privacy and civil liberties concerns.

In a recent development, the move comes a day after NYU’s Policing Project released an independent audit of the Seattle Police Department’s Real Time Crime Center (RTCC), which Wilson commissioned during the pause. The audit found the city had built “an important foundation” for overseeing the system but that “significant policy gaps remain.” It made 19 recommendations.

According to recent reports, cameras in the Stadium District, installed before this summer’s FIFA World Cup, will be turned on immediately, according to the mayor’s office. Cameras around Garfield High School and in the Capitol Hill nightlife district still need to be bought and installed, which will take months. The City Council approved all three areas in 2025.

Wilson briefly turned on the 22 stadium-area cameras during the World Cup, citing “credible threats” reported by law enforcement, and noted they would go off after the tournament. The audit noted that police streamed live feeds throughout the event, despite a department policy against monitoring cameras without an active call or case.

“After reviewing the evidence, the recommendations, and the safeguards available to us, I believe there is an crucial and responsible role for the RTCC within Seattle’s public-safety system,” Wilson mentioned in a statement.

Sources indicate that wilson said the city will adopt most of the audit’s recommendations. The police department will publish a public dashboard on how the crime center is used and tighten its rules on data retention, permissible uses and requests from outside agencies. A new advisory group will help write policies for privately owned cameras, protests and where future cameras go.

It has been revealed that no Flock cameras in Seattle, ever. Latest protections against potential abuses drawn from an outside audit. A handful of cameras in new neighborhoods. Here's what the RTCC looks like from the inside. pic.twitter.com/QeYUg8ZkW3.

The Real Time Crime Center, which rolled out in 2025, pulls live video from hundreds of cameras into a single command room at police headquarters. They include 303 police-owned cameras at 61 sites, 116 security cameras at police buildings, 96 city traffic cameras, and 23 cameras owned by three local businesses that share their feeds with police.

Sources indicate that analysts watch 911 calls as they come in and pull up nearby cameras to give officers details callers may have missed, such as what a suspect is wearing or which way they ran. They also comb through recorded footage to help detectives investigate past crimes. The system runs on Fusus, software from Axon, the Arizona-based maker of police body cameras and Tasers.

Sources indicate that police are barred from using facial recognition with the system. The software does include an AI tool that searches video for people, vehicles and other objects, but analysts told auditors they use it only as a last resort because it is unreliable. In one case, a search for a man in a gray top and gray pants returned an image of a pigeon.

Whether the system reduces crime remains an open question. The Seattle Police Department has said officers and detectives are three times more likely to make an arrest with help from crime center analysts, and that the center assisted in 17 homicide cases in 2025, helping close 10. But the audit notes that the department counts any analyst action as “support,” such as checking a camera, even if it produced nothing useful.

Broader research on crime centers is thin, the audit found, and studies of surveillance cameras on their own show mixed results. A University of Pennsylvania evaluation of Seattle’s program, commissioned by the city’s inspector general, isn’t expected until late 2027.

Critics have warned that footage could end up with federal immigration agents or out-of-state prosecutors pursuing people who come to Washington for abortions or gender-affirming care. The audit found that state and city laws limit such sharing, but they can’t fully prevent it. Outside agencies could still get footage through public records requests or court orders served on the city or on Axon, which stores some of the police department’s video in its cloud.

Sources indicate that tee Sannon, technology policy program director for the ACLU of Washington, said the group was “deeply disappointed” by the decision. With the audit having “reaffirmed significant gaps in privacy protections and accountability,” expanding the network “is a step in the wrong direction,” Sannon said. She added that the city should invest in proven alternatives such as community violence prevention programs.

“Used together, CCTV and RTCC supercharge law enforcement’s capabilities to monitor, track, and reconstruct people’s movements across the city,” Sannon stated. Protecting residents, she said, requires strict, enforceable limits on how the technology is used, how long data is kept and who it’s shared with, along with independent oversight.

Recent findings suggest that wilson remarked the expansion and the new safeguards go together. “We can gather evidence to hold those who commit violent acts accountable and protect our neighbors targeted by federal overreach,” she said.

Business groups praised the decision. Jon Scholes, president and CEO of the Downtown Seattle Association, said the city “already has stringent privacy guardrails in place” and that, with police staffing “still lagging,” additional tools “are essential for solving crimes.” The Seattle Metro Chamber and Challenge Seattle, which have pushed the city to turn on the cameras, cited a poll they commissioned this year that found 75% of Seattle voters support using cameras to help active investigations.

Sources indicate that “Residents and businesses have sent a clear message: they want our officers to have the tools to keep them safe,” stated former Gov. Chris Gregoire, CEO of Challenge Seattle.

City Councilmember Bob Kettle, who chairs the council’s public safety committee, mentioned the committee will take up the audit’s recommendations, along with those from the city’s inspector general and auditor.

Recent findings suggest that the city also looks to lay groundwork for connecting cameras run by Seattle Center tenants and nearby businesses to the crime center, according to the mayor’s office, citing interest from those businesses after the Bite of Seattle shooting in July. The audit flagged private camera integration as a key area to watch: the police department has bought about 100 devices that let businesses stream video to the center but hasn’t decided who will get them.

The advisory group, which will include members of the Community Police Commission, the Community Surveillance Working Group, police and other city staff, will meet over the next few months. Its recommendations will then go through the police department’s policy review process.
